“Yeah, that’s right, be shocked! I’ve got more- Uh, Gallant’s dating Glory Girl, who cares? Medhall- no!” Cherish’s voice was getting more frantic. “Hurry up, damnit!” she yelled. Who was she yelling at? She had Chariot and Othala- was she using one of them as an escape route?

“Fuckfuckfuck- Panacea- Panacea’s attracted to-!”

There was the beginning of a crash, an instant of static, and then Cherish’s broadcast cut out.

Amy grabbed a table for support, weak at the knees. Cherish had known- oh shit, she’d known about Amy, and she’d been planning to announce that to the whole city? She’d never have been able to come back from that- she’d have to leave the city, change her name, maybe change her face, she’d never be able to be anywhere near Vicky again-

She gripped the table harder and forced herself to inhale hard, exhale slowly, in and out, rinse and repeat. Dr Reese had taught her techniques to ground herself- she could see the table, a box of nitrile gloves, a bottle of antiseptic, a roll of bandages, her hands; she could feel the plastic of the table, her socks as she wiggled her toes, her sleeves brushing against her wrist, and the spider clinging to the nape of her neck, right below the hairline. She could hear her own breathing, and murmurs from the crowd, and-

“Cherish is down,” Alexandria’s voice cut into her thoughts, crisp and clear. “Othala and Chariot have been retrieved uninjured. Residual Master-Stranger protocols.”

Okay, she could hear that, and fuck was that a relief. Amy managed to straighten up and relax her grip on the table. Two things she could smell- the steriliser spray they’d used to clean the medical station, and there was some kind of power effect from outside that smelled like woodsmoke. One thing she could taste- she dug a hand into her pocket and found a pack of gum underneath the thing with the acid-spraying scorpion tail. She tore the packet open and popped a piece into her mouth, crushing the gum between her molars and focusing on the burning cold menthol taste for a second, taking deep minty breaths.

Cherish was dead, and Jack Slash and Taylor were going to teleport in soon. Focus.

 

 

The line moved surprisingly efficiently. The inmates lined up single file, some fidgeting or clutching their injuries, a few supported by friends, but after the first few, they understood how to do it. Hands out, give permission, hold still while Amy healed them, step aside for the next guy. Many of them thanked Amy as they left, even just a mumble, which surprised her- the worst prison on the planet, and they hadn’t forgotten their manners? But then again, how much healing did they get in here?

One man at the back of the line kept getting closer- a man with long brown hair and beard, who’d retracted his white armour into his body when he’d gotten in line. He kept his eyes on her as she worked, with a faint smile on his face.

The line moved forward- broken bones, stab wounds, cuts, burns and internal bleeding, and in one case minor radiation poisoning. The man kept getting closer, space by space, until suddenly he was standing in front of her, holding a hand out.

Amy didn’t want to take his hand. She didn’t want to get confirmation of her fears, to see the man who’d sired her.

But she also didn’t want to live in fear. She didn’t want to live in regret. She’d never get another chance like this.

Amy took a deep breath, and took Marquis’s hand. His biology flooded her mind- tall, lean, in very good condition. His skeleton in particular stuck out to her- no microfractures, no osteoporosis, no loss of collagen- just pristine bone all over. His skin was fine too, no scars to be found. There were signs of scarring in some muscles, some old damage to the kidneys, the remains of a deep burn wound on his shoulder, but otherwise he was in excellent shape. Nothing terrible in his DNA, nothing inherently monstrous in his physique. Just a man- a slightly unusual man, but a man nonetheless.

Marquis’s smile remained faint and polite, but she could feel his heart beating faster, see various neurotransmitters released into his bloodstream. He was excited, happy. “A pleasure to meet you,” he said.

Amy’s mouth was dry. She swallowed and managed to get the words out. “You’re Marquis.”

More happiness. “I am indeed. I was hoping we could speak in private, if that’s alright with you?”

She had Galvanate’s power coursing through her, making her strong and tough. Elpis and Alexandria and Eidolon would jump to her defence in an instant if he tried anything. But he wouldn’t- there was no hint of ulterior motive.

“Okay,” Amy said. “Should we-”

“I’ll provide us some cover,” Marquis said. His perfect skeleton erupted into needles that pierced through his muscle and skin, growing into thick spears that curved up and around, wrapping around and melding seamlessly together to form a large dome around the two of them.

As Amy goggled at one of the weirdest things she’d ever experienced with her power, she heard muffled shouting from outside, and then a boom.

Marquis frowned. “That sounds like Butcher’s teleport.”

Amy relaxed a fraction. Taylor was looking out for her. “I’ll make some light.” She pulled some insects out of her pockets and merged them together into a single organism; leave off the legs, the sensory organs, lots of photophores stuffed full of luciferase- and then there was pale yellow light.

Marquis stared down at the glowbug with a fascinated look. “That’s incredible. So your power is more than healing then?” A spur of bone grew out from the side of the dome, widening into a shelf.

Amy plopped the glowbug onto the shelf with one hand and slowly nodded. “Yeah.” First time she’d ever properly admitted that to someone. “So. You’re my biological father.” It was hard to tell with the bug’s light casting shadows across one side of his face, but there did seem to be something familiar about him.

Marquis kept that faint smile up, even while his emotions dipped. “I am, yes.”

“And who was my mother? What was her name?”

“Melinda Wickers,” Marquis replied readily, truthfully. “She was a follower of mine, and we enjoyed each other’s company for a while before she decided to leave. When she developed cancer, she got in contact again, asked me to take care of you.” His smile grew. “I couldn’t say yes fast enough.”

Big spike in oxytocin there. Amy felt her cheeks warm a little. “How long was I living with you?” She asked in a small voice.

“About a year. I must admit, I enjoyed our time together more than all the ill-gotten gains I ever had.” He smiled wistfully. “I still remember the princess costume I got you for your sixth birthday.”

Princess costume… The words stirred something in Amy’s memory, just barely out of reach. “Gold?” she hazarded a guess. “And lace?”

Marquis’s smile gained some teeth. “That’s right, tailor-made. I thought pink was too cliché. You loved that costume. Your stuffed rabbit was your faithful knight.”

“I don’t remember a rabbit,” Amy said.

“Ah. A shame.” Marquis’s heartbeat revealed what his smile didn’t- he was crestfallen, a little hurt.

“I think,” Amy said carefully, “I remember some other things. A big table, and writing my name.”

“Yes! I helped you practice your letters. You tried so hard. Many nights with inky fingers.” Fondness pulsed through his veins.

Which raised a question. “Why didn’t you stop?”

Confusion, a wrinkle in his brow. “Stop what? I’m afraid I don’t understand.”

“Stop being a criminal,” Amy clarified. “Weren’t you worried someone would find me? Didn’t you have enough money to retire?”

For the first time, Marquis’s expression truly matched his inner emotions- a mixture of shock and hurt. “Ah. Well. The truth is… The truth is I’m not sure. I was overconfident, I suppose? I picked my fights carefully, I had a long winning streak, I believed my civilian identity was secure. And I suppose one doesn’t become a crime lord if they don’t have the attitude to keep being a crime lord. Certainly I wasn’t the only family villain- Allfather’s brood were little terrors.”

“And then New Wave found you- found us,” Amy said. That part, she remembered; not clearly, mostly as the subject of childhood nightmares that therapy had barely scratched, but she remembered a small dark place with lots of smashing and screaming from outside, and then being taken to a strange place by big scary people.

“They did. I thought the people who managed to defeat me would be best suited to protect you from my enemies seeking revenge by proxy.” Slowly, carefully, he laid a hand on her shoulder. “And look at you now- a powerful healer, earning the respect of everyone around you. Even Butcher spoke highly of you, which is frankly bizarre.”

“Elpis is different,” Amy blurted. “She’s a hero.”

“Yes,” Marquis admitted with a bemused look, “That’s part of why it’s so bizarre.” He sighed, gazing at her tenderly. “I wish we had more time,” he admitted. “Time to refresh our memories, and to make new ones. I want you to know I’m proud of you, Amelia. You’ve become a wonderful young woman- impressing the best of the best before your eighteenth birthday.”

That caught her attention, but it took her a second to realise why. “I’m only sixteen. I had my birthday in March.”

Marquis frowned, concern written all over him. “No, your birthday’s September 7th. You should be turning 18- it is 2011, yes?”

“Yeah?”

“So you’re 17, going on 18.”

He was being completely honest- every part of his biology told her he was being confused but sincere. Something unpleasant curdled in her gut. “I was 16 in March. I had presents and everything.”

Marquis’s frown turned into a look of frustration. “They lied,” he said with growing anger, “about your birthday.” His fingers tightened ever so slightly on her shoulder.

“There must have been a mistake,” Amy said feebly. “I’ll check later.” She’d never been big, but her parents had occasionally said stuff about her being big for her age. She’d never looked up her adoption papers, she’d never felt the need- had they fudged the details, to obscure her identity and keep her safe?

Marquis closed his eyes and took a deep breath in through his nostrils, his pulse dropping as he reined in his temper. “Well,” he said brightly, “Before you go, may I give you something to remember me by? A little tangible reminder?” The bone in his fingertip stirred, extending slightly.

What the hell- Amy nodded.

Marquis took his hand off her shoulder and held is hand out palm up. A spike of bone punched out through the skin, shaping itself into a rod as thick as a pencil, and about half as long. More details took shape, a winding spiral forming around the main piece, finer details etching into the surface. Tiny scales emerged from the spiral, a pair of eyes at the top, even wood grain on the main rod. In a few seconds, the tip of Marquis’s finger held a rod with a snake twined around it. After a moment’s thought, a small loop grew out of the top, something to let it hang from a piece of string.

The rod of Asclepius, an ancient Greek symbol of healing, still used in modern medicine; not the caduceus, the winged staff with two snakes. It always annoyed Amy when people mixed the two up.

And Asclepius, god of healing, was the father of Panacea, the goddess of universal health. Amy’s eyes felt hot.

Then Marquis flexed his finger, and the rod snapped neatly off, accompanied by a bolt of agonising pain. Marquis didn’t react outwardly, but Amy saw it in detail.

“Oh my god!”

“What?” Marquis asked, confused. He glanced down at the bone. “Do you not-”

“It hurts when you break your bones? I thought your power compensated for it or something!”

“You saw that?” Marquis asked. “Yes, I’m afraid it does, but I’ve long since gotten used to it. Built up quite a pain tolerance over my career-”

“You shouldn’t have to build up a tolerance for it, that’s-” Amy scoffed and tightened her grip on his hand. “I can do something about that. Do I have your permission?”

Marquis blinked in surprise at her sudden change of attitude, but nodded. “Yes, of course.”

Amy reached out to his biology, focusing on that perfect skeleton again. The pain receptors were threaded through the whole structure, out into the dome Marquis had formed around them from his spinal column and his collarbones. If anyone so much as scratched the dome, he’d feel every agonising injury.

She didn’t really consider him family- she barely remembered him, and she wouldn’t see him again after this- but the thought of leaving him in pain didn’t sit right with her either.

This was very different from anything she’d done before- she’d healed people and she’d modified insects, but she’d never modified a person. She couldn’t just remove all the pain receptors- that’d leave him unable to properly perceive injuries and damage, which could lead to worse complications. Instead she reached out to the pain receptors and deadened about half of them, then reduced the sensitivity of the remainder.

“Okay, have another go.”

Marquis extruded another spike of bone and snapped it off without hesitation. There was still pain, but way less. It was like the difference between a kick in the ass and a kick in the crotch. “My word,” he exclaimed.

“Yeah, that should make it easier,” Amy said.

Her watch beeped- the ten minute warning to leave. “Uh, I should get back to healing people,” Amy blurted. “Not a lot of time left.”

Marquis nodded. “Of course.” He plucked the glowbug off the shelf and handed it to Amy, then tensed. The dome formed seams, split into segments, and retracted back into his regular skeleton in a couple of seconds, like a flower blooming in reverse. Amy blinked as the cell lights hit her eyes, dazzling her for a second. She turned off the glowbug’s light and stuck it in her pocket.

Marquis gently released Amy’s hand with a soft smile. “Thank you, Panacea,” he said politely. Then he turned and walked away.

Amy watched him go for a long moment, rubbing her thumb over the little bone sculpture.

The sound of someone clearing their throat startled her; she whipped her head around. Elpis was standing between her and the queue, no judgement in her expression.

“Good talk?” she asked mildly.

“…yeah. Yeah, it was… yeah,” Amy managed. She put the bone totem in her other pocket, melting down a spare bug to form a protective casing around it, and shook herself. “Okay, who’s next?”

 

 

People were cheering. The portal was shut, the ground around it had been glassed to ensure no-one and nothing had got out. Jack Slash was dead, Abattoir was dead, the Nine were dead. Nobody even needed healing right now.

Which meant that Amy didn’t need to hold herself together any longer. She turned her head up to look at Taylor. “I want to go home,” she mumbled.

“Me too,” Taylor said, shifting the arm she’d put around Amy’s shoulders. “Let’s get the hell out of here.”

A cloud of insects formed a ring around them, and Taylor led them away from the crowd. The Undersiders fell into step, the dogs flanking them, and Amy just trudged along. She was so tired.

“Hey, what about your gun?” Whirlygig asked.

“Forget it,” Taylor said. “Ammo’s gone, and we’re all tired.” A pause, then she continued, “Tactical thinks the PRT might keep it around for me, in case there’s anything in the future. But right now, I just don’t care.”

They made it past the outer cordon, troopers standing aside as the Undersiders passed through and came to a halt. “Amy, you want to ride with me?” Taylor asked as one of the dogs walked over.

“Mm-hm.”

“Okay. I’ll give you a leg up.” Taylor laced her fingers together into a stirrup for Amy’s foot.

“Amy, wait.”

Startled with one leg raised, Amy almost toppled over- Taylor caught her raised leg and swept her back onto her feet, facing back the other way.

Victoria was hovering a few inches above the ground, several feet away. Her tiara was missing, her hair was askew, and her costume was rumpled. Her eyes were red, like she’d been crying.

“Amy, please come back. Why are you going with them?”

“I’m tired, Vicky,” Amy mumbled.

“I know, I just- come with me, we can go home and rest. The whole family. We can make cocoa and cuddle up, like old times,” Victoria said, a touch desperately.

Amy remembered the old times- before either of them had their powers. She and Vicky would make cocoa with marshmallows, throw a big blanket over the couch, and watch their favourite movies together. Sometimes they’d fall asleep there and be woken by Carol shaking them awake, or Mark carrying them to bed.

Part of her wanted that- to go back and have a moment with Vicky, pressed close to her. To sink back into old habits, even knowing that they wouldn’t go anywhere.

Slowly, Amy shook her head. “I can’t. I have to go. I need space.”

Victoria’s feet slowly touched the ground. “…are you leaving?” Victoria asked.

Amy took a deep breath, tried to think of what to say, that she needed time away from her family to centre herself and decompress, using all the language that Dr Reeves had given her. But she started talking, and the words just tumbled out.

“I met Marquis in the Birdcage. He’s my dad- my biological dad- and he remembered me even though I didn’t remember him. And he said he was proud of me, and he didn’t say anything about me being a hero or anything, he was just proud of me, and,” Amy shoved a hand into her pocket and came out with the container she’d put the bone totem in. She peeled the flesh away like a banana peel and held it up, “and he made me this, and, and he told me my birthday-”

“Hoo boy,” she heard Tattletale mutter behind her.

“Your birthday?” Victoria asked, caught off guard. “What does your birthday have to do with-”

“They lied,” Amy said, louder than she’d meant to. She’d meant to look it up and check it later, but Marquis had been completely honest, and in some mean-spirited way it made sense that they’d want to keep her younger than Victoria. “They lied about my age. I’m seventeen years old.”

“That’s- well, maybe Mom and Dad-”

“Yeah, I know they probably did it to protect me, but I’m tired, Vicky!” Amy snapped. “I’m tired. I know they probably did it to protect me, and I know that Carol’s getting better, and I know Mark’s keeping up with his meds, and I know you’re not-” She cut herself off there. Victoria’s slipups weren’t something to talk about right now. “I know. But I’m tired and I just can’t deal with this right now. I don’t want to talk to anyone or touch anyone right now. For once in my life I’m choosing me. Just let me go.”

“Ames-”

“Stop it!” Amy yelled. “Please, just stop it!”

Victoria reared back like Amy had spat at her.

For a moment there was quiet, only Amy’s breathing and the low buzz of Elpis’s bugs to be heard.

There was a rustle of fabric behind her. “I picked this up from the lair,” Tattletale said quietly. Amy didn’t look around, still staring at Victoria.

“Amy. Please,” Victoria said, beautiful blue eyes welling with tears. “We can fix this, we can talk this out, just give it a chance.”

For one mad moment, Amy wanted to scream at her, wanted to yell at Victoria that she was attracted to her, even after all the progress she’d made. That Amy loved her not just as a sister, but as a woman. Something to push Victoria away so they wouldn’t keep leaning on each other like crutches.

A rustle of fabric behind her, and the sound of Taylor clearing her throat. Amy whirled around, halfway to a scream-

Taylor was holding her cape in her hands. Her sky-blue silk cape with the white amphora symbol in the middle, bunched in her grip like she’d come to Amy cap in hand.

“If you don’t want to touch anyone,” Taylor said, spreading the cape out, “I just thought maybe…”

Amy stared for a second. Then she nodded. Taylor gingerly stepped forward and carefully wrapped the cape around Amy’s shoulders like a blanket, taking pains to avoid touching Amy directly, even with her gauntlets on. The cape was heavy- all the chain-mail inside it pressed on Amy’s shoulders like a heavy coat. She clutched the ends closed with her hands and turned back.

Victoria was crying now, little tears running down her face. She still looked beautiful even when she cried.

“Just let me go,” Amy said. She took a step backward.

Victoria didn’t move; she just stared at Amy.

Taylor helped Amy into the saddle, and then climbed up after her, arms looping around her to grip the reins. “Let’s go.”

The dogs broke into a bounding loping run down the road. Amy didn’t look back; she just focused on staying in the saddle, leaning back against Taylor’s chest.

“Grue, give us some cover,” she heard Taylor say. Then everything went dark.

Chapter 133: Interlude 13- Amy 2

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Morning of Tuesday 7th June, The Lair, The Docks

Amy turned over in her bed, groaning. More sleep.

Unfortunately, memories of yesterday began to seep into her mind like blood under a door; the truce meeting, Siberian attacking the PRT building, Jack killing Abattoir, meeting Marquis…

Amy groaned and put her hands to her face, grinding the heels of her palms into her eyes. No chance of getting back to sleep now. She turned over in bed again, blearily cracking her eyes open.

This was not her bed, or her bedroom. Not her sheets, not her walls. And she was wrapped in a very heavy blanket.

Amy blinked hard a couple of times and pushed up on one elbow. The room was windowless, only a strip of light coming from under the door, but there was a digital clock that read 10:30 on the bedside table, and a moment’s fumbling found a lamp. When she turned it on, she saw the walls had posters for bands and films, clothes were scattered messily about in a way that Carol never would have allowed. There were shelves with books, and a bunch of little figurines made of china.

Right- they’d been headed back to the Undersiders’ lair last night. Someone must have put her to bed- she was still wearing her clothes, but her shoes and coat were off.

She sat up further, and saw her coat and shoes placed on a chair in the corner. As she shifted, she looked down at the blanket.

Not a blanket. Elpis’s cape. She awkwardly lifted herself up on her hands and tugged the cape out from under herself, and pulled it into her lap. The silk was so smooth, but she could feel the woven cables underneath as she ran her hands over it.

She’d done so many things she’d never thought she’d do, and a bunch of things she couldn’t take back. She’d healed Carol’s brain- just a little, barely anything that the stem cells wouldn’t have fixed in a few more months, but she’d done it. She’d met her biological father, along with some of the most dangerous people on the planet. She’d walked away from Victoria.

Amy pulled the cape up to her chin and flopped back down on the bed. Sleep wouldn’t come back, no matter how she tried to slow her breathing and snuggle down into the sheets. The weight of the cape helped, but not a lot.

The knock at the door startled her- she sat up again, the cape flopping down into her lap again.

After a second, a voice said “Amy?”

Amy relaxed a little. Taylor’s voice, if slightly muffled. “Yeah?”

“Do you want breakfast? I made pancakes.”

Now that she mentioned it, Amy realised she was starving. “Sure.”

“Okay. I’m coming in now.” The door opened at a careful speed, and Taylor slipped into the room, shutting the door behind her and flicking the lightswitch on, lighting the room properly. She was wearing a t-shirt and sweatpants, and carrying a tray with a plate of pancakes and a steaming cup.

“Please tell me that’s coffee,” Amy all but begged.

“Lots of cream, lots of sugar,” Taylor confirmed, padding across on bare feet and delicately setting the tray across Amy’s lap- there were legs on the bottom so it wasn’t balancing on her lap. Amy shuffled herself into a better sitting position and grabbed the coffee, taking a quick sip. Hot and sweet- the sip became a gulp.

“Better?” Taylor asked, sitting down at the foot of the bed.

“So much,” Amy said, setting the mug down and picking up the knife and fork to start tearing into her pancakes.

It took a few mouthfuls of syrup-soaked goodness before Amy started to wonder. “Whose room is this?” She asked, cutting another slice off her stack.

“Isabella’s,” Taylor said. “She shared with Brian.”

Amy paused. “So are they…” She trailed off, unsure how to finish that sentence.

“They’re something,” Taylor said with a shrug. “I don’t think they did anything besides cuddle- everyone’s too tired. Hell, even I fell asleep.”

“Wow, really?” Amy asked. As far as she knew, Taylor had only slept twice since getting her powers, and the second time was when Shadow Stalker had tranquilised her.

“Yeah- on the couch. Dad’s here too- I called him when we got back; he rushed over and I told him what happened.”

“I’m guessing you left some stuff out?” Amy asked. She’d only met Taylor’s dad once, but she got the impression he wouldn’t react well to all the details of the last 24 hours.

“Didn’t want to give him a heart attack.”

The conversation lapsed again as Amy worked away at the pancakes. She half-expected Taylor to fill the silence, but judging from the preoccupied look on her face, she was having a conversation with the Butchers.

Amy mopped up the syrup with the last bit of pancakes, then set her knife and fork down and sipped her coffee again, feeling a lot more human. “So… What’s going on with the rest of the city?”

Taylor’s eyes refocused on the here and now. “Well, the PRT left a few messages. They’ve double and triple-checked that Jack’s dead for good, and they’re giving me the credit for killing him, which means I can claim the bounty on him whenever I have the time.”

“Woah.” It hadn’t been Amy’s first thought, but the Nine all had Kill Orders and bounties on their heads, covered by the S-Class Truce. Even a minor member would have got a hefty reward. For Jack Slash, public enemy number one… “How much is it?”

Taylor’s eyes flicked upward for a second, and her lips twitched into a small smile. “A lot. Although I’m thinking I’ll put at least half into fixing up the city.”

“How do the Butchers feel about that?” Amy asked knowingly.

“Oh, they’re whining that I should spend it all on booze and women and stuff like that. I might treat them a little though.” Taylor leaned back on her hands. “Even without the money, I’m being publicly credited with killing Jack. I checked PHO and a couple of news sites a few hours back, and people are going crazy. I’ve got like a hundred thousand people following me on PHO now, and it’s still going up.”

“I can’t tell if you think that’s good or bad,” Amy said, cupping her hands around her coffee mug.

Taylor shrugged. “Bit of both. On the one hand, it seems to have finally got people believing I’m a real hero. On the other hand, I’m now internationally famous. I’ve already got people in the comments section being weird.”

“Weird how?”

Taylor pulled a face. “Weird like wanting me to step on them.”

Amy pulled a matching face. “Yeah, you’ll want to be careful about going too deep into net forums.”

“The Butchers have probably said and done worse, but yeah, I don’t want to see that. Sounds like you’ve got personal experience,” Taylor noted.

Amy snorted. “Oh yeah. After we both debuted, Vicky and I would look ourselves up, seeing what people were saying about us. After a while, we’d find someone talking about her short skirt, or if I was wearing anything under my robe; Usually the mods would ban them right away. Vicky said it was the price of fame…” She trailed off. The sudden burst of nostalgia was like a stomach ache.

“Do you want to talk about it, or leave it alone for now?” Taylor asked gently.

Amy stared into her coffee, then knocked it all back in a few gulps and set the mug down with a sigh. “I always thought of my biological dad as this,” she groped at the air, “shadow, following behind me. Like I could never be sure if I’d turn out like him, if I was already like him. And I spent so much time at the hospital working because I figured it was the least villainous thing I could do, and when it got too much I resented myself for resenting the patients, because that felt villainous!”

Taylor nodded slowly. “That’s rough.”

“And stupid. It took a bunch of sessions before I could even really put it into words.” Amy dropped her hands into her lap. “And Vicky- she was my rock. I never wanted to do anything, so she’d drag me out to parties and on double dates. She made friends, and I tagged along. And I comforted her when she was upset after breaking up with Dean for the thousandth time, or when some bad guy got away, or Carol was being extra Carol.”

“Sounds supportive.”

If you didn’t know that Amy was harbouring a big fat lesbian incest crush on Victoria the entire time. Not telling Taylor that any time soon- possibly never at all.

Instead she said “I don’t think it was healthy. Like I was using her as a crutch. It’s better for me to get some distance and work on myself, and that’s what I meant to say, but…” She bit her lip. “I just screamed at her. She was crying.”

“Hey,” Taylor said gently. “Everybody was emotional after all that. You were stressed out too. You’re allowed to take care of yourself. And if you’ve got to learn how to live without Vicky, maybe she needs to learn how to live without you too.”

It made sense- hell, it was something she ought to bring up in her next session with Dr Reese. But Amy kept thinking of Victoria crying from Amy’s words, and the thought made her want to run back and apologise for everything she’d said.

“You’re welcome to stay here as long as you want,” Taylor went on. “I’ll probably go out and pick some stuff up later- an extra bed and stuff shouldn’t be hard to find, and I can throw up some walls easily. That way you don’t have to keep borrowing Isa’s room.”

Amy sniffed. “Thanks.” She wiped her eyes with the sleeve of her t-shirt, then recoiled as she caught a whiff of herself. “Urgh. I think I need a shower.”

“Sure,” Taylor said, reaching out to take the tray. “Just don’t pull the big red handle. That’s for Butcher-level pressure- it’s like a hot riot hose.”

“Got it.” Amy flipped the sheets aside and swung her legs out of bed. “Here’s your cape back,” she added, holding it out.

“Thanks,” Taylor said, gently taking it and tossing it over her shoulder like a towel. “I think it’s time for me to put it on again. Do you want your coat?”

“No- Oh, hang on, the bone.”

“The bone?” Taylor asked, confused. “Wait- that thing Marquis gave you?”

“Yeah, I put it in the pocket.” Taylor stepped aside as Amy plucked her coat off the chair and stuck her hand into the pocket, rooting around and emerging with the little bone totem.

Taylor whistled softly as Amy held it up. “Nice. That’s Greek, right?”

“Yeah. Any chance I could get some string, or something?”

“I’ve got loads of silk lying around, I can get you some in a minute.”

“Thanks.” Amy turned the bone over in her hands- the snake was baring its fangs. “You know, I actually considered this as my symbol when we were designing my costume.”

“How’s a snake on a stick meant to represent medicine anyway?” Taylor asked.

“Well…” Amy wracked her brain for the details she’d learned trawling the internet all those years ago. “The staff represents the medicinal arts, and the snake represents renewal, because snakes shed their skin. Also I think there’s some stuff about using snake venom in medicine.”

“Right, like how poison and medicine depends on the dosage.”

“Exactly. But we decided on the red cross because people recognise that better than the rod and snake, and I didn’t want to have to keep explaining it to people.”

“Fair enough.”

“Marquis knew though. He just made this in a couple of seconds, for me.” Amy rolled it between her fingers. “He told me about my birthday,” she said suddenly.

“I heard you say something about that,” Taylor said, opening the bedroom door.

“He wasn’t lying- or at least he didn’t think he was. New Wave gave me a different birthday.”

Taylor tactfully said nothing for a while, simply stepping aside so Amy could get past her and out into the corridor. “Shower’s the last door on the right,” she said eventually. “And I guess this means I can get you a birthday present this time.”

Birthday present? It took Amy a moment to remember that conversation from what felt like years ago. “Yeah, I guess. It’s September 7th. I’ll be 18.”

The plate, mug and cutlery rattled against each other as Taylor suddenly jerked. Her face was rapidly turning bright red.

“18?” She asked hoarsely.

Amy took in the sight of her flustered girlfriend. “Okay, which Butcher said something gross? Was it Rotter?”

“Uh, I should really get these dishes washed up- I’ll have some bugs bring you the silk, have a good shower.” Taylor spun round and all but ran off down the hallway, tray rattling in her hands.

Amy watched Taylor go for a moment, smiling. Then she turned and padded the other way down the hallway towards the shower.

Chapter End Notes

Usual update schedule will be postponed until the New Year. However, I'll be working on some snippets in the meantime, so keep your eyes peeled.

Chapter 134: 14.1

Chapter Notes

First chapter of 2026! Woo!

Morning of Tuesday 7th June, The Lair, The Docks

“Ceeee-lebrate good times, come on!” Anchorage sang along to the radio as I worked four frying pans. Every station I’d checked had been reporting the news that the Slaughterhouse Nine were all confirmed dead. A couple had called it the Slaughterhouse Zero, or the Slaughterhouse None. The music stations were all playing upbeat songs, the kind of stuff you could smile and dance to.

I’d fallen asleep last night as soon as I’d finished giving Dad a quick summary of how we’d managed to beat the Nine, leaving out a few key details like how much damage I’d actually taken, or how close Jack had come to beating me. I’d got hours of refreshing sleep, but Nemean’s power or my own early rising habits had eventually woken me up. When other people had started stirring, I’d decided to cook breakfast.

One pan held bacon and sausages, frying up nicely; another held several kinds of eggs- sunny side up, over easy, and scrambled. The smaller pans contained fried mushrooms, tomatoes and baked beans at Rotter’s insistence, and the last one was being used to build a stack of pancakes. The toaster dinged and ejected another couple of slices, which I set on a plate to the side. I’d set out butter and maple syrup and a bunch of drinks as well.

“We should spend the whole week partying,” Butcher said. “This is our biggest win yet- that means biggest celebrations. I’m thinking music, kegs, fireworks, all that shit.”

“Not going to ask for hoes and blow?” Bearskin asked.

Butcher snorted. “Nah, Taylor’ll just shoot it down.”

“My god, he can be taught,” Vladimir fake-gasped.

“Up yours.”

Dad stirred from the armchair he’d fallen asleep in, grumbled quietly, yawned hugely, and then finally opened his eyes. “Morning,” he mumbled, pushing his glasses up to rub at his eyes.

“Morning, Dad. You okay?”

Dad slowly pushed himself up and out of the chair with a grunt. “Bit stiff from that chair, but not terrible.” He straightened his glasses and sniffed. “Something smells good.”

“I’m making breakfast for everyone. I was just about to make coffee if you want a cup.”

“That’d be great.” Dad sat heavily at the table and yawned again.

“Man, is he always like this in the morning?” Firecracker asked.

“No; but then, he doesn’t usually stay up past midnight talking with me about how I fought a bunch of villains, so,” I shrugged as I filled the coffee pot and set it to brew.

I’d agreed early on to keep any and all bugs out of everyone’s rooms, but I did have some along the corridor ceiling that were picking up the sounds of people stirring and moving about. Good timing, since the bacon was about done. I started transferring strips onto a piece of paper towel just as Brian came into the kitchen, scratching his bare chest.

“Goddamn,” Quarrel said with a whistle. “You should’ve taken a swing at that!”

“You say that about everyone,” I pointed out. Out loud I said, “You want coffee too?”

“Please,” Brian said, nodding to my Dad. “Morning, sir.”

“Good morning. Sleep alright?”

“Not bad,” Brian admitted as the coffee finally brewed and I grabbed a couple of mugs. “I feel like I could go another couple hours though.”

“I feel like a wrung-out towel,” I admitted, bringing the coffee over. “But also really wired at the same time- I think it’s feedback from the Butchers being stoked that the Nine are gone.”

“It still doesn’t feel real,” Dad admitted, taking his mug from me with a quiet ‘thanks’. “You’d always hear about the Nine, losing members, getting chased off- but they always came back eventually.”

“Well, they’re not coming back now,” Brian said, engulfing his mug in his hands. “The Protectorate turned Jack’s death spot into a glass floor. I don’t think there’s even DNA left there.”

“Even his reputation’s been destroyed,” Needler pointed out. “I imagine it won’t take long for word to spread that Jack’s power gave him an advantage against parahumans. Hardly so impressive when he was playing with cheat codes the entire time.”

“And got shot in the ass and chopped to pieces,” Tock Tick added with a snicker.

“He got Butchered,” Nemean said.

“Ooh, maybe we should make that a catchphrase,” Stoneknapper suggested. “Taylor, next time you beat someone, say ‘You got Butchered!’”

I snorted with laughter. “No, absolutely not,” I giggled.

Brian gave me a weird look. “Uh, context?”

I waved a hand. “Stoneknapper’s trying to get me to make a catchphrase, it’s nothing.”

“That doesn’t sound like a bad idea,” Dad said. “It could help with the heroic image.”

“Nobody who wants to be taken seriously uses a catchphrase,” I pointed out. “Name one serious hero who uses a catchphrase, outside of cartoons.”

“You used to have a catchphrase.”

“Wait, you had a catchphrase?” Brian asked. “I never heard that.”

“Dad, I didn’t have a catchphrase,” I said with a frown.

“No, not when you were Elpis,” Dad admitted. “But back when you were little and playing hero, you were always shouting ‘For Justice!’ right before you jumped off the couch or something.”

The Butchers laughed hysterically as the memory of tying a blanket around my neck as a cape and pretending to be Alexandria surfaced like a corpse that had slipped its concrete shoes. Brian spluttered with a mouthful of coffee. I just groaned “Da-ad, why?”

“Oh come on, you were cute! I know we’ve still got the pictures somewhere-”

“Dad!”

“Alright, alright, I’ll stop,” Dad chortled. “I’ve had my fun.”

Shuffling from the hall preceded Isabella, almost drowning in a Brian-sized shirt and with her hair covering most of her face. Altogether, she looked like she was auditioning for a remake of The Ring. She yawned something that could have been words and flopped into the chair next to Brian, immediately putting her head on his shoulder.

“So who wants food?” I asked, smirking as Brian froze, unsure what to do with his sleepy girlfriend.

“Yes please.”

“Please.”

“Wstfgl.”

I filled three plates and set them down, then grabbed a little bit of everything for myself, plus a glass of orange juice. I didn’t need the caffeine and frankly the others needed it more than me.

Tarquin came in next, wrapped in a blanket and scratching his head, Rachel and her dogs following. “You guys want food too?”

“I need to feed the dogs first,” Rachel said.

“Okay. I can fill you a plate while you get their bowls?”

“Yeah.”

“Why are you frying tomatoes?” Tarquin asked, tilting his head.

“Part of a Full English Breakfast,” I said with a shrug. “We don’t have any black pudding though.”

“Isn’t that made out of pig blood?” Tarquin said with a disgusted look.

“As opposed to thin strips of pig meat,” I said, gesturing to the bacon as I filled more plates, and added extra bacon to my own.

“I had black pudding a couple of times,” Dad said, cutting his sausages. “It’s pretty good.”

“Don’t know why you lot get so squeamish about it,” Dirty Rotter said. “And haggis- it’s good stuff.”

Once everyone else had a plate, I dug into my own, a lot faster than the others. I wasn’t sure if Needler’s regeneration affected my appetite, but I was famished. I cleared my plate before anyone else was halfway, and mopped it with a spare piece of toast.

Lisa chose that moment to emerge, rubbing her eyes. She still had streaks of dark makeup smeared around her eyes, meant to hide the gap between her domino mask and her face. I poured her a cup of coffee and handed it to her as she approached.

“Mm, thanks.”

I made her a plate, refilled my own, then finally sat down. Everyone was quiet for a while as we concentrated on the food and the coffee. Even the dogs were focused on their kibble more than anything else. The food vanished even faster than I’d expected- I’d have sworn there was still leftovers in the pans, but those disappeared too.

Finally Dad set his knife and fork down. “So what happens now?”

“Please tell me we’re not doing anything else today,” Lisa all but begged. “I’m this close to a migraine.” She held up finger and thumb barely apart.

“No,” I said, shaking my head as I drizzled maple syrup on my pancakes. “Short of the Triumvirate wanting to talk, today is nothing for us. We rest, we recover. The truce will last until the end of the week, so we have time.”

“And after that?” Brian asked, pushing his plate aside and resting his arms on the table.

“Kaiser lost his heavy hitter, his giant, and his healer got Mastered,” Tactical chimed in. “Depending on when the Protectorate withdraws the reinforcements, he might lay low or he might come out swinging to reestablish himself. As for Bakuda, I’ve got no idea. She’s the last cape of the ABB, but her powerset is perfect for leading from the rear.”

“There is also the challenge of the Teeth,” Muramasa said. “With their losses, they may choose to withdraw.”

“I doubt it,” Flinch replied. “The reputation you’ve won without them will probably make them even more eager to have the Butcher powers back. And being honest, they still have the capes most dangerous to us.”

That was true. I hadn’t been worried about facing Spree or Vex- I could cut through his clones and push through her forcefields easily enough. Reaver and Animos, on the other hand, could match me in speed and cutting power, or cancel out my power entirely. Squealer and Bilious were still alive, but they were more of an afterthought.

The real question was how to deal with the challenge. I’d agreed to the duel, since we needed all the hands we could get to deal with the Nine, but I still wasn’t comfortable with it. I’d killed clones when Noelle had gone berserk, I’d aimed to kill Abattoir when they’d broken the Truce, I’d killed inmates inside the Birdcage- but those were all moments of immediate danger where the lives of at least a whole city hung in the balance. Premeditated murder for a gang’s tradition was a different matter.

“The gangs will probably try to push again, but I don’t know what pace they’ll take. For once the heroes have the numbers advantage. We’ll just have to prepare and cross that bridge when we come to it.”

“Might as well enjoy the break while we have it,” Aisha said around a mouthful of pancake.

Isabella jumped. “Cono! Don’t do that!”

Brian’s expression went from startled to exasperated quickly. “Aisha, how long have you been there?”

“I got here before blondie,” Aisha explained, gesturing to Lisa with a fork that dripped syrup onto the table. “Couldn’t be bothered to turn my power off, so I just grabbed a plate.”

“Well, that explains where the rest of the food went,” Vladimir noted.

“Better topic,” Butcher interrupted, “The fight. You better not hold back. That’s the rule. You come at the Butcher, someone doesn’t walk away.”

“She doesn’t have to use your stupid rules,” Flinch snapped, glaring at Butcher.

Tactical cleared his throat. “She might have to. By now the whole world knows that Elpis killed Jack Slash, albeit with some help. The local gangs are weakened, and we’ll probably weaken them further. People will start to see this city, see Taylor, as a target. Finishing the Teeth off when they challenge would be a good way to establish what will happen to others, ward off some of the challengers.”

“It’d also fuck our standing with the heroes,” Firecracker pointed out. “Every other time, the heroes were joining in on the killing because it was that or kiss their asses goodbye. A Teeth deathmatch ain’t going to be the kind of thing they’ll let slide.”

My eyebrows drew together. Both sides had points, and I wasn’t sure which to pick.

“Debate later. For now we get re-armed and get the money for offing the Nine. How many do you think we can take credit for?” Anchorage asked.

The rest of the team were talking even as I managed the debate inside my head. “Where did you even sleep?” Brian asked. “You don’t have a room yet.”

“Who says I didn’t just sneak into one of your rooms and sleep there?” Aisha said, wiping syrup off her plate with a finger and sticking it in her mouth.

“Because we’d kick your ass if you did,” Isa said, finally pulling her hair out of her eyes to give Aisha a hard look.

“You’ll have to catch me first. And who knows what I’d be doing in the meantime? Rearranging your drawers, tying your shoelaces together; random wet willies.” Aisha took her finger out of her mouth and waved it threateningly.

“Where did you really sleep?” Dad asked. “I feel like you wouldn’t want a repeat of the last time you tried to sneak in.”

Aisha groaned. “Fine, I grabbed a bunch of blankets and made a nest downstairs. Happy?”

“That can’t have been comfortable,” I said. “Why didn’t you just sleep in the living room? There’s another chair.”

“You guys snore,” Aisha said, pointing between me and Dad. “So loud.”

Quarrel burst out laughing.

“I’ll sort out a room for you later,” I said. There was still a lot of free space in the loft- all I’d need was to put up a wall and move some furniture. “What were we talking about?”

“Bounty money,” Needler reminded me. “I think it depends on how we consider assists. We killed Burnscar after the Wards had knocked her out, the Siberian was killed by us guiding Flechette’s shot, Bonesaw died from a Bakuda bomb, and while I doubt there’s any way we can send money to Glaistig Uaine, Armsmaster and Piggot did help us kill Jack.”

“Fuck giving any money to Bakuda,” Nemean said at once.

Tock Tick nodded. “I’ll second that. I think the Wards deserve the Burnscar money though.”

“All of it?” Rotter asked incredulously.

“Hey, that’ll be chump change compared to the price on the other three,” Stoneknapper said. “We can afford to be generous.”

Isabella set her cutlery down and stretched. “Ugh. I might just go back to bed again.”

“Go for it,” I replied, pushing my chair out and grabbing the empty plates. “I’ll finish up here. I need to make something for Amy’s breakfast anyway.”

 

 

I was the only one who’d woken up before 10, so I let everyone else be while I got to work downstairs. My armour was battered, my weapons were worn, and all of it was crusted with blood and dirt and ash.

More than that, I needed to change my look. The polished picture-perfect look wouldn’t work now that the world knew who I was, but I didn’t want to stick with the grim and spiky aesthetic either. There had to be a midpoint between unrealistic perfection and nightmarish aggression that I could work in.

I pulled the armour apart and sorted the salvageable pieces from the stuff that would need to be remade entirely while the forge heated up. I could actually take out a lot of the innards, the mechanical equivalent of padding that made the armour look powered. Maybe thicken the plating as well, add a few more tricks. I pulled out my tools and set to work.

I was about an hour into heating and hammering and quenching when I felt Dad coming down the stairs. I looked up from the jawguard I was reshaping and waved. “Hey Dad. What’s up?”

“Just stretching my legs,” Dad said with a shrug, stopping a little way away from the forge. “Fixing your suit?”

“Yep. I’ve got the time for once, might as well. Think there’s anything I should add?”

“How many weapons do you have right now?”

I stuck the piece back in the forge to heat up again and counted on my fingers. “I’ve got my bow, my sword, my axe and mace; pistol, wristgun, saws in the shins. A bunch of knives… and the air cannon’s around here somewhere.”

Dad made a face. “Maybe something blunt? Like a nightstick?”

“I mean, my bare hands can do about the same. But yeah, good point. I’m thinking of making another grappler- it’s useful.”

Dad nodded. “And once you’ve got everything ready? What are you going to do with it?”

The firm tone of his voice made me pause. “Well, I’ll have to coordinate with the PRT, figure out how the gangs are going to move, plan out a response…” I shrugged.

Dad sighed. “Taylor, you’ve been through three S-class situations. You can take a break. I think you should take a break.”

“I’ve got the rest of the week before the Truce ends,” I pointed out. “And things will be quieter with a bunch of villains gone.”

Bearskin shifted at that, but said nothing. He’d been close with Purity back before he’d left the Empire, and despite years apart, her death had shaken him.

“That’s not what I mean,” Dad said. “I think- you should let yourself be Taylor again. Check up on your school friends, do something fun. I heard they’re trying to get summer classes going at the schools- you wouldn’t have to catch up when you go back to school.”

I realised Dad and I were thinking along very different lines. “Dad, I don’t think I’m going back to school.”

Dad blinked. “What do you mean? They’re already fixing up-”

“No, Dad, I don’t mean that the schools aren’t going to reopen, I mean I can do more important things with my time.”

“More important? Taylor, this is your education we’re talking about-”

“Dad, I’m a cape. I’m a cape with a laundry list of powers and a reputation. The city needs me to hold things together more than it needs me to pass exams. It’s not like I can just settle down and do a 9 to 5.”

“And how are you going to make a living?” Dad retorted. “I know independent heroes struggle with money if they don’t have a sponsor.”

“I’m going to collect the bounties on Jack, Bonesaw and the Siberian tomorrow. I’d be set for life with that alone. I figure I can buy up some wrecked buildings through proxies, pay the Dockworkers to fix them up or do it myself if I have to, get an income stream. People will be coming to see the city where the Nine died, we can lean into that- I could just build a boat and restart the ferry service myself. I’ve got a lot of options.”

Dad looked utterly poleaxed at my response. “I… I just…” He sighed, defeated. “We always figured you’d go to college,” he murmured.

I winced. Mom had taught at the local college- I remembered her bringing me with her to work a few times when I was little, letting me sit in the back while she gave lectures on literature. I’d always assumed as a matter of course that I’d attend properly one day. “I know, Dad. But things are different now. And there’s people out there that need my help.”

Dad blew a breath out through his lips. “I guess I can’t argue with that.” He looked me in the eye. “You have to promise me you’ll keep me in the loop. And that you’ll keep yourself safe.”

“I promise,” I said sincerely.

“Okay.” Dad smiled sadly. “Your mom would be proud of you, you know.”

I felt a sudden rush of warmth at that, so I took a couple of steps forward and threw my arms around Dad. He hugged me back, and for a second I felt like a little kid again.

After a second Dad said, carefully, “There might be some online courses. Maybe a GED. If you really don’t want to, that’s fine, but maybe you could think about it.”

I considered it. “Yeah, I’ll look into it.” I squeezed gently. “Thanks for understanding, Dad.”

“Love you, Taylor.”

“Love you too.”

“D’aww, that’s cute,” Vladimir cooed.

“Don’t spoil this for me,” I warned.

Chapter 135: 14.2

Wednesday 8th June, Downtown

People had recovered enough energy to start celebrating the end of the Nine; when I’d slipped out of the Lair yesterday to grab more food and bedding for Amy’s room, people had been drinking and dancing like it was 1999. As night had fallen, bonfires had been lit, and I’d passed one where people were eagerly burning effigies of the Nine. The Jack Slash dummy had no arms or legs- apparently that story had got around.

The Butchers had wanted me to join in, but I’d argued them down to hauling chips and soda back to the Lair. The whole team had spent the night arguing over the music selection and dancing badly, then going to sleep way past midnight again. I’d slept again, and woken up feeling great.

My new armour wasn’t finished, but I had pieces, so I set off to run errands with the helmet, the breastplate, and a few bits on the arms and legs. I also had my sword and bow, because I wasn’t going to fully trust the gangs to keep their word. My cape hung from my back, a little musty after weeks in a box, but it felt good to have it again.

As I jogged along the rooftops, teleporting across gaps, people looked up at the sound of the explosions as I arrived, and they waved and cheered; some called my name. It was a strange new feeling, but I welcomed it.

“This is so nuts,” Firecracker giggled as I waved back to a crowd before teleporting again. “You’re a freaking celebrity!”

“With freaking fans,” Dirty Rotter enthused. “Freak-y fans... Eager groupies, ready to please...”

“You just can’t help yourself, can you?” I said wryly as I teleported across another gap.

“Nah.”

A few more teleports got me within visual distance of the PRT building. They’d have heard the thundering teleports from blocks away, and I’d called ahead to let them know I was coming, but I still dropped to street level and walked the last block, a few hundred bugs buzzing around me.

The troopers guarding the front door straightened up as I approached. “Morning,” I said, slowing to a halt. “I’m here to see Director Piggot.”

The troopers on the right actually saluted me. “Yes ma’am, you’re expected. Go right on in.”

“Fuck, I could get used to this,” Tactical admitted.

The man at the front desk pointed me towards the elevator the moment he laid eyes on me, so I shrugged and stepped through the iris shutters. The ride was as quietly smooth as when I’d visited Amy, and I came to a halt almost at the top of the building. I’d expected that the office would be straight ahead, but I had to look around and turn a couple of corners before I found the door with a plaque on it that read Director Emily Piggot.

“I guess it makes sense not to give people a straight shot to the boss’s room,” Quarrel said as I knocked carefully on the door. When I heard a voice say ‘come in’, I turned the handle and entered.

Sure enough, Director Piggot was behind her desk, rising easily to her feet as I stepped in. Even after Amy had stripped away most of her body fat and fixed her health issues, she hadn’t looked great- more like someone who’d lost weight from a bad flu than anything else. But a couple of days had done her good; bright eyed and rosy cheeked. Even her unflattering bowl cut looked better on her.

“And to think she’d been holding off on healing for years,” Needler marvelled.

She wouldn’t be up for it though, would she?” Stoneknapper grumbled.

“Seriously guys, knock it off,” I insisted.

“Then get laid, for fuck’s sake!” Butcher bellowed. “I’ve got balls like a fucking Smurf here!”

“Changing the armour?” Piggot asked, drawing me out of my thoughts.

“Yeah, it’s a work in progress. I don’t need spikes all over; I might not even need the guns.”

Piggot nodded. “Well, I’d suggest a backup in case someone is crazy enough to try, but otherwise that sounds like a good idea. One of the hard things about heroes is making them look like heroes, so the public doesn’t get nervous about all the super powered people running around in costumes.”

“Someone’s definitely crazy enough to try,” I said, more to myself than to her, thinking of the Teeth’s challenge looming in the future.

“Mm. Anyway, the bounties?”

“Yeah. Siberian, Bonesaw and Jack.”

“What about Burnscar?”

“The Wards did the legwork on that. I just insisted on offing her to be sure, and so they wouldn’t have a death on their consciences. Split it between them.”

Piggot’s eyebrows rose. “Generous of you.”

“Well, like I keep telling the Butchers, the other bounties will be enough that I can afford to be generous.”

“In that case, we’ll add it to their trust funds,” Piggot said, writing something down on a notepad. “I’m sure they’ll appreciate it. As for the other three, I can have the money wired to an account of your choice, or the PRT is prepared to set up a secure account for your use.”

“I’ll go for the secure account. Not like I’d take it in cash.”

“Wait, was that an option?” Tock Tick interrupted. “No, take the cash! We can make a bed out of it and lie on it!”

Before I could even respond to that statement, the other Butchers started shouting. “Yes! Let’s make a throne out of it! We can post a picture of you on it to PHO!” Anchorage exclaimed.

“If we get it in dollar coins, we could swim in it like Scrooge McDuck!” Vladimir replied.

“But it’d be solid, not liquid,” Flinch began-

“We’re strong enough to burrow through it,” Nemean said over him.

“It’d be ridiculous to take in cash,” I said firmly.

Piggot gave me an odd look. “Do I want to know?” She asked cautiously.

“It’s like managing a bunch of horny, angry teenagers,” I said with a sigh.

Piggot snorted. “I know what that’s like.”

For a brief moment we shared a complicated look of shared suffering. Then we shook ourselves and returned to business.

“Out of curiosity, what are you planning to do with the money?”

“I’m thinking of investing in real estate. There’s a lot of trashed buildings that I could help fix up myself, get a constant income from that. Maybe a few other projects on the side- work on clearing the Graveyard, look into restarting the ferry service, that sort of thing.”

“I see. Very civic minded of you.”

“So now we’re becoming ‘legitimate businessmen’?” Stoneknapper joked.

Firecracker snickered. “If anyone asks, we’re in waste management.”

“Anything else I should know while I’m here?”

Piggot grimaced and nodded. “Unfortunately, yes. Cassandra and the Think Tank have confirmed that killing Jack averted the six-month’s apocalypse, but it’s still coming. We have no idea what starts it or what force could possibly destroy the world, but it’s a blind spot for every precog we have.”

The Butchers went quiet as a shiver went down my spine. “How long do we have?” I forced myself to ask.

“Three years,” Piggot said heavily. “We’re keeping it as quiet as possible to avoid a panic, but we’re reaching out to our allies and factions around the world, feeling out who’s willing and able to help us stop it.”

I nodded slowly. “If you need me to do anything, just call.”

Piggot’s eyebrows went up again. “That’s appreciated.” After a second she asked, “Is there anything that you need to tell me while you’re here?”

I couldn’t stop the wince, and she noticed it. “You know that the Teeth challenged me at the Truce meeting.”

“You’re not seriously going to meet them?” Piggot demanded.

“She’s quick on the uptake,” Bearskin conceded.

“It was the price for them helping,” I admitted. “And it’s a tradition of the Butchers- if someone formally challenges, they answer it.”

“Of all the stupid things-!” Piggot visibly reigned herself in with a deep breath. “I was under the impression that you didn’t have to follow the Butchers’ rules.”

“If I don’t stop them, the Teeth will just keep coming back and trying to make the Butcher return, no matter what kind of psychoes they have to recruit to do it. I need to end it, and I’ll never have a better chance than them naming the time and place.”

Piggot drummed her fingers on her desk for a second. “These challenges are to the death,” she said eventually. It wasn’t a question.

“The last time the Butchers spared a challenger, it was Muscular back in ’96, and he went and joined the Nine out of spite.”

This time it was Piggot who winced. “You’re the woman who killed Jack Slash. That kind of reputation is incredibly valuable. If you walk into a deathmatch with the Teeth, you’ll be throwing that in the gutter.”

“There’ll still be people coming after me for the mantle now that people know I’m still sane. If I don’t set an example soon, it’ll be a never-ending line of crazies coming to Brockton Bay looking for an upgrade, and people will get hurt.”

“A single neat cut now, or a dozen messy strikes later,” Muramasa mused.

“The mantle?” Piggot asked with a puzzled look.

“It’s what we call the position and the powers.”

“Ah.”

There was an awkward silence for a few seconds.

“We can’t condone heroes committing premeditated murder,” Piggot said eventually.

“I think I could argue self-defence,” I said non-commitally.

Piggot groaned and straightened up. “Where’s this challenge happening?”

“I’ve got no clue,” I said honestly. “The Teeth will get in touch at some point, but until then, best I can say is after the truce ends, hopefully outside the city limits.”

“...You’re really willing to go this far to set an example? To keep Brockton Bay safe?”

I shrugged. “It’s home.”

 

The conversation with Piggot dragged on for longer, and it left me and the Butchers arguing back and forth, but eventually I headed off to my next errands, and the Butchers got back on the subject of me being hilariously rich.

Rotter was in the middle of trying to remember the words for “We’re In The Money” when I arrived at City Hall. I’d made an appointment for this too, but people were a lot more surprised to see someone in armour with a bow and sword strolling up. There were a bunch of people in suits looking surprised to see me, and a couple of people hustling towards me, one of them holding a large camera-

“Oh my god, we’re getting interviewed,” Quarrel said in disbelief.

“Stan Vickery, Channel 12 News,” said the man with the microphone, flashing a friendly smile that I trusted about as far as I could throw him. Less, probably – I was very strong and he wasn’t huge. The guy holding a bag of wires and tripods and other stuff looked like he was barely out of high school, and the girl holding the camera was even smaller, built like a thirteen year old. If it wasn’t for her tattoos and all the piercings crammed into her right ear, I’d have thought she was just some kid Stan Vickery had paid to carry his stuff.

“Elpis, do you have a minute to comment on the recent events in Brockton Bay?”

My gut instinct was to say nothing, push past him and get on with what I’d come here to do. But what Piggot had said earlier, about the reputation of killing Jack Slash and what that could do, came back to me.

“Just speak clearly, and don’t give too much away,” Flinch said. “You’ve got this.”

I took a deep breath and forced a smile without too many teeth. “I can spare a moment, since you asked nicely.” I shifted the insects around me, moving the spiders and beetles and flies out of sight, then bringing the few butterflies and moths I had to flutter prettily around me. Vickery’s practiced smile grew a little wider, which I took as a good sign.

“Wonderful,” Stan Vickery enthused, moving around a little to the side. The girl with the camera adjusted her grip to get both of us in shot, while the guy with the bag just stepped back a few paces.

“First of all, there’ve been a lot of rumours regarding how you defeated Jack Slash. In your own words, how would you describe it?”

I held back a shudder. “Horrible would sum it up. But in more detail, the capes of Brockton Bay, and later, Protectorate reinforcements from New York, LA, and Houston, including the Triumvirate themselves, coordinated to take out the Nine until Jack was the only one left. He used a tinker tech device to isolate himself and me from the others, in an attempt to take my powers and escape.”

It was a good thing Piggot had insisted I hear the official story the PRT was putting out- I didn’t want to contradict them and accidentally clue people in on the clones or the Birdcage portal or any of that crap.

“But you were able to defeat him.”

“I had help- all the capes present contributed, but Director Piggot of PRT East-North-East personally put a bullet in Jack at a critical moment, and Armsmaster tossed me his halberd right when I needed a weapon. Jack fell apart after that.”

Quarrel cackled. I hadn’t even meant that as a pun, but the way the camera girl winced told me that I’d slipped up.

Stan Vickery didn’t even blink though. “The world is glad to see the end of the Slaughterhouse Nine’s reign of terror. I understand that one of your predecessors confronted Jack Slash when he led the Nine to Brockton Bay back in 1996. “

“Two of them, actually. Needler was Butcher V at the time, and fought Jack personally, and Firecracker was one of her subordinates. They still maintain a particular hatred for Jack Slash.”

Stan Vickery nodded. “The story of the Butcher and their, ah, line of succession, has been a hot topic for some time now.”

“Try 20 years, ass wipe,” Butcher sneered.

Stan Vickery looked uneasy for once as he continued “With that in mind, can you shed some light on the rumours that the previous Butchers speak to you, even after death?”

“Yes, it’s true. All 14 of the previous Butchers speak to me inside my mind.” I shrugged nonchalantly. “I realise that sounds hard to believe, but it’s the truth.”

“What’s it like?” Vickery said, sounding genuinely interested.

The Butchers all turned towards me, waiting to hear what I had to say. I considered.

“It’s...constant. They’re always commenting on what I’m doing, always giving an opinion or arguing with me and each other, or just shouting and demanding something. When I’m fighting, they offer advice; when I watch TV they heckle: the only time they really shut up is when I’m in the bathroom, and that’s just because it’s awkward.”

The camera girl’s face was a mask of horror, and the guy with the bag wasn’t much better. Vickery’s professional expression wavered.

“I see... There’s been a lot of discussion regarding your decision to turn the Undersiders into a team of heroes, and your recent success certainly seems to have vindicated that. Do you have anything to add on the subject?”

“He sure changed the subject fast,” Tock Tick noted.

Anchorage shrugged. “Nobody wants to hear about ghosts watching you shit.”

“I’d say that I hope this will encourage people to rethink their opinions on criminals in general and villains in particular; why people fall into that lifestyle and how we can get them out of it. Don’t get me wrong, there’s plenty of people out there who don’t want or deserve a second chance, but there are plenty more who would gladly take a way out if it was offered. The Undersiders, all of us, have proven that it’s possible to change for the better, and I hope we see more of that in the future.”

“That’s a very noble sentiment,” Vickery said. Before he could start another question, I shifted my weight and looked pointedly towards City Hall. He took the hint and said brightly, “Well, thank you very much for speaking to us today, Elpis. On behalf of Brockton Bay, let me just say thank you for your service.”

“You’re welcome. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have things to do.” I gave him a nod, waited until the girl lowered the camera, and then set off towards the doors again. People parted before me as I walked, butterflies orbiting around me.

The flies I’d left hidden around Stan Vickery and his crew let me listen to them. “That was gold. Pure gold. First ever to interview Elpis- we could get an award for this.”

“It’s only a few minutes,” the camera girl said.

“A few minutes of unprecedented footage, Nipper,” Vickery retorted. “The most anyone’s got of Elpis until now has been phone video and her PHO verification.”

“What the hell kind of name is Nipper?” Tactical wondered.

The corridors here were more clearly signposted, so I found the mayor’s office pretty fast. There was a stressed-looking secretary at a desk just outside, clearly reaching or something under her desk before she recognised who I was. “Oh, Elpis,” she trilled nervously.

“That’s me. I have an appointment.”

The secretary glanced hurriedly at her screen. “Uh, yes, that’s right. I’m sorry, but I’m afraid Mayor Christner is currently, uh, indisposed right now. I could reschedule your appointment for later in the week if you’d like?” she added nervously.

I glanced past the doors with blood sight. The shape of a man was slumped in a chair. “You know I can see him in there, right?”

The secretary’s harried expression grew more frantic. “I’m sorry, but Mayor Christner just isn’t available right now.” As I watched, the blood silhouette in the office reached for something on the desk and brought it to his lips.

“Our tax dollars at work,” Needler said in disgust.

“You never paid taxes in your life,” I pointed out, stepping past the secretary’s desk, ignoring her attempt to turn me back without actually touching me or raising her voice. I pulled the double doors to the mayor’s office open and stepped inside.

Mayor Roy Christner was sat behind his desk, cut-glass tumbler in hand, an expensive-looking bottle on his desk. I recognised his face from newspapers and adverts around town over the years- fifty or sixty, with horseshoe-pattern baldness and ears that stuck out. He looked a lot worse than he ever had in the ads- red eyes, rumpled shirt, flushed face.

And he was crying. Tear tracks marked his face, all the way down to the collar of his shirt, and his nose was embarrassingly snotty.

“Go away,” he burbled, gesturing at me with the glass.

“I have an appointment,” I said, stepping closer. This was not what I had expected.

“Sir, I’m sorry, I tried to stop her,” the secretary babbled.

“Not that she could have really done anything.” Needler said absently, her attention mostly focused on the mayor.

“Man, he looks like crap,” Bearskin said bluntly.

“I said go away!” The mayor threw the glass at me; I snatched it out of the air and sniffed. Scotch; expensive stuff too. The Butchers would drink anything, but they occasionally indulged in high brand liquor looted from the rich or traded for drugs or sometimes even bought, and this smelled really good.

I looked at him again. This wasn’t a happy drunk. There were plenty of people getting happy drunk with the Nine gone. This was a man who was drinking a lot of scotch and crying all alone.

I set the glass on the desk. “Who did you lose?” I asked softly.

Mayor Christner’s face crumpled like wet tissue, and he flopped back into his big leather chair with a sob. “My boy,” he cried. “My son, my boy.”

“Oh hell,” Vladimir muttered, not without sympathy.

I turned to the secretary. “How does he take his coffee?”

“Uh, cream, one sugar?” she managed.

“I think he’ll need a few cups. And maybe some water too.” I took another look at the man crying into his hands, and added, “And some tissues.”

The secretary nodded and flew the room, closing the doors behind her with a soft click.

I moved the glass and bottle away from Mayor Christner while he cried, then took a look around. After a second, I found a box of tissues on the mantlepiece in a fancy holder that made the tissues look like the sails on a boat and set the whole thing down in front of him.

Mayor Christner grabbed a few and clumsily blew his nose, then wiped his hands of all the snot. While he did that, I pulled up a chair and carefully sat down, sweeping my cape out so it wasn’t stuck under me. Then I waited.

At length, Mayor Christner lifted his head and stared at me blearily. “It’s my fault.”

“I doubt that,” I answered.

“It is,” Mayor Christner insisted. “My fault. He wouldn’t have been out there if it wasn’t for me. He got killed because of me.” Fresh tears welled in his eyes.

“What happened?” I said gently.

“Jack Slash!” he bellowed suddenly, slamming a fist on the table. “He- he killed him, that- that fucker killed Rory! Hit him with that thing so hard they wouldn’t let us look at him!” He turned bloodshot eyes on me. “You killed Slash. Did it hurt? Did he scream?”

“To his last breath,” I said.

“Good,” Mayor Christner snarled. “Good.” Then his face crumpled again. “But Rory... If I’d never, then he wouldn’t have- and he wouldn’t have been in the fight- it’s my fault. And now he’s another name on a memorial like all those other poor bastards. Except if I put up a memorial for him, they’ll say I’m spending taxpayer money on my son’s memorial. And I don’t want it to just say Triumph, he was my son, my little boy...”

Nemean swore. “Triumph...”

“Fuck me, no wonder he’s getting plastered,” Rotter said. “That’s definitely a closed casket job.”

“I mean, it was probably quick and painless?” Firecracker suggested hopelessly.

“Death by high-speed corpse is hardly a dignified end,” Muramasa countered.

“We could make him a memorial,” Flinch suggested quietly, hushing everyone else. As the only parent of the Butchers, he was probably the only one who could even begin to understand Christner’s grief.

“I could make a memorial,” I said aloud. The mayor slowly raised his head. “I came to talk to you about rebuilding the city. Adding a memorial wouldn’t be difficult.”

“Rebuilding?”

“Yes. Mr Mayor, I just claimed the bounties on Jack Slash, the Siberian, and Bonesaw. Do you know how much money that is?”

Mayor Christner slowly shook his head.

“$250 million for Jack Slash, $150 million for Siberian, $150 million for Bonesaw. All together, that’s $550 million in perfectly legal money.”

I’d asked, and Piggot had explained that it actually would have been more, what with people donating extra to the bounties over the years, but the government had eventually but a cap on the bounties and redirected the extra to charities helping the survivors of S-class events. The Butchers had cynically wondered if the feds had just given up on anyone actually managing to off the big three.

I wasn’t particularly happy that Bakuda and Crusader would probably be able to claim the $75 million apiece for Crawler and Mannequin, but it was still petty cash compared to my money. The Wards would have to make do with splitting Burnscar’s $30 million six ways.

Christner’s mouth fell open as I continued, “I’m willing to put the bulk of that into restoring this city. Clearing rubble, raising new buildings, finally get the Boat Graveyard removed. And once that’s done, people will flock to this city. We’re the town that killed the Nine; how many tourists will come to see where it happened and spit on the glass floor where Jack Slash died?”

“Spit on it?” Quarrel snorted. “People will want to shit on it!”

“Maybe we should set up a taco stand next to it,” Butcher said with a horrible grin. “Let ‘em load up first.”

I cringed on the inside as I kept talking. “And how many of them will want to lay flowers on the memorial? A memorial to everyone who lost their lives to the Slaughterhouse Nine, including the last of them; Brockton Bay’s own hometown hero, Triumph. I’ll make the damn thing myself if I have to, Mr Mayor.”

“Shit, that’s right,” Tock Tick realised. “I don’t think anyone died when we cornered Jack, and we can’t tell the public about the Birdcage portal, so as far as the world knows, Triumph was the last person who got killed by the Nine.”

Mayor Christner slowly reached for the tissues, wiped his eyes and blew his nose, then crumpled them into a ball and dropped it into a wastepaper basket. “Where,” he cleared his throat and continued more clearly, “Where would you put it?”

“Right by the Boardwalk, maybe,” I said. “Somewhere easy for people to find.”

“And it’d be- like the Leviathan memorial? An obelisk?”

I shrugged. “Maybe. It could be an obelisk, or a wall with people’s names on it, or something else entirely.”

“We could get creative,” Stoneknapper suggested. “Like a huge knife being shattered- or a nine-sided tower falling down.”

“We should have something for Spree and Vex, and the lovebirds,” Needler put in.

“Yeah,” Anchorage agreed, “But we should do something back at the lair too. We wouldn’t be able to do something really Teeth-y in public without scaring the normals.”

Mayor Christner nodded slowly, thinking it over; then his expression drooped again. “I don’t even know if I’ll be re-elected,” he admitted. “I don’t know if I’ll even run.”

“Well, that’s up to you,” I said. It’d be cruel to try and pressure him now, while he was grieving. “But whoever ends up in office, I intend to rebuild this city. And I intend to make sure Triumph is remembered as a proper hero.”

Mayor Christner’s eyes shone with fresh tears, but he blinked them away. “Thank you,” he said thickly. He sniffed hugely and looked down at his desk. “I never should’ve bought that fucking vial,” he whispered.

It was said so softly he couldn’t have meant me to hear it, but I had sharp hearing from Nemean, and a few bugs that I’d slipped into his desk and under his chair without even realising I was doing it. “What did you say?”

“A vial?” Nemean hissed.

Christner looked up. “Hm?”

“You said you bought a vial.” I stood up from my chair with deliberate movements. “What did you mean by that?”

“Easy, Taylor,” Flinch warned.

The blood drained from Christner’s face. “I- I didn’t say that. I didn’t say anything, I was just mumbling-”

“No, you weren’t,” I said, setting my knuckles on the desk and leaning forward, looming over him as he tried to shrink into his chair. “What did you mean, buying a vial? A vial that gives people superpowers?”

Christner’s face grew even paler. “How do you-”

“So you do know what I’m talking about. Who sold you the vial? Did you contact them, or did they contact you?”

“Is that why he was blaming himself?” Tactical wondered. “Did he buy Triumph’s powers for him?”

“Holy shit,” Bearskin murmured.

“I, I, I can’t tell you,” Christner stammered. “They said if I told anyone, they’d-”

“They? Who are you more afraid of, Mayor?” I asked, sharpening my teeth so pointed fangs flashed with every syllable. “Them? Or me?”

Christner swallowed heavily. “Them.”

“What?” Several of the Butchers asked.

“You’re not- you’re a hero, you’ve spent all this time proving it. And you’re just one person. These people, they’re bigger- they contacted me, they brought me to- I don’t know how far it goes, but it must be huge. I can’t tell you, I have no idea what they’ll do.”

I glared at him, swearing on the inside. A solid lead on the vials, a fragment of the mystery behind Case 53s, maybe even the secret of powers in general, and he was more scared of the shadowy conspiracy than an angry Butcher looming over his desk. What the hell was I chasing?

There was a knock at the door.

I didn’t look around, just moved some of the bugs I’d planted outside the door frame- when had I done that? It was the secretary, holding a tray with a silver coffee pot, a little jug of cream, a sugar bowl, a couple of mugs, and a pitcher of water.

“It’s your secretary,” I said, straightening up. I smoothed out the faint dents my knuckles had made in the wood.

Mayor Christner hastily sat up in his chair and tapped a switch on his desk. The doors swung open quietly, and the secretary quietly stepped in.

“Thank you, Millie,” Mayor Christner managed as she set the tray down on a side table. “Uh, will you want a cup, Elpis?” he added with a surprising recovery of composure.
