I gave him a hard look. “No, thank you. I’ve said what I needed to. I’ll leave you to your business. I hope you think carefully about what I said,” I stated heavily. Judging by the look on his face, he caught my meaning.

“Shame,” Dirty Rotter said. “That smells like a good cuppa.”

I turned and walked for the doors without a backward glance, calling the insects I’d secreted all over the place back to me. Maybe I could have left them in place, but it didn’t seem needed.

I turned back and gently closed the double doors as I exited, giving the Mayor one last look as Millie the secretary poured him a cup. Even if he didn’t want to talk, I could keep an eye on him, maybe glean a few more hints of the mystery-

I turned around as the doors closed, and I was standing in a cavern.

For a second I could sense the insects scattered throughout city hall before they were abruptly cut off. A portal, maybe, one that took me to a place carved out of stone, with tube lights set into the ceiling every few feet or so.

And at the far end of the wide, circular cave-like room, there stood two figures. Both women, one dark-skinned in a white coat, one light-skinned in a dark suit and hat.

“Good morning, Elpis,” said the black woman. “I felt it was time for us to talk.”

Chapter 136: 14.3

Wednesday 8th June, Unknown Location

“It could be an illusion,” Stoneknapper said as I stared at the two women across the room. “Check the walls.”

I reached a hand out to the nearest wall, brushing my fingertips against it. Stoneknapper’s fizz activated, recognising it as rock- granite, I thought. I also activated bloodsight and directed insects to sweep around me, looking for exits and entrances, hidden traps and weapons.

I pulled a lump of rock from the wall with ease, and bloodsight revealed only the two women standing there, but my insects brushed up against another presence- a non-presence, more like a shift of air currents, affecting certain bugs when it should have touched other bugs in front of or behind them.

The topographical sense I got from the movement’s of my bugs suggested a woman’s body, unclothed. Stranger still, it wasn’t entirely done when another appeared to my senses across the room. The same figure, moving in sync- probably not two people. One person, unseen and barely felt, a phantom in the room. Some kind of backup perhaps.

“I fucking hate Strangers,” Needler groused.

I moved closer to the women, stopping about ten feet away. If these were the people who sold powers, then they either started with serious firepower of their own, had picked out something powerful for themselves, or they had muscle on call. Best to keep a distance until I knew what I was dealing with.

The dark-skinned woman nodded. “You can call me Doctor Mother, and I am the founder of Cauldron.” She spoke with a slight French accent, and she was dressed neatly- blouse, skirt, lab coat, and a pin in her hair. She did nothing to indicate the other woman, or the phantom.

“Cauldron. So that’s what you call yourselves?” I wondered at the meaning behind that.

“Witch’s cauldron,” Dirty Rotter suggested. “Brewing stuff up for a price.”

“Three women,” Quarrel noted. “Three witches. If she’s Doctor Mother, does that mean the other two are the Maiden and the Crone?” It wasn’t a joke- a lot of capes chose symbolic names and themes that could reveal a lot about their powers and goals. I needed more information.

“Indeed,” Doctor Mother said. “And as you have already worked out, we are the organisation creating parahumans, including the Case 53s.”

Nemean had been simmering with anger since we’d stepped into this place. Now she boiled over, screaming with inarticulate rage. A few swear words were mixed in, flotsam on the river of fury.

I didn’t push her down- I was pretty fucking angry myself. “The Case 53s, Noelle- and how many other fuckups? At least some of the Travellers got powers from you, how many other villains?”

“The Travellers gained their powers without our knowledge or permission,” Doctor Mother replied without so much of a flick of an eyelid. “We have removed them from play.”

“What does she mean, removed from play?” Vladimir wondered.

“Nothing good,” Anchorage said darkly.

“Not denying the rest?”

“You have already figured it out,” Doctor Mother said calmly. “And that’s not why we brought you here.”

“Then why?” I demanded.

“The end of the world is coming, and we are preparing for it.”

“If Triumph wasn’t the only hero who got vial powers, they might have moles in the Protectorate,” Flinch pointed out. “This could run very deep.”

“Mountains of molehills,” Tock Tick muttered. “If the Travellers are the maximum amount of power you can get from a vial, and if you don’t need a trigger event- powerful, less fucked up… How many top heroes had a little drink?”

“You can still be fucked up without a trigger event,” Firecracker countered. “Some of their customers could be villains.”

“So you heard about the prophecy,” I said, keeping the anger out of my voice.

“We did, but we didn’t need to. Our organisation was founded with the goal of countering the coming threat.”

“WHAT?!” Butcher bellowed, the others not far behind.

“What?!” I shouted. “How long have you known?”

“Since the dawn of parahumans on this earth,” Doctor Mother said simply. “Everything we have done has been to advance that goal, and it is why we are speaking to you now.”

“If you’ve known the whole time, why couldn’t you stop it from happening in the first place?”

“The threat is a blind spot to all precogs, no matter how powerful. And this is not something that we can prevent from occurring. The end of the world is coming. Since we cannot stop it, we must prepare to fight it.”

“And you’re not going to tell me what it is,” I said flatly, feeling my anger rise again. My fingernails stretched and sharpened slightly, digging into my palms.

“I’m afraid not. Telling you would only accelerate the timeline, before we’re ready to act.”

“The Endbringers?” I guessed anyway.

“No. The Endbringers are a conundrum that we haven’t yet been able to solve, but they are not the greatest threat to humanity.”

“Fuck me,” Tactical whispered. “Worse than the Endbringers…”

I shook away the horror of that statement and pressed onward. “What do you want from me then?” I kept bugs orbiting around me, wary for an attack. If they wanted to kill me for my powers or take me for experiments, I wouldn’t go easily.

“Your cooperation and assistance,” Doctor Mother said simply. “You’ve achieved more in six months than most parahumans achieve in a lifetime, and now you’ve been thrust into the spotlight with the death of Jack Slash. We’d like you to collaborate with us for the next three years, to give humanity the best chance. We know you’re important, and so do you- Cassandra told you so.”

“A secret organisation that sells powers wants our help to save the world,” Bearskin muttered. “Sounds like a fucking conspiracy theory.”

“Or the plot of a B-movie,” Muramasa snorted.

“Do you guys think I should go for it?” I asked. I wasn’t sure that I trusted them, but the portal power that had brought me to wherever this was didn’t make it seem like I had much of a choice. If they could just scoop me up whenever they wanted, they were holding the cards.

Dirty Rotter shrugged. “I guess it’s like a truce thing, but longer. Even if we don’t trust ‘em, we all gotta work together, or we’re toast.”

“It sounds too good to be true,” Anchorage said. “What’re they going to want us to do? Deliver their stuff? Find customers?”

“Like we’re strangers to dealing drugs,” Stoneknapper snorted.

“Definitely get the details before agreeing to anything,” Tock Tick said firmly.

Then Nemean growled, long and low. “Ask them about me,” she demanded.

I stared at Doctor Mother’s calm face for a long moment. All the talk of the apocalypse had distracted me for a moment. “Tell me about Nemean,” I said carefully.

For the first time, the woman in the hat moved. She reached into her jacket and withdrew a cardboard file folder. 562 was stamped on it in black ink. She held it out to me without a word.

I took the folder in hands that shook slightly, pulling my claws in before touching it, and carefully opened it. The first thing I saw was a photograph of a black woman, badly injured. Fresh wounds crossed her face, arms and upper body, bleeding heavily. Her features were just visible under the injuries- a broad nose and full lips, her hair in thick braids with colourful beads at the end. She seemed familiar, like a half-remembered dream.

Kareela Drees, read the page. Earth Waw. Born 14/8/1972. Occupation: Mercenary. Family: Two Children, Alinta (1995) and Jarrah (1998). Wounded by an IED, retrieved and given D1632-Fang. Developed Hyper-durable skin and moderately durable body, flawless healing, enhanced senses, ability to extend teeth and claws. Mutations- total coverage of fur, digitigrade feet, slit pupils.

“This is more comprehensive than our usual files,” Doctor Mother said from far away as I slowly turned the page, revealing more photos- Kareela standing in a group of other men and women, all holding weapons; Kareela holding a newborn baby with an exhausted smile; Kareela clutching two laughing children to her sides. The girl was taller, with a feather in her hair, and the boy had a gap-toothed smile. “We did additional research for the purposes of this meeting-”

“Why.”

Doctor Mother stopped talking, but she didn’t respond to my question.

I raised my eyes from the page to look at her, the woman behind it all, and Nemean’s words tumbled out of my mouth. “Why did you take me? Why did you take my memories? I can’t remember any of this. I had children, AND YOU TOOK THAT AWAY FROM ME!”

“Kareela Drees was dying when we found her,” Doctor Mother said simply. “As many are. The vials can give a healing effect- we offered her a chance to live.”

“No you didn’t! Kareela Drees died years ago! You erased her memories, and Nemean woke up! Why did you do that?! Don’t tell me the vials erase memories, because I won’t believe it!” I snapped the folder shut and jabbed an accusing, claw-tipped finger at her face.

Doctor Mother was silent for a moment. It didn’t seem like she was emotional or taken aback- more like she was waiting to see if I had anything else to scream at her before she spoke again. “We cannot afford to let our secrets be released into the wild. We have to enforce total silence in order to operate effectively.”

“To your test subjects,” I snarled. “To the people that you abduct from other Earths and offer them a, a poison chalice! Not your paying customers, right?!” My mind was whirling, making connections like the world’s most fucked up game of connect the dots. “I’ll bet Triumph went home to his rich daddy without a single minute missing!”

“They are sworn to secrecy,” Doctor Mother said. “And if any of them consider going against it, we remind them of the terms of the agreement. Drastic measures are rarely necessary, but they are a possibility.”

“You murder them.”

“If we must.”

I stared at Doctor Mother, fangs gnashing, while she stared calmly back. I’d met thieves and kidnappers and murderers and sadists and perverts and straight-up monsters, but I’d never met anyone who talked about abduction and experimentation and murder in such a calm, clear voice. It was like she didn’t have any feelings for the things she did, like it was all just another day at the office.

“Fuck me,” Quarrel breathed. “She might actually be the worst we’ve ever met.”

I was angry. I was furious. I was incandescent with rage. But if there was one thing I’d learned how to do, it was to control myself. I swallowed deeply, and it felt like I was swallowing hot coals, but I managed to pull the claws in and the fangs back, and speak in a voice that trembled only slightly. “Is there anything else you wanted to tell me?”

“Only to repeat my earlier points. We would like to coordinate your efforts with ours for greatest effect. With the Slaughterhouse Nine gone, there will be others seeking to establish themselves in the power vacuum. And of course there will be various groups who will need to be dealt with to keep things stable- not necessarily lethally, of course.”

“Of course,” I said venomously.

Doctor Mother nodded. “Thank you for listening. Now, I have said everything I wanted to, and I can see that emotions are high. This will take you back to your base.” She gestured, and a portal opened to my left, to a well-lit area full of bugs.

I shot the two of them one last furious look, jammed the folder under one arm, and marched through the portal without a backward glance. At this point I didn’t care if it was a trap, I just wanted to be gone. The portal closed behind me, and I looked around to see where I was.

I was back in the Lair, on the ground floor. The doors were locked, the bugs were in their terrariums, I could make out the sounds of the others upstairs.

I wouldn’t be able to find them again- the file had all but stated they could move across parallel Earths. Who knew where that meeting room was, or their other bases? I’d never be able to find them unless they wanted to be found. Or unless they summoned me again, at their leisure.

Nemean screamed in rage, and my claws popped into meat hooks in response. My heart was pounding in my ears, my insects were thrashing around, I felt like there was fire under my skin. I was as angry as I’d ever been, and I was powerless like never before.

“Hey boss, I didn’t hear you come in,” said Isabella from the top of the stairs. “Uh, I’ve got some bad news- Weymouth Mall just called. Somebody made off with the Chariot-”

I spun around and smashed my fist into the wall with a roar, cracking the brickwork under my knuckles. Ten feet away, Isabella stumbled back and sat down heavily on the stairs. “I’ll leave you alone,” she squeaked, and bolted back up the stairs.

 

 

It took hours for me to calm down enough to speak coherently and tell everyone what happened, and even that required Lisa inferring a few things from my snarls and grunts. Eventually I shucked my armour and just hopped in the shower, blasting myself with scalding, high pressure water until the Butchers and I managed to calm back down.

When I emerged with a change of clothes and towel-dried hair, everyone else was sitting at the table, with the folder open. I caught a look of fear on Isa’s face, and felt a stab of guilt.

“If you didn’t want us to look-”

“It’s fine,” I said over Isabella. “I probably would have shown you guys anyway. We need to talk about this anyway.”

“It’s pretty difficult to believe,” Brian admitted. “A secret conspiracy kidnapping people across parallel dimensions? It sounds like something out of science fiction.”

“So did superpowers, once upon a time,” Dad said, turning a photo around to look. “So this is what Nemean looked like, before she had powers?” He looked at me in the slightly awkward way he did when I was relaying stuff from the Butchers. “You look- well, looked- nice, Nemean.”

Nemean managed a grumble in response, too worn out to speak. “She appreciates it,” I said on her behalf.

“I think this could explain even more than what they said,” Lisa said, writing stuff down on a notepad. “Haywire was one man, but if Cauldron can move across dimensions that easily, it might mean that parallel dimensions are involved in how powers themselves work.”

“What’s that mean?” Tarquin asked.

“So many powers seem to be pulling energy out of thin air, or matter. Legend can fire off enough energy to light up Manhattan- the human body couldn’t supply that if he was eating plutonium.”

“So you think that the passengers, the actual source of powers or whatever, they’re from another dimension?” Amy asked, leaning forward. Her pendant slipped out of her collar, dangling on a cord of finest red silk.

“Almost definitely.”

Rachel grunted. “Forget the powers stuff for a second. How do we handle these guys?” She tapped the folder with a knuckle to underline her point.

“We can’t.”

Everyone turned to look at me like I’d grown another head. “Wait, what?” Aisha asked. “You’re kidding right? We just put down the Nine, these guys-”

“Are far more dangerous,” I said. “They can create powers on demand and sell them to the highest bidder; and if they’ve gone this long without being revealed, then either they’re extremely good at keeping under the radar, or everyone with the capacity to find out is already in their pocket-”

“Or Cauldron killed them before they could blow the whistle,” Vladimir said grimly. I repeated his words out loud.

“Look, these guys scooped me out of City Hall and dropped me in here. That was deliberate, they were sending a message. They know where we are, and with moles in the Protectorate they know who I am. They’ve made it clear they can get to us whenever and wherever we go. And we still have no idea what powers they’re packing, if it’s possible to counter them…” I trailed off and shrugged helplessly. “Look, I’m the one who says we can move that rubber tree plant, but fighting them would be like spitting at a tornado.”

“And they left the folder for you,” Lisa said, hooking a finger under the page she was reading. “Letting you keep it means they’re sure you’re not going to go to the- gah!”

I hurried around the table to look. On the page Lisa had flipped to, one I hadn’t seen before, was a handwritten note in the most exact penmanship I’d ever seen. It read ‘We are grateful for your discretion, Ms Wilbourne. 12:37pm.’ And at the bottom was the upturned omega symbol of Cauldron.

Lisa yanked back her sleeve to look at her watch. “It’s 12:37,” she said shakily. “Exactly.”

“Fuck me,” Tarquin whispered.

“I’m with the kid on this,” Firecracker said.

“You know,” Lisa said, rolling her sleeve back down and pushing the folder away, “There were times when Coil would call, and I’d know that he was using his power to ask me questions in one timeline and give me the answers in another, before I asked the questions. And that really creeped me out.” She stabbed a finger at the note. “That’s scarier.”

“We can’t fight them,” Brian said.

“No, we can’t. We’re just going to have to proceed like they don’t exist,” I said. “Focus on what we can do.”

“Like what?” Isa demanded.

“Like use the $550 million dollars from the bounties and the fame and goodwill from ending the Nine to fix this city, and more.”

Dad’s head came up. “How much?” He asked incredulously.

“$550 million. And that’s not considering the stuff we can do ourselves. I’m thinking we can buy up property, fix it up ourselves, get some businesses going as a cash flow. Building a ferry boat might be a little much for Tock Tick’s power, but I could give it a shot.”

“Hell, it sounds like fun,” Tock Tick said.

“So long as there’s one of those naked figureheads,” Butcher said.

“Oh hell yes, I always wanted a boat,” Anchorage agreed enthusiastically.

“A ferry boat? Really?” Isa asked.

“I’ve been trying to get the ferry restarted for years,” Dad said. “Figured it’d bring jobs, make it easier for people to commute from one end of the city to the other.”

“And if we buy up properties, those people will be working for us, which gives us a revenue stream to go further.”

“Further?”

“Brockton Bay has more heroes than villains for the first time in years,” I said. “Bakuda’s all on her own, and the Empire’s down to six capes. Seven if Othala gets deprogrammed any time soon, but that could take weeks.”

“Night and Fog weren’t doing so well either,” Amy said. “I managed to fix whatever the fuck Bonesaw hit them with, but it took a lot out of them.”

“Thank you, Amy,” I said. “We have a chance to take this city, clean it top to bottom, and harden it against any new villains that try to move in. Brockton Bay could go from being a shithole to one of the safest cities on the East Coast.”

“My god,” Dad said faintly. “We could- we really could do it.”

“You’re serious?” Rachel asked.

“Absolutely. Plus when people have steady jobs and no pressure from gangs, they’ll be able to take in a dog or two, and learn how to treat them right,” I added, pressing Rachel’s motivation button as unsubtly as possible.

Rachel nodded decisively. “Sounds good.”

“I know guys in the other unions,” Dad said. “Honest guys looking for honest work. They’d jump at the chance to do this.”

“I heard some stuff from my cover job,” Brian said, growing more animated as he talked. “We could reach out to a few companies.”

“You’ll want to set up the right systems to channel the money,” Lisa said, flipping the folder closed. “I can handle that.”

Tarquin raised a hand. “I don’t know crap about business, but I’m good for clearing stuff out and knocking shit down.”

“Same here, I guess,” Isabella said.

“Alright,” I said, clapping my hands together. “Let’s get to work.”

And once we had Brockton Bay established as a base of operations, then the real plans could begin.

Flinch grinned inside my head. “This is going to be good.”

Chapter 137: Bonus Interlude 14.c

Wednesday 8th June, Cauldron Headquarters

“That went as expected,” Doctor Mother commented, sinking into her seat at the head of the table. Contessa took up her usual place standing beside and behind her.

The Number Man nodded. He looked the same as usual- blonde hair combed back, glasses polished, shirt ironed and pocket protector in place. “It’s a shame we couldn’t bring her in more directly.”

Alexandria took off her steel helmet and shook out her hair. The makeup she used to appear older and hide her ageless features had rubbed off, revealing the youthful face of Chief Director Rebecca Costa-Brown. “We can work with her as an independent factor. Presenting the Undersiders as an alternative to the Protectorate will keep more parahumans on the side of the law.”

“And her reconstruction efforts will increase employment, reduce urban decay, lower gang recruitment and overall membership…” The Number Man’s eyes flicked upward for a second as he calculated some complex formula, then nodded decisively. “Yes.”

“So, Elpis will act as a stabilising force in Brockton Bay?”

“Indeed,” Doctor Mother confirmed. “We can use her as an example for the PRT to move forward with further parahuman integration- bringing the less appealing powers forward and openly recruiting former villains.”

“While also creating a city that is all but run by parahumans,” Rebecca noted. “It’s a shame that we weren’t able to see how Coil might have controlled the city, but that’s a negligible loss compared to the gains we’ve had.”

“She won’t have enough money to expand across the East Coast without help,” Number Man noted. “I’ll handle that- some government subsidies, a few tax write-offs. Her Thinker won’t even notice.”

“Very good,” Doctor Mother said. “Even if she despises us, as long as she’s contributing to the work, it’s progress.”

“Do we have any idea what role she’ll play at the end?” Rebecca asked.

Doctor Mother shook her head. “The blindspot covers whatever she’ll do. Personally, I’d guess that she will act as a figure for people to rally around. She’s already proven capable of galvanising people to action before eliminating Jack Slash; with three years more work, people will listen to her when she calls for action.”

“Good. A possible leader unaffiliated with Cauldron could be a useful backup in case people aren’t willing to listen to us.” Number Man sighed. “People can be so distracted by morality even when their lives are on the line.”

“True,” Doctor Mother said. “Let’s move forward. Eidolon said he was testing a theory in the containment cells- did he give you any details, Rebecca?”

Rebecca shook her head. “No, but he seemed very excited. He said that he’d been thinking about what Glaistig Uaine said and came up with an idea. He wouldn’t elaborate when pressed.”

“We’ll just have to see what he’s achieved when he’s done,” Doctor Mother said. “Number man, how is our newest member?”

“Not well, I’m afraid. Even with me introducing myself as a, ah, friend of the family, she’s distraught over her loss. I think Contessa should speak to her.”

“Yes,” said Contessa. “Door to Riley.”

A portal opened beside her, and she walked through without a word. Doctor Mother glimpsed the sealed biological containment cell before the portal closed.

“That should be dealt with soon,” Doctor Mother noted. “We should begin acquiring materials for her to work with.”

“Easily done,” Rebecca said. “I was also wondering about her research notes. Do we let Dragon catch them, or allow them to be released to the general public?”

“Releasing them would cause disruption,” Number Man said. “it would be like catnip to every Biotinker on the planet.”

“The loss of the Nine and Elpis’ rising star should act as a counterbalance,” Doctor Mother said. “And it would provide a way for us to stir up trouble where necessary. We can release something into a specific area and claim that it’s the work of a Biotinker.”

“I say we do it,” Rebecca said. “We might be able to fold them into the Nemesis program as well.”

“A good point,” Doctor Mother agreed.

 

 

Later that day, a large cache of files that had been stored on a hidden server finally hit the countdown that had been running since the last time it had been accessed. The deadman switch activated, and the files were uploaded to multiple sites across the internet, both public and deep web, with inappropriately cheerful announcements.

Many of those sites removed the files as soon as they could, although the files had been uploaded with countermeasures to prevent that. Many people who saw the announcements started reading through the files out of morbid curiosity. Most immediately backed out on seeing what they contained. Some downloaded copies for various reasons. And a few sent copies off to others, for shock value or intellectual curiosity or because they thought the information could be useful.

And like the viruses that she had often engineered, Bonesaw’s accumulated research on parahuman studies, biotinkering, and the nature of powers themselves, spread across the internet, replicating and travelling.

And in some cases, it found a place where it could do serious damage.

 

 

Geoffrey Pellick, known to the rest of the world as Saint, leader of the mercenary and hacker group The Dragonslayers, stared at the wall of complex code on his screen. He knew how to interpret it and understand it, but he’d never seen anything like this before.

It disgusted him, on a visceral level. But Saint was a driven man, fuelled by the goal of keeping humanity safe from an extreme threat, and he was willing to seize an opportunity when it presented itself.

“Guys?” he called to his teammates, not looking away from the code as he hastily copied and saved the files, storing them on multiple backup drives. “I think I found something.”

Chapter 138: 14.4

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Thursday 9th June, The Lair, The Docks

“How are you feeling?”

Amy barely turned at my question. “Not great. Bad dreams.”

I winced sympathetically. “Can I get you anything? I was going to grab a drink.” Coffee and a doughnut, since it was Bearskin’s turn to pick.

Amy pulled the blanket around herself a little tighter. “No.”

“Oh boy,” Quarrel said. “Looks like she needs another heart to heart.”

I agreed even as I popped into the kitchen to pour myself a mug and grab a glazed doughnut, before sitting down on the couch by Amy, just far away enough to give her space.

I’d had half the coffee and the last bite of the cruller when Amy finally spoke. “I dreamed the world was ending.”

That last bite of cruller was suddenly so much harder to swallow. “Christ, what a way to start a conversation,” Dirty Rotter muttered.

“There were bodies everywhere, and body parts… They were so messed up I couldn’t tell where one ended and another began. And I couldn’t do anything. I was just standing there.” She pulled her gloved hands out of the blanket and rubbed at her face.

“That sounds horrible,” I said.

Amy dropped her hands into her lap. “Yeah.”

I didn’t want to make her talk more than she was ready for, so I just sipped the coffee while Amy stared down at her hands. Finally she said, “I think I need to see my therapist again.”

“Okay,” I said, setting my mug down. “We can get you there.” I wished we still had the Chariot, but since Squealer and the Teeth had apparently stolen the damn thing from Weymouth Mall, we’d have to settle for one of Rachel’s dogs-

“I mean… I mean I need to keep seeing Dr Reese. I feel better here; it’s quiet and safe, and nobody’s pushing me to get back to healing. But I can’t just wait for my problems to get better on their own.” She snorted. “I tried that before and it didn’t fucking work. I have to get better. And I need to do it fast.”

“Hey, you don’t have to rush it,” I said. “We have time-”

“We have three years,” Amy interrupted. “Taylor, I’m the most powerful healer on the planet. I can’t afford to sit around; we can’t afford to sit around.”

I halted. As much as I wanted to tell Amy that she should take things slow and get better at her own pace, there was a ruthlessly pragmatic part of me that agreed with her. The number of capes Amy had healed over the years; how many of them might be critical to preventing the apocalypse? And how many more could she heal with the PRT helping her- their resources, their connections?

I still wanted her to stay. I wanted to pause the world right here, curled up on the couch with my girlfriend with nothing to do right now. I wanted to help Amy finish putting her room together, and cook her dinner, and wish her good night.

But this wasn’t about what I wanted.

“She’ll come back,” Needler said reassuringly.

I swallowed heavily. “Okay. What can I do to help?”

Amy slumped a little, letting out a breath. “I need to pack my things. And I should probably call ahead.”

 

 

Even with me double-checking everything, and the rest of the team saying their goodbyes and offers of support to Amy, and Dad driving us over to the PRT building, it still felt like only a minute before we were sitting in Dad’s truck, parked about a block away. I had the entire area monitored with bugs, and groups of the nastiest bugs positioned along Amy’s path just in case anyone was stupid enough to try anything.

“You’re sure you’ve got everything?” I asked.

“Yeah.” Amy patted the little bag I’d found for her to put her stuff in. It was mostly clothes that the girls and I had loaned her to wear while she stayed with us, plus her costume.

“Okay.” I tried to think of something else to say- something supportive, but not sounding like I wanted her to stay. I did want her to stay, but not in a possessive way- just that I’d miss her.

Amy laid a gloved hand on mine, and words failed me. “I’ll call you,” she said, leaning over and giving me a quick hug.

“Right,” I managed, breathing in her scent.

Amy smiled briefly. Then she unbuckled her seatbelt, slipped out of the truck, and walked out of the alleyway Dad had parked in and towards the PRT building.

I tracked her with a few bugs I’d slipped onto the backs of her shoes, and with the thick clouds that lurked out of sight around every corner, making sure nothing and nobody could threaten her. There really was nothing- perhaps the remaining villains really weren’t stupid enough to go after Amy.

Amy made it to the double doors, and the troopers standing guard welcomed her as they rolled open. Amy put one foot over the threshold, then stopped and glanced back.

Struck by sudden impulse, I sifted through the bugs in my range, setting aside all the stinging and biting things I’d assembled for combat, and bringing up the insects I’d dismissed. They converged on the doors with fluttering wings- butterflies mostly, but also moths, dragonflies, and fireflies flashing with light. They formed into a thick cloud a few feet away from Amy, swirling and spiralling like a sea of wings.

Amy held a hand out, and I made a single butterfly land on her fingertip. Amy brought it up to her face and looked at it for a long moment. “See you soon,” she whispered.

Then she put her arm out again, and the butterfly took off, joining the rest as they dispersed back to where I’d found them. Amy turned and walked into the PRT building, and the doors shut behind her.

I let out a sigh and slumped into my seat.

“She’ll be alright,” Stoneknapper said bracingly.

“And she’ll be back before you know it,” Tock Tick added.

“Yeah,” Anchorage said, gesturing to me. “How can she resist all this?”

I snorted, but I appreciated the gesture.

“All set?” Dad asked from the driver’s seat.

“Yeah,” I said after a moment. “We should get back.” I sat up straight. “We’ve got work to do.”

 

 

Monday 13th June, The Lair, The Docks

The armour was finished, and I looked damn good in it.

I’d melted down the plates and reforged them with fresh metal, making them thicker and heavier. At the same time, I’d stripped out the internal framework I’d used to make it look bulkier, so that it would pass for a Tinker’s power armour. The end result was that the armour rested on me like a thick jacket and moved without a single clank or clatter.

No more rust or scratches or dirt- no more crude spikes and rivet heads. The steel was a matte graphite grey instead of the polished silver, and the paint stripes were cobalt blue instead of sky blue. The amphora was on my chest in white, with a blue butterfly in the centre. The same symbol was on my cape, freshly woven and clipped to my back.

I hadn’t completely removed all the nastier stuff- blades were still hidden in spring-loaded sheathes on my arms and legs, and my knuckles were covered with thick studs that I could shape into spikes at a thought. Past that, my fingers were only lightly armoured, and only on the backs- better for precision. The little openings at the tips meant I could pop my claws out too. The jawguard on my helmet had a mandible design now.

And down the length of my right arm, from the shoulder to the back of my hand, were symbols rising out of the metal, highlighted by the paint. On the shoulder was the same butterfly on my chest and cape- below that was a bow and arrow, then a katana and wakizashi side by side. A lion’s pawprint, an anchor and chain, a crosshairs. A roaring bear’s head in profile, a hammer and chisel, a pair of interlocked gears. A cartoon bomb with a fizzing fuse, a pair of crossed daggers, a biohazard symbol. An exclamation mark in a triangle, a bat with its wings spread; and on the back of my hand, a shiny cleaver.

Melee weapons- check. Bow and arrows- check. Anti-Brute pistol- in a compartment under my armpit. Various knives and shuriken secreted around my person. My air cannon had been stripped down and compressed as far as I could get it, and attached to my left forearm- not nearly as deadly as my wrist guns, but still able to knock someone on their ass. A new grappler was hidden under the plate of my right forearm, beneath the symbols.

“You look wonderful,” Flinch said approvingly.

“You look like you could kiss a baby any second now,” Firecracker chimed in teasingly.

“Or help an old lady across the street,” Bearskin added with a chuckle.

I laughed a little, turning away from the mirror. “Glad you approve.” I did feel pretty heroic, even with the revelations of Cauldron weighing on me- not to mention some very scary tricks I’d been working on for the last week. I walked towards the rest of the Undersiders, who were finished with their own prep. Grue’s coat was cleaned and patched, Whirlygig’s pockets were full of ammo, Imp had her devilish mask and a belt full of tricks; Tattletale’s goggles and crossbow were both polished and tweaked, Ironclad’s armour gleamed. Cerberus and her dogs stood ready, and the spear I’d made her shone with a razor edge.

“Alright,” I said with approval. “Let’s get out there.”

“About time,” Cerberus said, hauling herself up onto Brutus. The others climbed up onto Judas and Bentley, while Ironclad folded his wheels out of his armour and set them on the ground. I grasped Firecracker’s teleport and focused on a point up on the rooftops. The main doors opened with the twitch of an ant against a switch, and I set my feet.

“Undersiders, move out!” I called, leading the way out into the city. The dogs followed, Ironclad bringing up the rear.

With the Truce ending today, we’d coordinated with the PRT and New Wave. The Protectorate would resume patrols throughout the city, New Wave assisting in pairs. Once we’d secured Weymouth Mall and made sure that the villains weren’t going to target it, we’d join them.

Much as I’d wanted to launch a strike against the Empire or Bakuda, and several of the Butchers had agreed with the idea, Tactical and Armsmaster had talked me down. The gangs had had a week to rest, recover and rearm- there were even unconfirmed reports that the Empire had a new cape. Even with Lung timelocked and Othala still in custody being deprogrammed, they’d be ready. If we committed to attacking one, we’d be leaving ourselves open for an attack from the other. It was the constant problem of heroes- while villains were active, they had to be reactive, and the heroes couldn’t be everywhere at once. Villains could choose the time and the place, and the heroes were constantly playing catch up.

I needed to change that. We had three years to build up the resources and connections to try and stop whatever was coming for us, and having villains messing with that wasn’t going to help anyone. To address that, I needed a solid base to work from- so I needed to make Brockton Bay a place where I wasn’t having to constantly deal with the gangs’ bullshit.

First, Weymouth Mall. People were glad to see us, many of them cheering for us. I weathered it politely, shaking a few hands and patting a few eager kids on the head while I checked- supplies were doing well, the water filter was working fine, reconstruction was actually ahead of schedule; volunteers were helping to speed up the process during the Truce, and more were clearing abandoned buildings, marking places that had been emptied of supplies or were too dangerous to stay in. A lot of those buildings were marked with an amphora symbol, I noticed.

“Marking territory,” Butcher noted as I finished up with the managers. “We can probably have this whole city marked up by the end of the month.”

“It’s a nice idea,” I said. “Might take a little longer than that.”

“I say we take out the Empire first,” Vladimir interjected. “Now that we’ve got your bugs and Quarrel’s aim, we can just take them out at range. Night and Fog might be a little difficult, but the rest are squishy.”

“Also a nice idea.” I thanked the managers and headed for the front, politely stepping around people as I went. A few kids held up chunks of wood or rocks, or half a brick for one gap-toothed little boy. I obligingly shaped each one into something with Stoneknapper’s fizz- a lion, a horse, and a narwhal for the half-brick kid.

“I like that boy’s style,” Tactical commented as I made it out of the doors.

“Mmm.” The Undersiders were waiting for me outside. Ironclad would stay behind on guard- I’d managed to talk to his parents in costume and convince them to let him stay in the Undersiders instead of trying to force him to stay home or join the Wards, but they’d insisted that I try to keep him safe. He was okay with it- with Crusader, Kaiser and Fog in the Empire’s lineup, he’d be a bad matchup right now.

The rest straightened up as I approached- except for Whirlygig. She was staring through the doors at the people inside.

“Whirl?” I asked. She shook herself and looked at me.

“Sorry boss. I’m here.”

“Something on your mind?”

Whirlygig looked at me for a moment, then back at the mall. “All those people… All the little kids… It just hit me all of a sudden. Three years- most of those kids won’t even be in high school.”

“Oof,” Quarrel winced.

“We won’t let that happen,” Nemean said at once.

I laid a hand on Whirlygig’s shoulder. “We’re going to fight it. We’re going to build Brockton Bay into a fortress, and we’re going to find whatever causes the shit in three years, and we’re going to stop it.”

“…It’s scary,” Whirlygig admitted.

“I know. I’m scared too,” I said honestly. “But we’re going to get through it together.”

Whirlygig managed a nod. “Okay.”

“Right. Now let’s go kick some ass, huh?”

“That sounds really good right now.”

 

 

The next step was to check Dolltown, since Parian was still defending her little community all on her own. I’d planned to hand it off to Tattletale, but she’d convinced me that I should try and mend bridges with Parian. I wasn’t exactly eager to do it, but it needed doing.

“Do the butterfly trick again,” Muramasa suggested. “It will help to show you mean no harm.”

“It’s not just me she’s afraid of,” I pointed out as I jogged and teleported along back towards the Boardwalk. “It’s being targeted by the Empire, the ABB- not to mention the reputation from you guys.”

“Yeah, knowing there’s ghosts ogling you puts a lot of people off,” Stoneknapper admitted.

“Not always,” Rotter chuckled. “Remember that one goth girl? With the scorpion tattoo?”

The Butchers laughed and started reminiscing about their various conquests over the years, both individually and as a collective, while I moved onward. The streets below were looking better- most of the major debris from Leviathan had been cleared, even if there were still buildings that would need tearing down and holes that needed to be filled. Things got better closer to the Boardwalk- glass was already being replaced in some buildings. I’d have to offer to fix some stuff while I was here- Stoneknapper’s power would make it a snap-

Something caught my eye, rising into the air above the buildings. A thin stream of smoke, in the direction of Dolltown.

I broke into a sprint, jumping the small gaps to keep the teleport for the big movements. My mind was filled with horrible images- Parian’s shop, with its reams and reams of flammable fabric… I speed-dialled the PRT with the headset in my helmet, passing on a message as I sprinted across rooftops.

My bugs caught sight of the scene before I did- piles of burning fabric were crumpled in the street in front of Dolltown’s main entrance. A cartoonish dinosaur made of blue and black fabric was charging forward, even as flames licked at it, trying to get to the attackers before it fell apart. Parian stood at the border of Dolltown, desperately weaving spare scraps of fabric together, salvaging what was left of the burnt fabric. The people in Dolltown were pulling out extra clothes for her to use, towels and curtains- I saw one old man pulling his sweater off and tossing it to Parian. Smoke was streaming from some windows, and a few of the people were obviously hurt.

The dinosaur charged towards the main threat- a seven-foot tall thing made of orange and yellow flames. A massive flaming fist slammed into the dinosaur’s face, and then both hands grabbed it, forcing fire down its throat. The dinosaur struggled for a bit more, but the flames ate away at it from the inside out, and it crumpled to the ground. The fire monster tossed it aside dismissively.

I almost didn’t spot the other two standing behind the fire monster. I recognised Crusader at a glance with his armour and spear, but the other one was new- a woman, I thought, in Nordic style armour; breastplate, armoured skirt, helmet, and a thick cloak trimmed with fur. There was a hatchet on her belt, but her real weapon seemed to be the waves of cold mist that poured down off her, out of her skirt, and spread out across the ground. It parted around Crusader and the fire monster while it advanced on Dolltown- the bugs that touched it felt cold and lethargic at once. The dozen Crusader ghosts standing around didn’t seem affected.

“It’s a good day for dead Nazis!” Anchorage whooped as I focused my next teleport on the ground between Parian and the Empire, and appeared in a burst of flame that scorched the ground and drove back the mist. Extending the claws on my toes triggered compartments on my shins, firing twin metal rods up to shoulder height. I snatched them out of the air and flicked both of my shock batons out to full length, the tips crackling with electricity.

Shouts of shock from the civilians behind me, quiet curses from the villains in front of me. I saw the fire monster take a step back in fear. Off to a good start.

“You clowns just couldn’t wait to start hurting people again, huh?” I called out, drawing insects in. I kept them above the cold mist, drawing out lines of silk. The fire monster would just burn through them, but Crusader and the mist woman would be vulnerable. “I’d have thought you’d have better things to do, Crusader. Did you forget about the Mannequin money?”

Crusader snorted. “The money will be good for the cause,” he said. “But punishing race traitors is something I’ll do for free. Since dolly here,” he gestured behind me with his spear, “Is happy to refuse our offers and protect this bunch of camel fuckers instead of helping her own kind, I thought the newest members of the Empire could cut their teeth on her.”

I focused a group of bugs behind me. “Huh. Middle Eastern to a man,” Needler said.

“Well, points to Parian for looking after them,” Flinch said. “It’s not easy being brown in this town.”

“It’s about to get easier,” Bearskin growled, glaring at the villains.

“And who are these latest members of the Inbred Eighty Eight?” I jeered. “Dumpster Fire and Icy Queef?”

“Silence,” the fire monster rumbled. “I am Musphelheim, and my fires shall burn away the impure.” Nothing showed on bloodsight- he was all fire. Harder to fight, but not impossible.

“I am Niflheim, and my mist shall freeze your bones,” called the woman in a twangy voice.

“Two whole new kinds of hell for you, Butcher,” Crusader said.

“Shame you didn’t bring Jotun along, you could have had three of the Nine Realms,” I said, flipping the batons around in my hands and flicking them the other way. They redeployed tipped with spear heads, and I connected them together at the handles to form a single double-ended spear. “But since unworthy deaths send people to Helheim, I’d say you’ve got more to worry about.”

A couple of bugs on my shoulders undid the catches on my cape, letting it tumble to the ground. “Parian, keep your people safe,” I said in a low voice. “I’ll handle these guys. Reinforcements are coming.”

“I don’t have much fabric left,” Parian whispered.

“Just do what you can,” I said. “Get ready. Three, two-”

I aimed the teleport directly over Crusader’s head and blinked over, aiming the spear down. A ghost burst out of him as I dropped, and I landed on its shoulders while Crusader dodged, more ghosts coming off him. I kicked the ghost I was standing on in the head with clawed feet, popping it and falling to the ground; then I hit Niflheim with a blast of pain while I fired my air cannon at Crusader.

Niflheim dropped like a puppet with the strings cut; Crusader staggered, but was caught by his ghosts. I sent swarms of insects after Crusader with silk lines while I lunged with my spear at Niflheim, knocking the hatchet from her grip and then jabbing at her armpit. Electricity crackled, and she thrashed as the shock rendered her senseless.

“Get off her!” Musphelheim was charging towards me, coming to help his teammates. I threw the spear at him and fired my grappler at Crusader, Quarrel’s power guiding it to hit his breastplate and latch on. A hard pull yanked him off his feet, and I hauled him in hand over hand as he split off more ghosts to try and pull him backward.

The spear went right through Musphelheim without hurting him, planting in the asphalt as he kept coming.

“Weird,” Firecracker said. “He touched the dinosaur earlier. Is it by choice, or can he only handle flammable stuff?”

“Let’s find out,” I said, dropping down to grab Niflheim by the scruff of the neck and tossing her at Musphelheim like a sack of potatoes.

“Shit!” Musphelheim’s flames disappeared in an instant, turning back into a man in similar armour, but with a cloak patterned in red and orange flames. He stuck his arms out to try and catch Niflheim, but her weight simply knocked him on his ass.

I stepped forward, Bearskin’s clouds of rage pouring off me. Before Musphelheim could think to set her aside and transform again, the rage reached him, and he threw himself at me to attack with fists and feet. I stamped on his foot to pin him, then punched him in the side, the armpit and the head- all weak points highlighted by Needler’s power. He went over like a tree.

That just left Crusader, who had more ghosts splitting off to pull him by the legs as he tried to saw through the grappler cable with the blade of his spear. I released the grappler, letting him shoot backwards and belly-flop to the asphalt, and sprinted forward to finish him off. The two ghosts who got to me first received claws to the throat that popped them immediately, but Crusader got a palm strike to the side of his head as he tried to get up. He crumpled, and the ghosts all disappeared as well.

“Good job,” Tock Tick said. “Nice and clean.”

Butcher snorted. “I don’t know what these fuckers expected.”

I grabbed Crusader and his spear and dragged him over to the other two. A moment’s search stripped them of weapons, phones, and anything they might use to escape, before I tied them all hands and feet, and then to each other. After that, a quick call to the PRT to confirm that the villains were handled, and a call to Tattletale asking her to swing by to see if she could pry any secrets out of them. She was  eager to try.

“Hey, since we beat Crusader, does that mean we get the bounty money for Mannequin now?” Dirty Rotter asked.

“I don’t think it works like that,” I admitted as I noticed Parian approaching. She’d cobbled a puppet together out of the remains of the others, dripping with water and extinguisher powder. It held my cape in one hand as a shield. Some of the Dolltown civilians followed a few feet behind her. I rearranged my bugs, setting some stingers on the villains for insurance while bringing out the pretty ones to flutter around me.

“Is it over?” Parian asked, looking down at the villains.

“Disarmed and seeing stars,” I said. “How are your people?”

“We’ve got the fires out at least, but there’s burns, and we definitely lost a lot of our things…” Parian put her head in her hands. “Why couldn’t they just leave me alone?”

“I’m sorry, Parian,” I said honestly. “I can help fix things up a bit while I’m here, if you like.”

Parian brought her hands together, twisting the fingers around each other. “Can I think about it?” she said eventually, in an uncertain tone of voice.

“Of course.”

There was a groan, and then Niflheim stirred weakly. “Aw fuck,” she groaned.

“I hope that hurts,” Parian spat, angrier than I’d ever heard her. “You come to my home, you attack my- my people, and for what?”

“Fucking sand niggers and towel heads,” Niflheim slurred her slurs. “You picked them over us… You coulda been like us…”

“I’m not like you!” Parian yelled. “I’m nothing like you, I will never be anything like you! It’s this stupid-!”

Her gloved hands went to her mask and yanked. “Habibti,” said an older woman behind her in alarm, reaching out as Parian pulled her china doll mask off and smashed it on the ground. A moment later she pulled the mass of golden curls off her head and threw that away too.

Parian’s real face was dark skinned, Middle Eastern. She had full lips and big dark eyes- very pretty, even as her expression twisted her features with rage. Bands of metal extended from a hoop around the edge of her face to the middle of her cheekbones, her forehead and her chin- probably mounts to help keep the mask on. She pulled that off too, and threw it aside with a huff. She pulled some pins out of her hair bun, and the whole thing uncoiled into a long, glossy sheet of black hair.

“My name,” Parian snarled, “Is Sabah Basrawi. I’m Iraqi, I’m an immigrant, and I’m a lesbian. You people threatened my business, you attacked my family and my friends, you damaged my home- I am done! I’m not taking this anymore!”

Parian’s- Sabah’s family gathered around her, a few patting her shoulders reassuringly. The woman who’d called out drew her into a hug. I could see a resemblance between them; Habibti meant “My darling” or “My love” in Arabic.

“Well,” Quarrel said, “That’s one question answered, I guess.”

Vladimir burst out laughing. “Hahahaha holy shit! Oh god, I wish we could see Kaiser’s face when he hears about this!”

“Ah crap,” Tactical cursed, even as he chuckled along with Vladimir. “The Empire’s probably going to go even harder on her now.”

“Not if we hit them first. They just lost three of their capes,” I pointed out, smirking a little inside my helmet.

“If Crusader was the only one who could handle the bounty from Mannequin, then they just lost their meal ticket,” Nemean noted with a wicked grin.

“Even better!” Stoneknapper crowed, laughing along with the others.

Niflheim stared blearily at Parian and her family. “Fuck,” she said succinctly.

I cleared my throat carefully. Several of Parian’s family gave me fearful looks when they realised I was still here. “So, Sabah. That’s a pretty name.”

Parian sighed. “I disguised myself to keep myself safe. I was going to unmask myself later, spark discussion about assumptions of capes and their identities. I never expected them,” she gestured to the villains.

“I’m sorry you had to go through all that. I know we’re not really close right now, but if you need help, don’t hesitate to ask.”

“Well, if they’re coming to destroy my little territory, I think my neutrality is gone, whether I like it or not,” Parian admitted. “We could definitely use the help.” Her puppet stepped forward, holding out my cape. I took it gently and clipped it to my back again.

After a bit more talk, and me sealing the villains in asphalt up to their knees to make absolutely sure they couldn’t run off, Parian and her family agreed to let me in to help clear up. Mostly that meant hauling out burnt furniture, but there was also enough broken glass gathered up for me to meld it all together and replace more than half of the windows, which earned me some goodwill. With my cloak of butterflies and what bits of Arabic I had from Needler’s memories, after half an hour I had little kids trying to climb my cape, a few men asking me what I remembered of the old days of Brockton Bay, and Parian’s aunt plying me with little date cookies called kleicha. Parian herself kept a little distance, but I noticed her smile once or twice.

“She’s pretty,” Dirty Rotter said out of nowhere.

“Oh, don’t you start,” I said tiredly as one of the kids showed me the cuddly rabbit Parian had made for them.

“I’m just saying,” Rotter said defensively.

“I mean, if Amy is into an open relationship-” Anchorage began.

“She did say she’s a lesbian-” Needler started.

I shoved all three of them down while I agreed that yes, that was a very cool bunny.

The PRT showed up with a wagon to transport the villains about ten minutes later, but I asked them to wait a few more minutes for Tattletale to arrive. Three minutes later, she bounded up with Cerberus and practically leapt off Bentley’s back to walk up to the villains with a big grin on her face. I stood by with the troopers, spear in hand at maximum charge. Crusader and Musphelheim were conscious again, if still woozy, but I’d shock them again if they so much as twitched.

“Well, well, well,” she purred. “Who do we have here? Hey Parian, liking the new look,” she added.

“Don’t tell me you already knew,” Parian said flatly.

Tattletale shrugged. “Honestly, I didn’t. You were staying out of everything, so I didn’t see a need. Guess that’ll show me, huh? But for the really interesting secrets,” she circled around the villains, “Let’s find out what you know.”

“You’ll get nothing from us,” Musphelheim grunted.

“Oh, I will,” Tattletale purred. “I can already tell by you naming yourselves after entire mythical worlds that you’re eager for recognition. You haven’t really met a lot of other capes, so you think you’re a lot better than you really are. That’s why you were so eager to come down to Brockton Bay when Kaiser called- you thought you could handle the city that survived Leviathan and ended the Nine. Hilarious.”

“Shut up,” Niflheim snapped.

“And then there’s Crusader- bounty money filling your pockets, and what did you do with it? Ahh, you didn’t give it all to the cause, huh? Saved yourself a little nest egg, probably because of that little tidbit Cherish dropped in her final moments.”

“What’re you talking about?” Musphelheim demanded.

“Oh, she said something about Kaiser not really believing in the values of the Empire,” Tattletale said airily. “Did nobody tell you? No, they didn’t, did they? But they’re all thinking about it, right Crusader? You were definitely thinking about it- and with that bounty money, if you weren’t satisfied with Kaiser’s leadership, you could afford to break off and form your own group, right?”

“What?!” Niflheim demanded, twisting to try and glare at Crusader.

“She’s lying,” Crusader insisted. He didn’t sound very convincing.

“Of course, I think Kaiser was one step ahead of you. That’s why he sent you on a very visible mission not too far from our territory. He knew Elpis could kick your ass and remove his troublesome subordinate- and with you in prison, he can drain all your hidden accounts and funnel that money to “the cause”, she said with air quotes. “By which he means his wallet.”

“He wouldn’t,” Crusader said, but I could tell he didn’t believe it.

“Ooh, you think he had a better reason for sending you off, that’s cute,” Tattletale cooed mockingly. “And what is that? Something personal- personal to him, but familiar to you. He’s looking to find…”

Tattletale trailed off, then straightened up. “Okay, load them up, we need to go.”

“Care to explain?” I asked as she started jogging back towards the dogs.

“This was just a distraction. Kaiser’s kid just went AWOL, and they’re hunting him down now,” Tattletale called over her shoulder. “Are you coming or what?”

Chapter End Notes

Don't worry, Amy is not gone from this story. Not even close. She just needs to get her head sorted.
The symbols down the arm are an idea I've had for years, and it's great to finally put it into words.
As for Musphelheim and Niflheim- they are very technically canon, in that their names are mentioned as part of the Empire roster when they move to Boston, but no powers or description. Basically blank slates.

Chapter 139: Interlude 14.T

Monday 13th June, The Towers, Downtown

Aster squirmed and fussed as Theo fastened the baby carrier to his chest. “It’s okay, Aster,” he said, gently lifting her up and into the carrier. Once she was properly nestled against his chest, she settled down, little hands grasping at the front of his shirt.

Theo pulled on his jacket next, then his backpack, and finally grabbed his suitcase. He’d packed everything he thought they’d need- clothes for the both of them, toiletries, baby food and bottles, various favourite possessions and knick-knacks, and as much money and valuables as he could find. Even the pockets of his jacket and cargo pants were heavy. He felt like a thief, taking the jewellery that had belonged to his mother and step-mother, but he told himself it was for a good cause. Maybe Aster would want it when she got older, or if things got desperate, they could sell them.

If things got more desperate, he corrected himself. He was running away from home, after all.

After Kayden’s death, the defeat of the Nine, and the Butcher achieving global fame overnight, Father had been more difficult to live with than ever. The Empire was low on capes and high on enemies. Theo had done his best to avoid Father, making excuses about taking care of Aster, which drew the usual cold stares and remarks from Father about his only son being better as a babysitter than an heir.

Unfortunately, that wasn’t enough. Crusader had visited out of costume, as Justin, and had talked with Father in his study for a long while. When they’d finished, Father had looked pleased, but Theo could see the tell-tale vein throbbing in his forehead indicating concealed anger.

Justin had made an excuse of grabbing a drink before he left to corner Theo in the kitchen. There, he’d told Theo something unbelievable- that the Slaughterhouse Nine’s newest member, Cherish, had revealed in her last moments that Kaiser didn’t believe in the Empire’s doctrine. And he’d asked if Theo thought that was true.

Theo had denied it at once- he’d spent his whole life listening to his father’s comments about the filth polluting the city, about homosexuals and blacks and Asians corroding White America. Surely it was just a desperate attempt by a lunatic to save her own hide.

Justin hadn’t looked fully convinced, but he’d thanked Theo and made his way out. Father had stayed in his office making calls, which had given Theo time to think. Crusader had been part of the Empire for years, and had followed Kaiser faithfully, even if Theo had wondered about him getting closer to Purity while she and Kaiser were separated. If he was asking about Kaiser’s ideals now, then the seed had already been planted.

The Empire’s followers didn’t really need facts or evidence to build their views- that was just a bonus. What they went on was emotions and gut feelings. So if one of Kaiser’s capes was now questioning his leadership, others would follow.

That meant a few options, none of them good. Either Kaiser would perform some great deed to reaffirm his commitment to the Empire’s doctrine, or he’d purge the naysayers and threaten the rest into compliance, or the doubters would move faster and there’d be a war for control of the Empire.

Theo didn’t intend to wait around to find out what would happen and get caught up in it. Kayden had been the one person in the Empire who’d really shown him any kindness, distant and awkward as it was. With her gone, it was time for him to leave as well.

The elevator was still not working, so Theo had to take the stairs. Not for the first time he regretted that Father insisted on a penthouse apartment. He was breathing heavily within a few flights. Theo had always been large- another thing for his father to be disappointed in, to be unlike the athletic Max Anders.

He made it down to street level and looked around carefully. Father hadn’t replaced the doorman after Jack Slash had murdered the last one, so the lobby was clear. There was still the possibility that Father had someone watching the cameras. If that was true, then as soon as he stepped out the door, he’d be on a time limit.

He could go back. He hadn’t crossed the line yet. He could just go back and pretend everything was normal, put Aster back in her crib and weather the storm. Assuming that the Empire didn’t fall apart around him. Assuming Father didn’t get worse. Assuming that Kaiser didn’t find out about what had happened to him and make him join and fight and kill…

Theo shook himself, took a deep breath, and stroked Aster’s little head one more time. His sister cooed happily, bringing a faint smile to Theo’s lips.

“Okay,” he said to Aster and to himself. “Here we go.”

He walked across the lobby, feet ringing on the marble, and out the door. He forced himself not to run. If he didn’t look like he was in a hurry, people wouldn’t think he was escaping. And he’d need to save his breath for if he really needed to run.

The streets were fuller than they had been since Leviathan had hit- people were talking, eating, laughing and smiling. With the Slaughterhouse Nine dead, the Teeth decimated, and Lung frozen in time, the villain population of Brockton Bay was at its lowest in years.

“I’m just glad Purity’s dead,” Theo heard someone say. “Fucking bitch.”

Theo flinched at that. Kayden hadn’t been a bad step-mother to him. But, he had to admit, she hadn’t been a good person outside of that. Even when she’d left the Empire for a time, she’d only targeted minorities for her idea of justice She’d hurt plenty of people. It was expected that some people would be glad to see the end of her.

Telling himself that didn’t make his heart hurt any less, but it let him keep going.

There was a shelter about halfway between The PRT building and the Undersiders’ territory. He couldn’t go to the PRT as the son of Kaiser and Heith, and he certainly couldn’t go to the Butcher. But they were the safest territories around for him to hide in, as long as he wasn’t recognised. If he kept his head down, he could wait out the worst of it and then buy a bus ticket to leave town.

He’d have to join a group at some point- he needed some way to support himself and take care of Aster. Better to do it somewhere people didn’t have personal grudges against the Empire. Boston, or maybe New York. They were tolerant cities, or so Father had occasionally disparaged them as such.

He was most of the way there when he saw something off in the distance- a thin plume of smoke. It might be nothing- people had been lighting bonfires for weeks, to stay warm or to celebrate Jack Slash’s death. He quickened his pace a little regardless, absently stroking Aster’s head again.

It was a few minutes later when he felt as much as heard something, and looked back. Nothing on the street- but up in the sky, something was closing in.

Theo turned back around, strangling the urge to sprint. His best bet was to avoid drawing attention. He kept walking, as casually as he could, and took the next right, then ducked into an alleyway and waited for a few seconds before exiting in a different direction, zipping his jacket up around Aster to hide her. Keep walking, head down, hands in pockets-

A shout made him look up. The flying thing was a chunk of concrete, and there were people on it. There was a girl in a hooded black and red robe-Rune; a woman and man in black and grey cloaks- Night and Fog; a man in chainmail and a helmet with antlers- Jotun…

And in the centre of the platform, hands clasped behind his back, a man in elaborate armour, his helmet crowned with blades. Kaiser. Father.

Theo abandoned stealth, breaking into a run down another alleyway. He couldn’t beat Rune’s flight speed, but maybe he could lose them in cover. Aster whined against his chest, not liking the bouncing.

The platform swerved to follow him. Theo dodged down the narrow alleyways on one block, trying every door he passed- maybe he could duck into an empty building.

No such luck. This part of town hadn’t been so heavily damaged and looted. The doors were locked.

He kept running, turning at random and doubling back as much out of rising panic as strategy. His breath came in hard pants, his pulse pounded in his ears, the contents of his pockets thumped against him.

Something crashed down to one side as he turned down another alleyway. When he looked, a wall of ice was forming out of clear fragments, forming a barrier too high to jump and too slick to climb. Before Theo could turn back, a scraping noise came from behind him. Steel blades were emerging from the ground and walls, lacing together to form a grid of edges. If he tried to climb that, he’d lose fingers. A second grid was already emerging to the other side.

That left one way out- forward, into a sun-drenched little plaza behind an apartment building, surrounded by plant pots. The concrete platform was already landing at the other end, the passengers hopping off. Kaiser formed a small staircase with his power and disembarked with the self-possession of a king.

Theo swallowed heavily. Aster was fussing now, squirming and batting her little hands against his chest. He stroked her head again, thinking- then pulled his zipper down carefully, making sure none of her hair got close to the zipper. With his jacket hanging open, she was more visible. He tugged the kerchief around his neck up to cover his nose and mouth, then set down the bags and stepped out into the plaza, hands in his jacket pockets.

Kaiser brought his arms around from behind his back and crossed them in front of his chest. “Boy,” he said in a voice of simmering rage, “Explain yourself.”

What the hell could he say? There was no possible excuse he could give that would disarm Kaiser’s anger. Apologising had never worked, trying to act tough had never worked- he couldn’t say it wasn’t what it looked like.

Maybe Kaiser actually wanted to watch him stumble his way through an explanation, to mock him before issuing punishment. The thought cleared Theo’s head a little; that Kaiser’s disdain for him was not an end result, but a goal in itself. And Theo didn’t want to give him the satisfaction.

He took a deep breath and spoke clearly, enunciating every syllable. “I’m leaving.”

“What.” Kaiser’s arms unfolded, clenching at his sides. The other Empire members either stared at Theo, or glanced nervously at their leader.

“I said I’m leaving. And I’m taking Aster with me.”

“And where will you go, boy?” Kaiser demanded. “To the lessers? Will you throw yourself on the chinks’ mercy and hope they don’t cook your sister in front of you? Are you going to let the PRT put you in a cage?”

“The penthouse is pretty much a cage too. Locked in, only leaving with your permission.”

“Clearly I was too permissive,” Kaiser growled. “I think I’ll have Night and Fog take charge of your discipline from now on. Maybe that will teach you to show respect to your elders.”

Theo could tell that wasn’t an empty threat, and it made him feel weak at the knees. Every cape of the Empire Eighty Eight was violent as a matter of course, but Night and Fog scared him more than anyone else. They were products of Gesellschaft, the Empire’s European allies- created somehow, and brainwashed to be fanatically loyal to the cause. Their powers made them a nightmare in battle, and their eerily detached, composed, even enthusiastic personalities made them a nightmare everywhere else.

“You won’t,” Theo licked his lips, “You won’t try to take me here. You won’t risk Aster.”

“You won’t hurt her either,” Kaiser countered. “Night, Fog- take my daughter away from him. Then you may begin your instruction.”

Theo caught the horrified look on Rune’s face, and the grimace on Jotun’s as the couple advanced in lockstep. Night’s high heels clicked across the concrete paving slabs, as steady as a metronome.

Concrete then. Theo balled his hands into fists inside his jacket pockets, pressed them to the scavenged pieces of broken concrete he’d stashed there, and pushed as hard as he could. His hands sank into the cold cement like he was pushing them into a puddle.

The concrete in front of Night and Fog rippled with a glimmer of energy, like Kaiser’s powers produced. That was the only warning before two massive fists burst out of the concrete at the right angle to punch Night and Fog in their stomachs, sending them tumbling backward.

Theo extended the fingers of the fists and laced them together into a short wall, then dropped the connection. Through the slabs in his pockets, he could sense every other piece of concrete around him- smaller fists emerged from the concrete and grabbed Rune and Jotun by one ankle each, then set in place. Another push, and two more hands emerged to grab Night as she tried to sit up. There was no point in grabbing Fog- he’d just use his Changer form to escape easily. Theo would just have to hope he could outrun him.

Kaiser’s eyes were just visible inside his helmet, blown wide. “You triggered,” he rasped.

“Yes,” Theo said. One lonely night, after the death of Kayden, after Father had disparaged his weakness and fatness and cowardice for the thousandth time, and Theo had been left all alone in the penthouse yet again, and Aster had started wailing. He’d clutched the wall for support, and it had all come crashing down-

The only blessing he had was that he’d managed to draw back the first hands he’d made, and Father hadn’t noticed a thing.

“And you dare to strike at your own kind with it?” Kaiser demanded.

“I’m leaving,” Theo repeated. “That’s all. I don’t want to fight you.”

“You’ll have to,” Kaiser snarled, a blade forming out of the ground next to him, crossguard and hilt emerging at the top. Kaiser snatched the sword up in one hand and levelled it at Theo.

That was a distraction, Theo knew. His father didn’t bother with melee- his power let him skewer his opponents at a distance without lifting a finger. Kaiser wanted him to focus on the weapon and not his surroundings.

Fog was getting to his feet, dusting himself off and glancing at his wife, who seemed very accepting of her capture. Jotun was swearing and tugging at his leg without effect, but Rune simply crouched and traced a fingertip over the concrete fist. A second later it and the slab it had grown from ripped itself free from the ground, Rune balancing on it like a skateboard. Her platform behind them rose up, ready for use.

He kept his fingertips pressed against the concrete, ready for action. He hadn’t been able to sense Kaiser summoning that sword, but maybe Kaiser couldn’t sense his power activating either. He focused on his hearing instead, listening for that tell-tale scrape of blades.

At the edge of his hearing, he did hear something- a hissing rustle, growing louder…

Insects poured out of the plant pots, out of the neatly tended hedges, out of the little patches of grass, out of the alleyway behind him, and dropping out of the air. Theo felt his heart drop as bugs of every description filled the air. Oh no, he thought. Please, no…

The insects came together, piling themselves up into mounds that grew and grew, until they were the size of people, and rearranged themselves further into the shapes of people- heads, shoulders, chests, hips, even a suggestion of legs. Fireflies glowed in their faces, a crude imitation of eyes. Rune shrieked, Jotun swore.

Then the insects buzzed, clicked and hummed, again and again, stretching out the sound and mixing it together. Theo’s knees went weak as the sound sharpened into something recognisable.

“Tzz-tnn. Tezz-tenn. Tezz-tinn-guh. Tezting. Ahh, found it.”

“Butcher,” Kaiser rasped, bringing the sword up in a guard like he actually meant to use it.

“Butchers, plural,” The figures buzzed and hissed. “Good, isn’t it? Took a lot of practice to pull it off. Now all of us can have a say. How’s it going, Bucket Head?”

Blades spiked out of the ground, stabbing into the concrete hands holding the others down. Jotun ripped his hands free and formed axes of ice in his hands, while Night hopped to her feet at once.

“Family squabble, huh?” One of the figures on the left said, turning its ‘head’ to look at Theo. “And you must be Junior. And Junior the second,” it added, its firefly eyes glancing down at Aster, who was wiggling, apparently not liking the noise. Theo took a step back, one hand instinctively coming up to shield her.

“Easy, Rotter,” said a figure near the other end of the line. “Don’t worry kid, we’re not going to hurt you.” A couple of butterflies emerged from the cloud and flitted over towards Theo, circling around over Aster’s head. She cooed as she saw them, chubby little hands reaching up to bat at them.

“We’ve got no problem hurting you though, Kaiser,” said a bulky one in the middle. “And your cronies. Elpis already flattened your other goons.”

“You killed the Heims?” Jotun said, aghast.

“Don’t be stupid,” said the next one across, which was shorter than most of the rest. “She’s got standards. Odds are they’ll be pissing blood for a while though.”

“Face me, Butcher,” Kaiser demanded, a blade shooting up through the bug figure that had just spoken. “Or are you too much of a coward?”

“Why would we fight your way?” asked the stabbed one, reforming around the blade.

“You know us,” said the sixth from the left with what might have been meant to be a cheerful tone. “Fighting fair’s for morons.”

“I know how low you sink,” Kaiser snarled. “I live with the memory every day.”

Mother. Theo had never really known her- she’d died when he was small, in a scuffle with the Teeth. The Butcher had struck the fatal blow and left her to bleed out.

“That was an accident,” the fifth figure said, turning towards Theo. “Truly, it was.”

Theo said nothing. He had no idea what to say.

“Boy,” Kaiser snarled. “Get over here, help fight, and maybe I’ll be generous enough to forgive your transgressions.”

A supposedly peaceful Butcher or a supposedly forgiving Kaiser? Both sounded like lies, both would cost him and Aster dearly. The Undersiders didn’t openly operate like the Teeth, but who knew what they were doing behind closed doors? On the other hand, he had a pretty good idea what the Empire did behind closed doors. The devil he knew, the devil he didn’t…

“Boy!” Kaiser barked. “Come here, now!”

“Stop calling me boy,” Theo managed, sticking both hands back in his pockets, touching the concrete again. Aster started to whimper.

“What should we call you then?” asked one of the Butchers. The third from the left.

Theo had thought about that. About the hate he’d been fed since childhood, expected to swallow and regurgitate. The ideals of the Empire, and how he wanted to reject that. About things of clay and stone, made to protect the innocent from persecution.

Time to make a choice. He took a deep breath, and enunciated clearly. “Golem.”

“…what?” Kaiser didn’t even sound angry, just utterly confused.

“Oh my fucking god,” Rune said, staring at Theo.

The bug Butchers buzzed even louder, crackling with rhythmic pulses of activity. It took Theo a second to realise they were laughing, their figures wavering as they doubled up or clutched their sides or threw their hands up, pantomiming hilarity.

“HAHAHAHAHAHA! OH MY FUCKING GOD! YES! THAT’S PERFECT!” The Butcher at the very left, the start of the line, motioned like it was slapping its knee. “Ah fuck, I like you, kid! You just made my day! Golem! Ha!”

“You worthless little shit!” Kaiser howled. “You dare-”

A steel arrow whipped through the air and slammed into the concrete slab at Kaiser’s feet. He stumbled back with a shriek, swinging the sword around.

“Go, we’ll cover you,” said one of the Butchers as they all dissolved into a thick screen of bugs between him and the Empire.

Theo picked a direction and ran, jabbing his hands into the concrete as he ran, forming large hands as a shield wall in case of a loose shot. He could hear the Empire’s shouting as the bugs assaulted them from all angles, a smash and crackle as Jotun’s ice broke and spread, and an explosion. Metallic clangs and pained yells followed a second later. Aster was wailing now, beating her tiny hands against his chest. He couldn’t stop to comfort her, even as it tore at his heart.

The insects followed him, but they kept a distance, and they left the way ahead clear for him to see. Theo burst out of the alley and into an open street.

Two massive creatures stood there, and two girls. He recognised Tattletale in the purple and black, and Cerberus in the brown and bronze. Tattletale grinned like she’d just heard a good joke, while Cerberus, whose helmet was tucked under her arm, merely scowled at him.

“Hiya,” Tattletale said cheerfully.

Theo stuck his hand in his pants pocket, pressing his fingers to the chunk of asphalt hidden there. The other hand came up to gently stroke Aster’s head as she cried and wriggled.

“Woah, easy,” Tattletale said, her grin shrinking slightly. “Not here to hurt you kid. Trust me, we both get it.” She indicated herself and Cerberus with a gesture. “Running away from shitty families is how we both got started.”
