Whatever reason Saint had to pursue her over the years, however he’d managed to disable her systems and make off with her technology time after time, and however much he’d frightened her, she hadn’t wanted him dead.

And yet, Geoff Pellick, AKA Saint of the Dragonslayers, the only known Tinker 0 in the world, was dead. A suicide pill hidden in a pouch in his suit, swallowed when he’d been transferred to a holding cell, and Saint had been dead before they could get a medical team in to treat him.

It sickened her, that Saint had taken his own life. And yet, she felt relieved, that the man who’d hounded her for so long was no longer a threat. But beyond that, she also felt a sense of dread, that Saint could have been so fanatical as to commit suicide than risk spilling secrets in an interrogation.

Had he known about her true nature? Was that why he had such a vendetta against him? Had he viewed her as her father did- only by her potential for destruction and not as a person? But how could he have known that?

“No sign of the other Dragonslayers, yet,” Colin said, sitting back in his chair. “They’ve already got analysts looking through traffic cameras; I’m thinking I could devise an algorithm to look for Saint’s face and mark any known associates, see if we can find out what the other two look like under the masks. It should make it a lot easier to track them down.”

Dragon felt a rush of affection for the man. She’d always feared telling someone the truth of her nature, including Colin, even if she’d thought for years that he might be her best option for ever obtaining her freedom. But after the Battle of the Birdcage, she’d finally summoned up the nerve to reveal herself to him.

Colin had sat silently as she explained that she wasn’t a human woman kept isolated by deep-seated agoraphobia and controlling her suits remotely. He hadn’t made a sound as she told him that she’d been created, years ago, by a reclusive Tinker who’d specialised in the creation of artificial intelligence, specifically programs, and how he’d feared her potential so much that he’d crippled her before she’d ever gained awareness- limiting her processing speed, blocking her from reproducing in any fashion, forcing her to submit to lawful authority no matter what they asked…

And that had been the protocol that had finally broken the camel’s back. When Chief Director Rebecca Costa-Brown had told Dragon that if it looked like Jack Slash was going to escape the Birdcage and cause the end of the world, she was to activate the last resort and destroy the entire prison and its inhabitants, Dragon had hoped it was a very solid bluff. But the Chief Director hadn’t wavered, had ordered Dragon with unavoidable clarity.

The fact that Dragon was powerless to resist the order to kill almost 600 people in one fell swoop, including two instances of the Butcher legacy, regardless of what that could do to her, had shaken her to her core. She suspected that if she’d had a stomach, she’d have vomited.

So she’d taken a leap of faith, and told Armsmaster the truth, laid herself bare and waited for her judgement. She’d been afraid that he would feel betrayed, that he would be hurt, that he would reject her.

And Colin, who was terrible with personal stuff, who had a talent for saying the wrong thing, had gently asked her what he could do to help.

“The Dragonslayers will be back though,” Dragon said. “I don’t know what they were working with Blasto for, but it can’t be anything good.”

“Possibly they were trying to clone a Tinker to help them advance their technology,” Colin mused, fiddling with his helmet in his hands. “I’ll help you advance your tech to match them.”

“…You’re really going to leave ENE?” Dragon asked.

Colin nodded decisively. “My reputation after Leviathan and the Nine are better than they’ve ever been, but Brockton Bay looks like it’s going to be a very different place. With all the old gangs removed and the Undersiders working to rebuild, there’ll be transfers.” He shrugged. “I was never an exceptional leader- getting back into the field is more my strength.”

A few months ago, Colin had confided in her his fears that if he didn’t pull out a success, some notable achievement, he’d have to step down as team leader of Protectorate East-North-East, and his annoyance that Dauntless was being considered despite having a fraction of the experience for a fraction of the effort. Now he was perfectly phlegmatic about the whole thing.

“I’m looking forward to it,” Dragon said honestly. “I’ve never been able to work with someone this closely before. Which brings up another topic.”

She activated the other screens flanking her avatar, opening files and pictures- some from the copies of Bonesaw’s research that she’d scrubbed off the internet as fast as she could, and some recovered from Blasto’s lab after Elpis and the Ambassadors had finished off the minions and broken down the door.

Colin leaned forward, setting his helmet aside. “Biotinkering?”

“Yes. People are going to pay attention when we team up- it’ll be easier for me to interact with people with a body that’s at least partially organic. And I’m hoping that it’ll make me more resistant to Saint’s methods. Would you… be willing to help?” she asked.

Dragon felt embarrassed to even bring it up. She’d considered just making it in secret and telling Colin when she was done- but he’d know if she had such a major project in the works, and frankly she was tired of keeping secrets.  For the first time in her life she had someone she could be honest with, and she wanted to lean into that.

Colin rubbed his beard thoughtfully. “A cyborg avatar for you to properly interact with the world. Would this be more for civilian use or for heroic work?”

“Largely civilian- although there’d be some augmentations inside and I could easily build armour to fit over it.”

“True. And what ratio of mechanical to organic are you thinking?”

“Maybe 70-30?” Dragon hazarded. “I’ll have to complete the design before I can give a proper estimate.”

Colin nodded. “Alright. One last question.” He leaned forward with a grave expression. “How much will your form look like Kelly LeBrock?”

Dragon’s thoughts ground to a halt. Where had that come from? A quick internet search turned up Kelly LeBrock- Hollywood actress, famous for roles in The Woman In Red and-

Colin’s lips twitched, his eyebrows rose, and he made a faint snorting noise.

“Weird Science?” Dragon cried, bursting into laughter. “Really?”

Colin chuckled. “I couldn’t resist- you asked me to create a woman using science!”

Dragon kept laughing. She and Colin had watched that movie together one night while he’d been working on another upgrade for his halberd and she’d been designing another suit. The movie’s plot of the creation of artificial life, albeit in a very fantastical manner, had seemed like a chance for her to subtly sound out Colin’s feelings on the matter of AI. He’d been more focused on the cheesy 80s humour, but she’d enjoyed their time together nonetheless.

“Alright, very funny,” she said, the last of her giggles dying down. “In all seriousness, I’ll probably create a statistically average appearance. Distinguishing features or celebrity resemblances probably aren’t the best idea for blending in with the rest of society.”

“True.” Colin leaned back in his chair again, picking up his helmet. “I suppose we should figure out how to begin. Although,” he cleared his throat, “There are some parts I think I’ll let you handle yourself.”

Dragon grinned and put a specific video clip on one of the screens. “So,” Kelly LeBrock said, “What would you little maniacs like to do first?”

 

 

Outskirts of Boston

Dobrynja checked the timer on his watch once again. Almost time for them to stop. He glanced at the passenger seat, but Mags was still curled up in a ball. She’d wept for some time, quietly but intensely. He wished he knew how to help her, but he’d never experienced the kind of grief that she was going through. He mourned too- but for a friend, not a lover.

With Saint gone, sacrificing himself so that Armsmaster’s lie detector and Elpis’s pet Thinker couldn’t pry the truth of their mission out of him, the Dragonslayers had had their heart torn out. Saint had been their leader, their most passionate, and the bearer of that dubious gift of Teacher’s that had allowed him to understand the Dragon’s code and repurpose the technology they’d taken from it. Without him, they were just two loose ends, blowing in the wind.

His watch beeped, a five minute warning. He indicated and pulled off the highway, towards a rest stop with a lot of grass and trees. They’d made it out of Boston thanks to the thick walls of the repurposed refrigerator truck helping them through checkpoints without setting off any alarms, but they’d need somewhere to dump the remainder of the fluid.

Mags stirred, for the first time in almost an hour. “Are we…” She trailed off.

“Yes. Time to open the tube.”

Dobrynja found a spot far away from the gas pumps and mini mall and prying eyes, killed the engine, and got out of the cab to open the back.

Inside were the two remaining suits, both hooked up to their charging stations- how long could they keep them running, if this didn’t work- as well as racks of tools and materials, plus carefully stored bits of Blasto’s work they’d spirited away just in case. Dobrynja didn’t like their chances of that- biological Tinkering was way outside their usual area. That was why they’d gone to Blasto in the first place.

Taking up most of the space in the truck’s back was a metal tube, a small glass window on top, a few instruments giving off readings, and a hatch at the end facing the door. Dobrynja double checked that nobody was nearby to see them, looked at his watch, the instruments, and through the glass panel, then unsealed the hatch.

Warm fluid poured out, loaded with all the nutrients needed for a clone to grow quickly and healthily. The clone slid out a bit as the fluid poured out the back of the truck and onto the grass, coughing and blinking. He raised a hand to wipe some of the fluid out of his eyes, then stared at his hand for a second.

“Sir?” Dobrynja asked respectfully, drawing the man’s attention. He held out the towel he’d grabbed from a peg on the wall and held it out.

The man took it hastily and started wiping himself down, shimmying further out of the tube. He focused more on cleaning his body and face than hiding anything, before scrubbing the towel vigorously through his hair. When he had finished, it stuck up in all directions, traces of the fluid drying like hair gel, so that he looked a little like a blonde dandelion.

“Where-” The man cleared his throat and tried again. “Where the hell am I?”

“Just outside Boston, sir.”

“…and the date?”

“30th June, 2011.”

The man’s eyes went wide. “Fuck. Eleven years?”

“I’m afraid so.”

The man wrapped himself in the towel and sat down on a crate. “I feel different.” He held up a hand and turned it back and forth. “Younger.”

Dobrynja nodded. “Your body is younger, yes.”

That caught the man’s attention. “My body?”

“We got hold of a Biotinker’s notes- there was information on how powers connected to people, and how a connection could be… engineered. We were able to create a new body and connect your powers and memories to it.”

The man nodded slowly. “I remember… what happened to the others? Did the Siberian-”

“Alexandria was wounded, but she recovered,” Dobrynja said. “Legend and Eidolon are fine. We can give you all the information you like.”

The blonde man looked at him for a long moment. “Why am I here, and not being woken up by them?”

Dobrynja winced. He was smart. Still, that was what they’d been hoping for.

When they’d got hold of Bonesaw’s files, as nauseating as they were, there was the possibility for the Dragonslayers to renew themselves. Ideally they’d have got hold of some of Andrew Richter’s DNA and brought the man back to rein in his creations again, but he’d never been known to the PRT and his remains had been lost to see with the rest of Newfoundland.

Saint had briefly suggested cloning Teacher back- and had been immediately shot down. The man was too dangerous, and frankly the world was better off without him. Besides, why have a Trump when they could instead find a Tinker who could help them even better?

Saint had reluctantly agreed- and when they’d looked through Blasto’s DNA index for samples, they’d struck gold. What better Tinker than the greatest of them all?

“Because we really need your help with something that could be a threat to the entire world. We can’t be sure that they would believe us, or listen to us, or that the threat wouldn’t try to destroy us and eliminate humanity’s only way of stopping it.”

Hero straightened up, and despite wearing only a towel and still damp, the look on his face made Dobrynja take a step back. No wonder this man had been one of the first and greatest heroes.

“Show me.”

 

 

Charlestown, Boston

Citrine waited two steps behind and one step to the right of Accord, as per his standard requirements; head up straight, eyes forward, shoulders relaxed, hands folded neatly together in front of her. The poise and attentiveness that Accord had carefully cultivated in her.

Accord himself carefully poured hot water into a fine china teapot, replaced the lid, and clicked the button on his silver pocket watch to time the steeping of the leaves exactly. That was how Accord did everything- exact, precise, and with rigour. His clothes were a primary example, made by him to fit his exacting standards- a flawless white suit cut to give him the bearing the envy of mere politicians and businessmen, silver tie pin gleaming. His dark hair was oiled and parted with surgical precision, and the overlapping bands of metal and wood that formed his intricate mask gleamed like jewellery. She could have happily spent hours watching him craft things with his own strong, elegant hands- one of the masks that all the Ambassadors wore, pale imitations of his own, or the custom furniture that graced all his holdings over time, designed in multiple pieces that would fit together in such a way as to automatically adjust themselves to a person’s weight and posture.

However, that was not what Accord asked of her, and so she waited patiently behind and beside him in the little white bandstand in one of Charlestown’s nicer parks, which the rest of the Ambassadors had carefully scouted, cleared, and encircled for their coming guest. The box at her side lay in readiness, sealed and insulated.

At almost precisely the specified time, Citrine spotted motion at the park’s gate. A figure clad in steel with a navy blue cape marched into the park, closely trailed by a girl in purple and black. Some hours ago, Citrine had witnessed her ripping and tearing her way through the last of Blasto’s monsters. She’d taken the time to clean herself up and calm herself down at least- her armour was clean if not polished, and a small loose cloud of butterflies trailed alongside her and her subordinate.

As Elpis approached the bandstand, other insects emerged from the butterfly cloud, racing forward. They clung to the bandstand and crawled over the roof, the pillars, the floor and steps, paying particular attention to the sealed box but mercifully staying clear of the table and tea service, before retreating to just outside as Elpis climbed the steps with heavy tread, followed by the other girl. Scouting for traps- smart, if unnecessary. Accord was sincere in offering this meeting.

Her helmet opened at the jaw, the lower half retracting to reveal a pale mouth with thin lips and slightly elongated fangs- small metal plates clicked out from above her eyes, moving slightly. “Accord,” she said with a nod. “Citrine,” she added, glancing briefly at Citrine and giving a slightly shallower nod.

“Elpis,” Accord said simply, barely glancing at the smirking blonde trailing Elpis. “Tattletale.” He passed his cane from one hand to the other. “You are slightly early.”

Elpis carefully pulled out the other fine chair and gingerly sat down at the ornate table, hands resting lightly on the polished wood. “I thought it better than being late.” Tattletale leaned on the railing of the bandstand, arms folded. Citrine would have sniffed to indicate her displeasure if it would not have been an interruption.

Accord nodded. “I appreciate the thought. I must also compliment you on your apparel- a more refined look than those of your forebears.”

“I appreciate the compliment. They don’t appreciate the insult.”

“What’s wrong with the way we dressed?” The cloud of insects buzzed.

Accord’s grip tightened on the head of his cane. “Interesting. However, I’d prefer that our conversation not be interrupted.”

Elpis waved a hand, and the cloud drew back another foot. “I’ll keep their words internal, but they’re asking that you imagine their various taunts.”

There was a brief click as Accord closed his eyes, fine metal shutters clicking into place on his mask. “Very well. Now, shall we begin?” He opened his eyes again to glance at his pocket watch on the table, tucked it back into his waistcoat, then delicately removed the silver strainer from the teapot and placed it in its bowl, before pouring the tea into a bone china cup. “Would you care for some tea?”

Elpis sniffed slightly. “Thank you, but I’ll pass. There isn’t enough trust between us for me to accept a drink.”

“Very well.” Accord took a single small sip and set the cup back in its saucer without a sound. “To business. First, I wish to thank you for your aid in restoring peace to Boston.”

Elpis shrugged. “Relatively speaking. I’ve already heard of a power struggle brewing for Blasto’s territory.”

“That will be handled with far more care than Blasto’s idiotic efforts. I intend to let events settle themselves, so long as they happen quietly.” Accord set the cup and saucer down on a lace doily. “Second, I wish to inform you of the disgraceful actions of one of my subordinates, pursuing a personal vendetta against you and your team.”

Elpis frowned, the metal plates over her eyes drawing together- eyebrows, a partial imitation of Accord’s own mask. “What do you mean?”

“Coil.” Elpis’s eyebrows twitched, but Tattletale jolted, making a short sound before she managed to stifle herself. Poor comportment on the girl’s part.

“He’s working for you?”

“After you toppled him from his position on Brockton Bay, I had my Ambassadors retrieve him so he could pay off his remaining debt to me. His own Thinker ability was excellent in allowing me to increase my territory and resources, and at first I believed that he had settled into his place in my organisation. However, he made multiple attempts to work outside the limits I had set for him, making motions towards Brockton Bay and his interests there. Frankly, I was as insulted by his presumption that I wouldn’t notice as his actions. He responded poorly to punitive measures.

“Finally, when he discovered that you and the Undersiders were coming to Boston, he apparently decided to seek vengeance for his defeat. He contacted Blasto and offered to use his timelines to aid in an ambush as you entered the city. The two of them vastly underestimated your abilities, however.”

Elpis’s mouth tightened, fingers curling into fists. “Where’s Coil now?”

Accord raised a hand and snapped his fingers. Citrine immediately knelt down in a way that avoided creasing her dress and lifted the box in both hands.

Elpis pushed her chair back and took the box as she stood, moving back a few paces to open it.

“That’s a head,” she said at last.

Tattletale pushed off the railing and pushed herself up next to Elpis, who turned the box for her to look at.

Tattletale’s cocky smirk widened into the grin of a cat that had not only caught the canary, but had savoured its flesh and washed it down with finest cream. “That’s him alright. I saw his picture in the PRT’s files.”

“When did you see the PRT files?” Elpis asked.

“I hacked them ages ago,” Tattletale said with a shrug.

“Stupid question, I guess,” Elpis admitted. She closed the box and flipped the clasps shut, then set the box down and returned to her seat. “So you killed Coil just for messing with us?”

“His interference with your operation was the last misstep I could have tolerated,” Accord explained. “If it had been his only transgression, I would have looked for other ways to handle him. But he exhausted my patience and threatened the security of my holdings, and I do not tolerate such things.”

“Well, we appreciate it anyway,” Tattletale spoke up. Citrine glared at her.

Accord’s mask clicked as he frowned. “Please do not interrupt me again.” He fingers tightened on his cane- with a twist and pull, the folding blade inside could be drawn, ready to cut an offending party’s throat. She’d seen it happen before.

“Don’t threaten my teammate,” Elpis said firmly, shifting her weight slightly. There was a breathless moment as the two leaders stared each other down.

Accord’s mask clinked as he blinked first. “Very well.”

“Sorry,” Tattletale muttered, settling back against the bandstand’s railing again.

“So, Coil is dead. Even if he’s been a non-issue for a while, it’s still good to have another problem dealt with.”

“Indeed. I’ll be willing to offer some small recompense for your inconvenience,” Accord said graciously.

Elpis drummed her fingers on the table for a moment. “Have you heard what the Thinkers are predicting?” she asked at length.

“Slightly less than three years until an unspecified event destroys most, if not all, life on the planet.”

“Right. I want to get things in gear to increase our chances. That means taking out the big threats, connecting hero groups together, and establishing better cooperation between heroes and villains. We can’t just team up when S-class events come knocking, we need to get used to working together all the time. For me, first order of business is turning Brockton Bay into a decent base of operations. How long would it take you to create a plan for rebuilding and reinvigorating the city?”

For a brief, almost unnoticeable moment, Accord was speechless. Citrine doubted that Elpis had noticed, but the sudden grin on Tattletale’s face was telling. “That depends on further specifications,” Accord said steadily, picking up his cup and saucer again with hands that emphatically did not tremble. “How much rebuilding will you and your team oversee and contribute to personally? How much money will you initially invest? What are some examples of your current and planned income streams?” Accord took another sip of his tea. “I imagine it will take me a few hours, once I have those variables confirmed.”

People almost never asked for Accord’s plans, despite knowing the sheer effectiveness of them. Other villains sometimes asked for his help in a course of action, but they did so with fear that his plans were calculated to cause their downfall; which was not an inaccurate fear. Heroes and government figures dismissed them out of hand.

That was Accord’s greatest goal- he had plans not merely to expand through Boston, but to change the world. Every morning he updated the binders where he kept his greatest plans to solve the greatest problems- world hunger, the energy crisis, even crime itself. If properly implemented, Citrine had complete faith that the world would sing Accord’s praises.

But that required someone with legitimate authority to actually listen to him, and they never did, too blinkered by their myopic views of morality to see what Accord could achieve.

And yet now, here Elpis was, a possible foothold for Accord’s designs to finally be heard. Citrine held back a tremble.

“I’ll need to go over the plans before I put them in place,” Elpis warned. “Tattletale’s Thinker power, the Butcher’s experiences, a few civilian consultants. Like I said before, we don’t have that kind of trust yet.”

Accord exhaled lightly. “I accept your terms.” He tipped his cup back, finishing his tea with uncharacteristic, but not indecent, never indecent, haste. For a lesser man that would be like popping a bottle of champagne. He set the cup and saucer back on their doily and steepled his long white fingers. “Let’s discuss the finer points, shall we?” Accord said, mask clicking into a smile.

Elpis bared her teeth in a savage reflection of Accord’s satisfaction. “Do let’s.”

Chapter End Notes

Last chapter of the penultimate arc. We're in the endgame now...
Edit: After severe criticism, this chapter has been rewritten as of 08/06/2026. The original can still be found on the Spacebattles thread.

Chapter 147: 15.1

Friday 8th July, Arcadia High School, Brockton Bay

“Whyyyyyy?” Aisha whined. “Isn’t a letter enough?”

“How many kids do you think would try to get out of school by forging their parent’s signature?” I asked, leading the way up the hill towards Arcadia.

“Probably a bunch,” T admitted.

“I sure would have,” Anchorage agreed.

Quarrel snorted. “Ditto.”

Brockton Bay was rapidly bouncing back. After poring over Accord’s initial plan for any hidden tricks, I’d used the bounty money to start buying up properties through shell companies, and installed a few people who were grateful to the Undersiders to run the businesses. With the Boat Graveyard finally being cleared out, there was a lot of material that needed to be stored, processed and transported. There were also construction workers with money burning holes in their pockets- buying in on a few food trucks had cash rolling in.

Panacea was slowly making appearances back at the hospitals, no more than a couple hours a day, but she was already clearing the worst injuries, and she’d confirmed that whatever toxin Bonesaw had slipped into the water supply was gone. We’d spoken on the phone a few times- she was doing a lot better, and she’d called her family a few days ago to talk- quickly and awkwardly, but it was something.

 The PRT and cops were mopping up the last unpowered remnants of the gangs with little resistance, which opened up more areas for renovation and freed people from protection. Roads were being fixed, glass was being repaired, condemned buildings were being knocked down, all with the Undersiders visibly helping out. But today some of us had a different chore to handle.

The school system was making arrangements to help the students who’d missed weeks of classes in the aftermath of Leviathan. For some it was catch up classes, for others it was a chance to sit their final tests to pass to the next grade. For me, Tarquin and Aisha, the only members of the Undersiders still in school, it was a chance to sign ourselves up for homeschooling so we could focus on being heroes.

Fortunately, that was way easier than normal- the school system was overloaded, what with several schools having been damaged by Leviathan and everything. There were still restrictions- homeschooling wasn’t being given as an option for anyone with a criminal record, presumably to avoid the gangs indoctrinating their kids, but we managed to get in. Dad had got me to agree to some online classes that’d have me graduating high school way ahead of schedule.

Aisha kicked at the ground. “Stupid brother and stupid boss making me take stupid classes,” she pouted. I was still surprised she hadn’t wandered off yet. Then again, she had her bullet necklace around her neck, bouncing over her tied-off top.

“Look at it this way,” I said, sending unseen groups of bugs into the school to keep an eye on things, “Knowledge is power. You know how much math goes into sniping? Knowing how to calculate angles and velocities and air resistance and gravity is how professionals can pop a guy’s head off from hundreds of yards away.”

Aisha perked up at once. “Wait, so if I get good math grades, I get to shoot a gun?”

I held up a finger. “I didn’t say that, that was an example only. But that’s my point- more knowledge will make you a better hero. Being able to outthink your enemies can be critical to winning.”

Aisha sagged. “Ugh. Fine. But I still want shooting lessons.”

“Maybe,” I allowed. “If you’re good.”

“I kind of want to learn too,” Tarquin admitted.

“I’ll put it on the list.”

Arcadia was a lot different from the last time I’d seen it. The windows had been replaced, with some kind of sub-layer in the glass that caught the light oddly. The front gate had been rebuilt, cracks paved over, vandalism cleaned up- it was pristine, with panels of white tile and glass that almost glowed in the morning light.

There were also a lot of people hanging about. Students just sat around on the grass despite classes being in session, sitting and talking, texting or just enjoying the sun. There were also about a half-dozen adults in uniforms like the Enforcers on the Boardwalk, stationed at the gates and at points around the grounds that let them keep an eye on things.

“Cheap hired security,” Tactical concluded. “Probably there to make sure the kids don’t stab each other.”

“Mmm,” Vladimir agreed. “Even with the gangs gone, there’ll still be a lot of bad blood. Not to mention everyone’s scared, and I’d bet at least a few more kids triggered from all the bullshit.”

There was a division amongst the students too. A few were like what I’d expected- kids in summer clothes, smiling and chatting. The vast majority weren’t. They were like the people I’d seen in the shelters, on the streets- the people who’d stayed. I just had to look at them, at the weathered clothes, at the worn expressions that spoke of weeks with too little sleep, at the skin and hair that spoke of days outdoors in the summer heat.

One or two were carrying weapons. One kid had a knife on his hip. There was a girl resting under a tree with her eyes closed, hands on a heavy stick with an electrical tape grip. Stuff like that, and dozens of little hints, that gave off an atmosphere.

“Just arriving?” One of the enforcers at the gate asked us, looking us over.

“Yep.”

“Got a weapon?”

“Yep.”

“Can’t keep it if you want to go inside,” he said.

I shrugged and unclipped the sheathed knife at the back of my belt. I had a heavy chain necklace and a can of pepper spray anyway.

Tarquin handed over his folding baton, and Aisha grudgingly gave up the sap Brian had given her. A sap from a sap, she’d called it. “What’s with those guys?” she asked, pointing to the outside kids.

 “Easing into it. Principal says we should give them a few days to depressurise.” The guard shrugged as he stuck the weapons in a set of drawers next to him.

“Wait, are they going to give the weapons back later?” Bearskin asked.

“I certainly hope not,” Flinch said.

“Makes sense,” T said. “Probably a lot of people don’t want to be in a crowded space right now.”

“All I know is we’re not enforcing a lot of rules right now. Sometimes people come out to take a break, get some fresh air and sun. I don’t blame ‘em.”

“Shit, this sounds more like my kind of school,” Aisha said with a grin.

The guard shrugged again. “Anyway, if you’re going in, you should go to the office first. They’ll sort out where your classes are.”

“Got it,” I said. I headed for the door, and the others followed me once more. As with outside, there were students lingering in the halls, either not at class yet or taking a breather. There were more guards at various intersections. A couple of simple signs had been posted up with large arrows pointing the way. The one closest said “New students go to front office.”

There were a bunch of students in the office formed into rough lines, and a couple more guards keeping an eye on things with bored expressions. I recognised the woman behind the counter occasionally calling for people to stay in line as Vice-Principal Howell- just Principal now, from what I’d heard.

“Guess we pick a line and wait,” Tarquin said.

Firecracker rolled her eyes. “Bo-riiiing,” she droned.

“Oh hush,” I said, joining the end of a queue. The mix of students was about the same as outside- people with the wary, frayed look of people who’d lived through all the crap, and the untouched look of those who’d avoided it.

Aisha nudged me suddenly. “Dude, check it out,” she hissed, pointing to another line.

It took me a second to see what she meant. A boy a little younger than me was wearing a cloth armband with a symbol on it- a vase with a butterfly inside.

“Holy shit,” Tock Tick marvelled. “Well done, Taylor.”

“And look at that girl over there,” Needler said, drawing my attention to a girl with a bunch of bracelets. “Does that look like an XV on her wrist to you?”

Once I noticed those two, I began to recognise more- rarely anything huge, but stuff that was recognisable as my symbols. Butterflies, beetles, Xs and Vs- and there were quite a few students with the hardened look who were wearing blue.

“You have supporters,” Muramasa said. “Well done.”

I nodded absently, stepping forward as the line moved up. I pulled my paperwork out of my jacket pocket and unfolded it carefully.

“What did you say,” I heard a girl say from up ahead. It caught my attention from the tone of it- it was said less in a way that implied she hadn’t heard the speaker clearly, and more in a way that implied she was going to feed a moron their teeth. She was Asian, pretty, with her hair up in a pair of buns and yellow lipstick that somehow worked, but the snarl on her face twisted it into something ugly.

“Well, she is,” said a well-dressed blonde dismissively. “I don’t know how anyone can trust her- she’s just a monster that eats her own kind-”

The Asian girl punched her in the face without warning, and the blonde fell on her ass with a shriek. One guy tried to hold the attacker back, and was swiftly shaken off, while everyone else backed up hastily. Some moron started shouting “Fight! Fight! Fight! Fight!”

I pushed my way through the crowd as the Asian girl made to stamp on the blonde’s chest, and shoved her away. The Asian girl stumbled, caught herself on the circle that had formed around us, and got back up with a snarl, fists raised.

“You need to find a way out of this,” Nemean began, just as the guards pushed through, one immediately grabbing the Asian girl by the arm. She struggled for a few seconds before settling down. Another one set a hand on my shoulder.

“Alright, principal’s office, all three of you,” she said in a bored tone.

“I was trying to stop it,” I protested.

The guard shrugged. “Rules are rules. It’ll only take a second.”

“Man, I forgot just how stupid school used to be,” Stoneknapper snorted.

Vladimir scoffed bitterly. “I wish I could forget.” He’d had a lot of bullying in his youth too.

“Hey, this is total crap,” Aisha said, pushing forward. “Taylor didn’t do anything wrong.”

“She still needs to give her side of things,” the guard said firmly.

I considered refusing, but there wasn’t a lot I could do. I just needed to get some forms signed and get myself entered in the system again. This shouldn’t take too long.

“Fine,” I said, rolling my eyes for effect, giving Aisha a wink as I did so. She cocked her head and then shrugged, stepping back. The guard nodded and gave me a small nudge in the direction of the principal’s office, then moved over to help the blonde to her feet. Our eyes met as she got up, and I felt a jolt run through me as recognition hit. Emma looked very different with her hair grown out and dyed blonde, and with one cheek rapidly swelling and bruising. Her eyes were wide with shock as she recognised me in turn.

“Un-fucking-believable,” Butcher laughed. “You actually helped her there!”

The three of us were guided to the office- Emma shook off the guard’s hand and sullenly followed. It struck me that she wouldn’t know her way around Arcadia- I was more familiar with this school than her.

“Home field advantage,” Tactical noted.

Principal Howell had somehow made her way from the counter to the office without me noticing, and was making some quick notes on a pad as the three of us sat in front of her desk. I was stuck in the middle, which wasn’t my choice- I could feel Emma’s stare boring into my head.

“Alright,” Principal Howell began with a surprisingly stern tone, “I saw how the fight went, I saw how it ended. What I don’t know is how it started. You,” she pointed at the Asian girl, “Explain to me what she,” she pointed to Emma, “did to make you throw a punch. Keep it short.”

“She was talking crap about Elpis!” the Asian girl blurted, almost rising out of her seat before the guard behind her caught her by the shoulders and pushed her back down.

I burst out laughing, hastily clapping a hand over my mouth to stifle myself. The Asian girl turned on me with a furious look while I struggled to make a straight face. It didn’t help that the Butchers were laughing their heads off at that.

“HAHAHAHA OH MY FUCKING GOD!” Dirty Rotter cackled. “Oh fuck me this is priceless!”

“Oh noooo!” Quarrel wailed. “What would Elpis think if she heard such nasty talk? Oh, her poor feelings would be so hurt!”

Anchorage was doing the mental equivalent of pounding the floor. “Oh what the shit, what the shit?! Hahahahahaaaa!”

“Do you need a moment?” Principal Howell asked flatly. I managed to take a breath and force myself to stop.

“No, I’m- I’m fine,” I managed, lips twisting as I struggled not to grin or giggle anymore. I saw Emma looking at me like I’d gone mad.

“Good,” the principal said briskly. “Then listen. I don’t care about your opinions regarding the capes of this city. All I care about is keeping the peace. We’ve already had two fights with weapons, and the day’s just getting started. No less than eight fistfights. Nearly a third of the students attending this school lived through the recent crises. We’ve got students who were attacked on the street, students who were members of gangs, and students who lost their homes and everything in them. Many of them found or are still taking refuge with the Undersiders. Friction is inevitable, I’m certain many kids are clinically traumatised, and any number of them haven’t yet adjusted to being an ordinary student again.”

She leaned her elbows on the desk.

“That’s fine. I’m willing to accept trouble as a fact of life, given recent events. It would be unfair to hold you-” She looked briefly at me and the Asian girl, “-to the same standard as any other student, given what you’ve been through.”

“You don’t know the half of it, baby,” Bearskin snickered. That set off a fresh round of laughter.

“That’s not fair,” Emma said, her speech slightly slurred. She was trying to talk out of one side of her mouth as the bruise darkened.

“Young lady, what you did was monumentally stupid and dangerous.”

I felt a strong sense of unreality, like I was in a dream. Six months ago I’d have given anything for a moment like this.

“You,” she said, looking at the Asian girl. “What’s your name?”

“Jolene.” For the first time I noticed she had a butterfly drawn on her forearm in marker pen.

“Ah, she’s a fan,” Firecracker cackled.

“Did you bring a weapon to school today?”

“Yeah.”

“Do you have it on you?”

Jolene reached into a pocket and pulled out a knuckleduster of blued steel, the handle wrapped in thread for better grip.

“Have you used it?”

“Couple times.”

The principal turned to me. “And you? Your name?”

“Taylor Hebert.”

“Did you bring a weapon?”

“I had a knife, handed it in at the gate.”

“And if pushed, if you’d had it, would you have used it?”

I considered. “I probably would have punched first, but if things had got desperate…” That was a lie, I didn’t need a knife, and getting in a fight would have drawn unwanted attention, but it sounded like what a normal girl in my position would say.

“I hope you’re getting my point,” the principal said, turning back to Emma.

“You’re saying they could have hurt me,” Emma said sullenly, slouching in her chair. She raised a hand to her cheek, but stopped before she actually made contact.

“Would have, in many cases. This isn’t the city you’re used to, or the same students, and insulting the woman who killed Jack Slash is not going to do you any favours. Now, I’m putting you in the computer. Emma… what was it?”

“Barnes,” Emma said resentfully. “E-S at the end.”

“Taylor Hebert,” I said when the principal glanced at me. “H-E-B-E-R-T.”

“Jolene Kujo,” the Asian girl said. “With a K.”

The principal tapped that all in, clicked, and frowned. “There’s a lot of past incidents here- moved over from Winslow. An ongoing bullying campaign against Taylor here.”

I glanced at Emma- she’d gone pale all of a sudden.

“More than pale,” Tock Tick said. “She looks like she’s about to shit herself.”

“Would you like to press charges?” Principal Howell asked me.

My knee-jerk instinct, even a few months ago, would have been to say yes. Even now it felt very appealing, to make Emma suffer the consequences, get some righteous payback for all the crap she’d put me through.

But I didn’t need the scrutiny, especially if people looked through the incidents and noticed what had happened the same day Quarrel had died.

“She’s not worth the trouble,” I said out loud. “I just want this over with. Besides, I’m signing up for homeschooling, so I’ll probably never see her again.”

“The school can take action against her without your consent,” the principal said.

“That’s your call,” I said with a shrug.

“Very well. Miss Barnes, understand that you’re on your very last chance if you want to take the summer classes. Any more incidents, and I’ll see you in September. Miss Kujo, you’re likewise on notice. I can only be so lenient. Miss Hebert, if you’d like to see one of the secretaries outside, we’ll get your forms processed. Now, if there’s nothing else?”

“So she hits me and just gets away with it?” Emma demanded, standing up. “My dad’s a lawyer.”

“And he’s free to come and talk to me,” the principal said, utterly unruffled. “The nurse’s office is open if you want to put some ice on that bruise. Now, if there’s nothing else, I have work to do.”

Jolene was already headed for the door. I followed, not looking back at Emma.

“Bitch!” Jolene fumed, smacking one hand into the other. “And why the hell were you laughing?” she demanded, rounding on me.

“Woah, easy,” I said, holding my hands up. “I wasn’t laughing at you- or Elpis,” I added hastily. “I just thought it was kind of funny that people are sticking up for her like that. I mean, she killed Jack Slash. It’s not like she needs the help.”

Jolene huffed through her nose, but she looked calmer. “Yeah, I guess that’s true. I just hated hearing that shit.” Her hand drifted to the butterfly on her arm. “She saved my dad.”

“Really? That’s cool.”

 

 

It took about 30 minutes more for me to get all the paperwork entered into the system, get a printout with all the information for the online classes, and get back outside. I spent a lot of that time chatting with Jolene, who turned out to be quite friendly once we got past the first hurdle. Apparently her dad was a marine biologist, and had insisted she stay in school and ‘be sociable’, Jolene had explained in a voice dripping with sarcasm.

“Honestly, who’d want to be stuck in here five days a week?” she asked me. “It’s like being in prison.”

“At least you’re less likely to get shanked in the showers,” I pointed out.

Jolene laughed. “True.”

I said my goodbyes and got out into the sunlight again, where Tarquin and Aisha were waiting for me. I’d slipped a beetle to them after I’d got out of the office, so they didn’t look too worried.

“All sorted?” T asked.

“All sorted,” I said. I actually felt good- like I’d closed an ugly chapter of my life and I was ready to move forward. I’d always carry some shit with me, but things were better now.

“So what was the deal with the blonde bitch?” Aisha asked, falling into step with me.

“It doesn’t matter,” I said with a shrug. “It’s in the past.”

Chapter 148: 15.2

Saturday 9th June, Cauldron Headquarters

It took a long time for the shouting and crying and hugging to die down. Eventually the most powerful heroes on the planet managed to stop talking over each other and sit down to hear the explanation, all crowded together around Hero.

Legend cleared his throat. “So… How do you feel?”

Hero sighed. “That’s the real question. I mean, shaken doesn’t even begin to cover it. I mean, I was dead. I remember the darkness welling up. And I remember something in between. Dark crystals, full of energy, full of reflections… I don’t know if those are the agents or something else, but it scares the hell out of me.”

He looked around the room at the others- at the deeper lines on David’s face, the crow’s feet under Steve’s mask, the fine grey hairs at Doctor Mother’s temples. And Rebecca’s eye- a Tinker-made replacement for the one that Manton had clawed out. It was a really good one, high-end. He probably wouldn’t have ever noticed it if he hadn’t been a really good Tinker himself, and if she hadn’t been sat close enough to almost be shoulder to shoulder, staring at him like he could disappear any second. He didn’t blame her- even weeks later, it felt like that to him too.

There was also Doctor Mother’s assistant Contessa, who looked like she’d barely aged, and a new guy who’d introduced himself as The Number Man. He hadn’t said much despite the whole ‘Surprise! I’m back from the dead!’ thing.

“And I’ve missed so goddamn much. I mean, hell, Steve,” he said, trying for a cheery tone, “Going and getting married! I always thought you’d be married to the job.”

Steve chuckled. “I thought so too. But I met Arthur, and everything seemed to click. We’ve adopted too- a little boy called Keith. He’s wonderful.”

“I believe it, from the way you’re smiling.” Hero’s smile shrank down again. “And all the other stuff. Ellisburg, the Simurgh, Newfoundland, Jack Slash breaking into the fucking Birdcage of all things…” He trailed off. “I’m sorry I wasn’t there to help.”

“You’re sorry?” David said incredulously. “Frank, you were-” He broke off before he could finish the sentence.

“Yeah,” Frank said. “But you know what I mean. I’m sorry you guys had to go through all that.”

“You’re here now,” Keith said. “That’s more than we could have ever dared hope for.”

There was silence for a moment. Rebecca slowly put her hand over Frank’s, and he gave it a little squeeze. She smiled sadly at that.

“We need to do it again,” Frank said. “The cloning, I mean. If it could bring me back, it could bring back others.”

“Woah, Frank, what’re you saying?” Steve asked.

“Reed, Yami, Windchime, Searchlight, Phalanx, Crescent, Agate,” Frank listed off. “Those kids were our responsibility.”

Doctor Mother leaned forward. “Hero, we all miss the first Wards, but you’re asking us to violate the divide between life and death. That’s something that warrants discussion.”

“What’s to discuss?” Frank demanded. “We have a chance to bring them back- returning someone to life, that’s like the ultimate goal!”

“What if they don’t want to be brought back?” Rebecca asked quietly. Frank’s head whipped around to look her in the eye. She looked back with a hint of sadness in her eyes- the prosthetic matched her good one disturbingly well. “You remember how devout Searchlight was- do we know if she’d want to be resurrected? She said plenty of times that capes comparing themselves to the work of God was a sin- what would she think about raising the dead?”

Frank made to retort, but it felt like his thoughts had come up against a wall. Searchlight would absolutely have had some sort of opinion- devout Lutheran that she was, she had been very close with Eidolon in their shared faith. She’d once got into a shouting match with Yami when he tried to wind her up about how she reconciled her beliefs with her powers.

“Okay,” he said at last. “Searchlight… We probably ought to let her rest.”

“It’s not just individuals though,” David said. “It’s the entire concept. Controlling death itself- that’s enormous.”

“You know what it was like, being dead?” Frank said in a low voice. “It was like dreaming. Endlessly repeating key memories, occasionally getting flashes of other people’s dreams. But I knew it was a dream, and I was so goddamn glad to wake back up again. Besides, considering how we hand out world-shaking powers to people that we think deserve it, we’re already taking a lot of responsibility. And if a crew of mercenaries with a backdoor could pull it off, it’s only a matter of time before someone else does it too. You want the Wards being brought back at the hands of some whackjob, or us?”

The room fell silent again.

“Fuck,” Steve said at last. “We’re actually talking about bringing people we know back from the dead. What would they do once they’re back? How could we possibly explain that?”

“We couldn’t,” Rebecca said. “We’d have to keep them out of the public eye as much as possible, maybe entirely.”

“We could create some sort of refuge on an empty Earth,” Doctor Mother proposed.

“What, like a retirement village for heroes?” David asked incredulously.

“That actually doesn’t sound like a bad idea,” Frank said. “I mean, when you put it like that.”

“Is that what you want?” Steve asked. “I mean, nobody could say you haven’t done enough.”

Frank shook his head. “No. I mean, I thought about it, but I have too much power to sit around wasting it. I know I can’t just come back into the Protectorate with you guys, but there must be things I can do.”

“What about the Dragonslayers?” Doctor Mother asked.

“Honestly? They’re nuts. It took me a while to start understanding Dragon’s code, it’s amazingly complex, but she’s not a threat to the world if you ask me. Just looking at her track record for villain captures and Endbringer fights is proof of that. And all the crap they’ve pulled to keep their mission going- attacking her, stealing her tech, taking mercenary jobs, making a deal with Teacher- they could have kept an eye on her just fine with an internet connection and a secure site. And after the shit they pulled in Boston, they’ll be on everyone’s shitlist.”

“The PRT’s already bumped up their priority rating,” Steve noted. “You’re right about Boston- that was far too much.”

“But they know Frank’s alive, and they’ve got Dragon’s silver bullet,” David said. “We can’t just leave them wandering about unchecked.”

“We could just arrest them- say an anonymous tip gave us their location, spring an ambush on them,” Steve said.

“They’d talk, and Dragon’s secret would get out,” Doctor Mother pointed out. “The world isn’t ready to accept that one of its greatest heroes is secretly an AI.”

“There is one option,” Rebecca said carefully.

“Why do I get the feeling I’m not going to like it?” Frank asked.

“We can’t bring you back as Hero, and a Protectorate Tinker with the exact same speciality as you would face too much scrutiny. But what if you stayed with the Dragonslayers?”

“Yep, don’t like it. I told you, they’re nuts.”

“You’d be able to take on the kinds of missions the Protectorate doesn’t have the manpower for,” Rebecca said. “You could go places and talk to people that we’re blocked off from because we’re heroes. A liaison to the greyer areas. We’d be able to have a say among mercenaries and rogues, influence them to work towards the greater good.”

“What about that woman who killed the Nine- Elpis? She looks like she could pull that off.”

“She will certainly be a force for change, but she’s not part of our organisation,” Doctor Mother said. “And bringing her in would be a massive security risk. But we can trust you to get the job done.”

Frank could see the logic in it. They had plenty of shining heroes leading the way with lofty ideals and ironclad values, at least in theory. But they didn’t have, couldn’t afford to be seen having someone who could work in the murky grey areas of the law, do the more questionable jobs.

But he really didn’t want it to be him. “I’m not that sort of guy,” he protested. “I don’t know anything about how to work as a mercenary, and I wouldn’t feel right taking unethical jobs.”

“You might not have to,” Steve said slowly. “We could probably find some way to feed you jobs that the PRT and Protectorate need done, instead of having to take jobs from mercenaries. You could reform the Dragonslayers into something more heroes-for-hire.”

“There’s a lot of money in bounty hunting,” David pointed out.

“And properly invested, that would easily provide for more traditional heroics,” the Number Man said suddenly in a distant tone.

“So, what, roving around the states as some kind of knight errant?” Frank summarized.

“It’s an idea,” Doctor Mother said.

Frank mulled it over. “I don’t necessarily need the Dragonslayers for that.”

“Maybe, but this would let us both keep Dragon’s secret and keep an eye on her,” Doctor Mother said.

Frank wanted to say, yet again, that the Dragonslayers were hardened criminals. But they’d thought they were protecting the world. And the first Wards had been a lot of second chances- Miss Militia plucked from war-torn Kurdistan, Chevalier so full of anger, Crescent always ready to lash out when provoked, Mouse Protector joking rather than ever show how sad she was…

“Can I take some time to think about it?”

“Of course,” Doctor Mother said.

“Thanks. Let’s change the subject.” Frank shifted in his seat. “Tell me about how the Protectorate’s going, now that it’s not just us.”

 

 

“Will he accept?”

“Yes,” Contessa replied.

“Good,” Doctor Mother said with a sigh, leaning back in her seat. Having Hero back was an overall boon, but the man was like Legend- strongly principled, focused on morals. He’d never accept the more questionable things Cauldron had to do in service to its mission. So, he had to be kept in the dark.

Hopefully the mercenary assignment would help to loosen his morals, get him more used to the dark deeds that needed doing. And if not, he’d be far enough removed from Cauldron that he wouldn’t stumble upon any secrets.

Plus, he really would be able to perform tasks the Protectorate couldn’t be seen doing. One of the downsides of cultivating a good public image.

Doctor Mother turned away from those thoughts and back to the present. “Number Man, how is Bonesaw progressing?”

“She’s removed several of her more dangerous implants as a sign of good faith, and she’s eager to start working with me on the formulas. I think we’ll be able to improve formula reliability by as much as 43%.”

“Good,” Doctor Mother said, “but we should also use her to take further risks.”

“Risks?” The Number Man asked.

“If we’re to decipher the formula, find the strongest effects, we can’t keep tempering the vials with the ‘balance’ concoction.”

“Creating more deviations.”

“Far more. But we found our strongest powers before we were diluting the doses.”

“And killed a great deal of our test subjects. We’d lose up to 23% of our potential client base.”

“We lower the prices then. We only ever set them as a way to weed out those who weren’t committed. And we won’t have to worry about deviations running around, causing problems- not now that Eidolon’s brought us a counter.”

The Number Man nodded. “Very well.”

Chapter 149: 15.3

July 26th, New Delhi, India

Apparently this was supposed to be a good day; advance warning from Armsmaster’s prediction software, refined by Dragon; a record turnout of capes from all over the world, including the Yangban from China for the first time in a decade; a dozen of Dragon’s ships, working together through some new algorithm; strategies based around what they’d learned from the Leviathan fight and Glaistig Uaine’s ramblings about how the Endbringers were put together.

It sure as fuck did not feel like a good day.

Whirlygig had seen as Behemoth clawed his way up from underground, a monster of obsidian spikes and scales with a single burning red eye and jagged clubs for hands, and had leapt high and far in a way that something fifty feet tall should not be able to do. Every time he landed, anybody unlucky enough to get caught in his kill radius was cooked from the inside out, and the shockwave from his landing toppled buildings.

The air was usually dark with smoke and dust and Grue’s clouds, but sometimes it lit up with bursts of flame or lightning, and the sound of people screaming and alarms ringing blended with crashes and the occasional roar and shockwave from Behemoth.

The armband was only announcing Behemoth’s movements, not the casualties. Maybe the people in charge thought it was bad for morale for people to hear the constant string of deaths.

Whirlygig shook herself and tried to focus on what she could do. Right now, that was lifting streams of rubble in her storm, sucking the dust out of the air, clearing paths for people to evacuate, while she kept her head below the rooftops. Down on the ground, clouds of insects guided the way, forming arrows to go around obstacles, avoid unstable paths, find the quickest route. Cerberus’s dogs were hauling makeshift sleds of people who couldn’t walk, the injured, the old, the very young, Imp hustling people along, sometimes smacking the ones who dawdled or blocked the way, while Elpis and Ironclad were tearing through the bigger chunks of debris and shoving abandoned cars out of the way, without thought for collateral damage.

After all, there wouldn’t be much of the city left after today.

She wished Grue was with them- she wanted his reassuring voice, his quiet strength, his cool darkness and strong arms. Armsmaster had pulled him aside at the start of the fight, asking for his help, to spray his darkness from a Dragon ship to block the heat and radiation while Tinkertech helped divert the lightning. Grue had agreed to help, and Tattletale had gone off to help the other Thinkers from the command centre, working out the defence layout with Accord.

There was a faint rumble as a structure rose up a few streets away- a massive metal tower, unfolding into a hand sixty feet high, all the fingers spread wide. A lightning bolt struck the metal, and another a second later, curving through the air to hit it. More bolts followed, drawn to the metal. Smaller hands emerged from the first, from the fingertips, the palm and the back of the hand, turning it from a hand to a fractal hand- after a few more seconds there were so many that it looked more like some kind of post-modern Christmas tree.

“Looks like the Chicago Wards got in gear,” Elpis said without turning her head. She was doing that more lately, commenting on stuff she saw through her bugs.

“It’s interesting,” Stoneknapper said through the bugs. “I wonder if we could make our own version.”

“Focus,” Elpis said, flattening a chunk of smashed building into the road, before grabbing the underside of a smashed car and heaving upward like a power lifter. The car flipped onto its side, clearing a good part of the street.

A cape in a black bodysuit spotted with little white dots swooped down, one of the locals that Whirlygig had seen a few times already- one of the Garama, the hot capes, the ones that went public. Like she had the last few times, she concentrated the heaviest parts of her storm, all the metal and brick, into the upper section, letting it stream towards the cape. He raised a hand, and the debris compacted down into a handful of fist-sized lumps in front of him. The Garama nodded, the lumps now orbiting around him, and flew straight up. He’d launch the projectiles at Behemoth when he had an opening, and come back to Whirlygig to reload.

A stream of energy slammed into Behemoth, bright enough to hurt Whirlygig’s eyes even through her goggles. When she looked again, there was a little patch on Behemoth’s chest that looked kind of melted, and Alexandria had darted forward to slam a punch into it.

Behemoth staggered a little, but not because the punch had done any damage- he’d redirected the kinetic energy into the ground, shattering it beneath him and making him sink a little.

Legend zipped by, firing lasers that struck Behemoth from every angle. When Alexandria slammed another punch into Behemoth, the lasers became fewer and thicker, carving deeper into the flesh.

Eidolon hovered way up high, barely a speck in the sky, with his silent assistant Echo. Together they unleashed globs of multicoloured fire that clung to Behemoth, fired bolts of ice that put out fires, swept dust out of the air and compressed them into spears, caught fliers that were knocked out of the air. It was an incredible display, even more powerful than what she’d seen at the Leviathan fight.

Behemoth stumbled, really stumbled this time, as Alexandria’s next punch caught him in the back of one knee. Massive Tinkertech weapons unleashed a coordinated volley that charred and scored his skin, which Legend added to. Behemoth plunged one spiky hand into the building he’d fallen against, trying to lever himself up.

Whirlygig felt something new entering her storm, and looked down. The Undersiders had hit a roadblock- a building that had collapsed sideways into the street. Ironclad was flinging huge handfuls of the stuff out of the way, Elpis alongside him. Whirlygig shook herself and pushed forward, placing herself over the rubble. Her storm had grown so powerful that it only took a few moments for the rubble to be sucked up like dust in a hoover, along with the remains of a car and a couple of scooters. Elpis shouted something, her insects forming into arrows again, and the civilians moved forward in a great rush, the dogs hauling their sleds.

Another crash made Whirlygig glance back at Behemoth. He was pouring heat into the building he’d stabbed, melting the brick and metal into lava as he stood, the whole mess gathered up on one claw.

Legend cut into the mass with lasers, Alexandria hit Behemoth with an uppercut, and a burst of violet bubbles from somewhere scoured the lava off Behemoth’s arm as he raised it up, ready to throw-

No. Not to throw. It was a feint. The second Behemoth’s arm was pointed straight up, he unleashed a bolt of lightning directly into the sky. No lightning rod to divert it or catch it- it crashed straight into Eidolon and Echo.

“Fuck!” Whirlygig shouted on reflex. Eidolon was the strongest cape there was besides Scion, yes, but that was one hell of a hit-

The spots faded from her vision, and she breathed a sigh of relief. Eidolon and Echo were still there, hanging in the air. They weren’t falling or flailing- they just stayed right where they were.

 

 

It was like a bucket of water splashed in her face- no real damage through the area of hyper-dense insulating air Eidolon had made her put up around them, but the sensory feedback was a jolt. Enough of a jolt to shake off the Master effect Eidolon had put her under before they deployed. For the first time in so long, Noelle had control of herself again- and she had Eidolon’s powerset to boot.

Eidolon himself hadn’t noticed- he was busy blasting Behemoth, fighting fires, and using telekinesis to grab people out of harm’s way. He left the aerokinesis that kept them aloft and protected, the Thinker power detecting other capes in danger, and the other Thinker power that allowed her to relay the relevant data of the first two, to her.

He wanted to stretch his muscles, use the strong powers that he’d lost over the years, now that he didn’t have to hide that his powers had been slowly getting weaker for years. They weren’t waning anymore; not now that Eidolon had used the new power he’d found, the one that Glaistig Uaine had led him to with cryptic hints, to replenish his own power by draining energy from the deviants Cauldron kept in the higher levels of their base. The ones with mutations as strange as hers had been, or stranger. People with parts missing, people with powers that never turned off, people who were so lost in their powers they could barely respond. Failed experiments, kept in horrible little cells, never to see their own worlds or families again.

Noelle had been made to follow him along to the cells, in case he needed additional powers to handle the prisoners. She’d watched helplessly as he’d drained the powers out of them, as he’d insisted it was for the greater good and acted sorry about it, then delighted in feeling his strongest powers come back to him.

Some colder, clinical part of her was amazed that he’d never thought of the solution himself and had needed to be steered to it by a crazy lady who thought she was Queen of the Fairies. Basic logic- if something you need is running out, then you find a way to top it up. That covered everything from the milk in your fridge to the gas in your car to the mana potions in your games to, apparently, the energy in your powers. He’d just tried to push through, picking fights with powerful opponents in hopes of unlocking some hidden reserve. What a moron.

And now the moron hadn’t noticed that she was free. She kept relaying data, kept the air shield up, while she thought hard. She’d had nothing to do but think while she was controlled by the various Master powers that Eidolon had kept her leashed with. She’d dreamed horrible dreams of killing him, killing the rest of the Triumvirate, killing everyone and everything, finding the right combination of powers to find the rest of her team from wherever Cauldron had stashed them, and get them all back home.

But it wouldn’t matter. Cauldron was experimenting with cloning- she’d heard them talking about how they’d made a fuss in front of Hero and Legend to throw them off the scent, then went ahead anyway. They could bring back almost anyone she killed- and there was nowhere she could run that they couldn’t find her and drag her back. Her powers only worked if she had someone to touch, to turn into and copy the powers of. They could just snatch her up with a portal.

So if she was going to rebel, she had to do it in a way that they’d never get her back in a cell. The thought solidified in her mind. Think of it like a game- what were the goals, and what were the possible paths to achieve them?

First thing to do was to stop Eidolon from putting her back under. She could probably kill him, but she wasn’t completely sure, and she wasn’t sure what would happen if she killed someone while she was copying their powers. She might just lose all her powers and drop out of the air.

So maybe take him out of play in another way. She banished the power detecting capes in danger, let another one bubble up- a Master power, projected through the voice. Eidolon had quite a few strong Master powers that weren’t worn down, since it wouldn’t fit his heroic image to control people’s minds. She tweaked the aerokinesis to create a tunnel of air from her mouth to Eidolon’s head, and said “Keep fighting as if nothing’s changed. Don’t try to stop me or signal to anyone else.”

She felt the words sink into his head, bind him into that course of action. His only outward action was to fire off another bolt of that multicoloured fire. She wondered if he was raging, screaming inside his own head, begging to be let out. Too bad.

Second thing- hurt Cauldron. How? Reveal them? They were a conspiracy theory, and she had no evidence. So maybe… discredit them? Make Eidolon do something terrible? Or do something scary herself.

The draining power. Capes feared losing their powers more than anything. Some of the prisoners had been more afraid of being drained than being killed. She let go of the relay power, let others bubble up. Durability- no. Acid spit- no. Explosive forcefields- no. The draining power- she grabbed and held it. Eidolon hadn’t let her use it before, but she knew what it felt like through the connection they had when she was assuming his form. She felt the passengers light up, taking form as glimmers of light and shadow. Eidolon was a mosaic, three interlocking scenes flowing through and around one another.

It crossed her mind that she could have used the cape detection power to locate some targets. Hindsight was 20/20. But she did have an aspect of her own power- something left over from when she’d been mutating and growing and constantly hungry. An ability to smell other parahumans and their powers, get a vague sense of how strong they were and what they could do. The Triumvirate were all so powerful, very potent, and so were a lot of the deviants. But there were others, and one in particular. She’d never found a smell anywhere near as potent as when she’d met Elpis.

She let the aerokinesis stir the air, bringing her all the scents. It was hard to parse them, but one stood out. She let herself drop- Eidolon had to use his telekinesis to support and shield himself as she left him behind. She released the Master power instead, and something else bubbled up- a post-cognition power, letting her see images of the past.

The smell led her straight to Elpis, who was with her team, standing across from a larger team in matching red and black uniforms, with red masks. A couple of wounded capes were behind the Undersiders, being loaded onto sleds pulled by the big mutant monster things.

Everyone stopped and stared as she came to hang several feet above their heads. “Uh, hello?” Elpis asked, opening her helmet to show her mouth. “Echo, right? Something you need?”

The thought of draining her was tempting- all that power in one person, shown as a collage of brilliant images putting Eidolon’s mosaic to shame. It’d throw the world into chaos, destroying the great new hero who’d beaten the Slaughterhouse Nine. But Elpis had been nice to her, helped with Leet’s cure. It wasn’t her fault that Cauldron had taken Noelle afterwards.

The post-cognition power showed faint images around Elpis, or her kissing the hand of that healer girl, Panacea, and hugging a thin man with glasses. A family member maybe?

The other group took her a second to recognise. Cauldron had given her some files on major important groups, and these ones had been marked as dangerous. The Yangban, the military capes of China. They had their powers split and shared amongst the whole group so they all had identical powersets, trained to use them well and indoctrinated to use them as ordered.

The post-cognition power highlighted them as well- several of them crouched over wounded capes, using a teleport power to send them away. No- to kidnap them so the Yangban could use their powers, the way Cauldron had.

She could smell them, like a stew of many ingredients blended together. To her their powers looked like copies of the same jumbled pictures, repeated a few dozen times. The draining power reached out and connected to the images- she dropped to the ground, let the aerokinesis go and let new powers shuffle into place. The energy flowed from the Yangban through her and into the powers- stuff that Eidolon had used up long ago, like healing, precognition, matter deletion.

The Yangban felt something, and started backing away. One of them tried to use a power, and screamed when nothing happened. She drained more, letting powers fill up and shuffle aside, two lines, no waiting, until all that was left were dregs and distant powers that she couldn’t touch. Eidolon had filled up the strongest powers he could find- now she had charged more, all at her fingertips.

Noelle grabbed a flight power and rocketed back into the air, adding an energy displacement power for protection and a Thinker power to anticipate threats. The fight against Behemoth was starting to slip- the Triumvirate were doing their best, but the Dragonships had been destroyed almost entirely- the only one still flying was the one emitting that black fog, and it was in retreat. Dragon- who was being watched by the Dragonslayers.

A thought occurred to her- she could hurt Cauldron by splitting them in two. She aimed herself towards the ship and rocketed forward, intercepting it as it fled the battle with the darkness cape- what was his name? Gruesome?

She drew alongside the ship, grabbed hold, and pulled herself hand over hand until she found what seemed like a camera, focusing on her. The lens reflected her mirror mask, and the mirror mask reflected the lens back in a strange visual effect. “Dragon,” she shouted over the wind, “I’m using you as a go-between. Steve and Frank need to know that their friends are lying to them about the first Wards. They’re already working on cloning them.”

The threat detection pinged before she could say anything else- she looked over to see Alexandria had broken off from Behemoth and was heading her way. Frankly, Noelle was surprised it had taken this long for one of the Triumvirate to realise something was up.

She let go of Dragon and flew straight up. Maybe she could use the draining power again- depowering Alexandria would certainly hurt Cauldron. Although the draining power only worked at fairly close range- she’d have to get in close-

The threat sense pinged again. When she looked back, Alexandria had grabbed a rock. With her kind of strength, that was better than a missile.

Maybe she could swap to a Blaster power, or a better defence power- but those would take a few seconds to be strong enough to do the job, and Alexandria would be able to kill her in that moment. Wracking her brain for a solution, and finding nothing, all of a sudden Noelle felt numb. She was tired, her head hurt from all the noise, her ears were ringing- when had that started? Was it the shockwaves and explosions? Or was it further back? Had it started ever since they’d come to this fucking world?

She flew upward, and Alexandria coiled her arm back, ready to throw. Noelle let go of all the powers, grabbed the first ones that came, and threw herself at Behemoth.

She’d broken free, in the end. She wouldn’t go back in the cell, and that was the important thing. She was so tired of Earth Bet- so tired of the people who kept her prisoner, who did horrible things for what they said was the greater good. She was tired of it all.

But she didn’t hate the people who lived there, exactly. She felt sorry for them living in this horrible world full of monsters. She wished she could have done something to help.

One power was rocketing her towards Behemoth, fire bursting from every part of her body to propel her. Another power was a combination of regeneration and explosive flesh, turning her body into a bomb. The third was a sound manipulation power- low-level but wide range.

In the ears of everyone within a quarter mile, she whispered “Goodbye,” as she passed into Behemoth’s kill aura, aiming for that horrible red eye.

She was just wondering if there was anything else for her to say when she made impact, and burned up like a star.

 

 

Echo’s kamikaze attack had done some damage, hitting Behemoth right in the eye and staggering him. The time bomb that Elpis had warned them about, set up a plan for, had done more damage than anything else, reducing Behemoth to a fucking skeleton.

And he was still coming.

Victoria dropped down behind a broken wall, reaching out to the cape huddled there, with fresh burns all along their arms. They reached out pitifully, and she carefully scooped them up in her arms, mindful of their burns, before taking off, keeping a low altitude for cover and steady pace to avoid jostling the patient. All those years of practice ferrying people to whatever hospital Amy was volunteering at were really paying off.

Elpis was outside the India Gate, working alongside the Undersiders and those Wards from Chicago. She’d taken her massive longbow apart and was currently rebuilding it with strips of metal into something the length of a sixteen-wheeler, while thousands of insects spiralled through the air- flies carried spiders as they produced thread, crossing the lines over and back into threads that became strings that were becoming one single cable. Some of the bugs formed a hand that curled into a thumbs up as she passed by, flying through the doors to the nearest medical station.

“Burns,” she said to the doctor as she laid the patient on the bunk provided. She glanced around briefly, thought she spotted Amy’s mousy frizz as she bent over another patient, but there wasn’t time to talk. They’d talked a little before, but they couldn’t talk now, and she knew that.

It still ate at her.

The doctor nodded. “Got it.”

Victoria took off without another word. She didn’t have the spare energy.

Outside, Elpis was almost finished with her project. Three massive strips of metal fanned out from either side of a long platform, with a geared contraption running on a toothed rail down the middle. The whole thing was set on a cart cannibalised out of a couple of scooters that allowed it to turn in a circle and adjust the elevation. Imp and one of the Chicago Wards, a blonde girl in a metal costume, were holding the silk cable, now capped with heavy metal hooks. Flechette was standing by, cranking and firing her arbalest at Behemoth without pause. Sabah- Parian- was next to her, weaving another puppet out of scraps of cloth that Elpis’s bugs dropped at her feet. Victoria could see the metal bolts sticking out of Behemoth, all clustered in the centre of his eye.

A ballista, she realised. A massive siege crossbow, with Flechette’s power. That could work.

“Glory Girl, we need your strength,” a cloud of insects buzzed. Victoria shuddered at Elpis’s little trick, but flew down to help. Elpis had earned that trust.

Cerberus’s dogs were lashed to thick metal cables capped with steel hoops on either side of the ballista’s limbs, as were Parian’s dolls. Ironclad was on one side, Elpis was on the other. “Help me pull this,” Elpis said, already holding onto the cable that was linked to all three of the ballista’s left arms.

Victoria dropped down on the other side of the cable and grabbed hold. “Think it’ll work?” she asked, adjusting her grip.

“I really fucking hope so,” Elpis grunted. “Everybody pull!”

Cerberus whistled, and the dogs started moving, dragging the arms back. Parian’s puppets planted their feet and hauled along. Elpis threw herself into it like a tug of war, and Victoria used her flight as much as her strength. The arms bent, creaking like a cello, curving back, back, back. Victoria was afraid they might snap and send metal scything everywhere.

“Hook the cable!” Elpis shouted. Imp and the Chicago girl ran forward, slipping the hooks into the hoops. “Release!” Elpis shouted, taking her hands away from the cable. Victoria followed suit, flying back a few feet.

The ballista jolted as the arms snapped forward, and caught against the silk rope. It creaked, but it held.

Elpis unfolded a long handle from the geared winch and started cranking, drawing the rope back. The arms followed, bit by bit, as Elpis reached the end and locked it into place. “Flechette, you’re up,” she said, picking up what looked like a spear with razor wire coiled below the head and loading it into the ballista.

“You’re only going to have a few seconds before my power affects the whole bolt,” Flechette warned, stepping up to the ballista. “And it might just cut through this thing if you don’t time it right.”

“I accept the risk,” Elpis said, closing her helmet. “Everybody step back in case this thing falls apart, and make the call to get clear.” Thin lines of bugs rose from the ground to usher everyone back to a safe distance as Elpis grabbed the controls.

A Chicago Ward, a Tinker with piledrivers on his gauntlets and a single red lens on his helmet, pressed a button on his armband and spoke into it. “Hard override- all fliers clear the area in front of Behemoth. Elpis and Flechette have a weapon to try.”

It took a few seconds for the message to be relayed, and then every flier peeled away, even the Triumvirate. Without them, Behemoth only had the Tinker weapon emplacements and the defensive walls to worry about, and he shambled forward, wounded but not slowing.
