Flechette laid a hand on the tip of the bolt for a moment. “Fire,” she said, hastily stepping back from the weapon.

Elpis pulled the trigger, and the ballista jolted back half a foot as the bolt was launched out from it. As it flew, the coils of wire unravelled, spinning around the bolt. Behemoth suddenly jinked sideways, like he was trying to dodge, but Alexandria and Eidolon struck together, arresting his movement for the bolt to strike him just off centre, between his shoulder and where his heart should be. It cut through the Endbringer’s flesh like it wasn’t even there, the trailing wires slicing through the surrounding flesh. Behemoth’s arm drooped, barely attached, and thick chunks of flesh fell to the ground.

Alexandria hit him, and the arm came free, smashing to the ground and crushing a building.

A cheer rose up from the defenders at the greatest wound ever inflicted on an Endbringer. The attacks resumed with new vigour, lasers and missiles and exploding polygonal shapes. Elpis roared in triumph even as she hurried away from the controls to the uppermost right arm, where the cable had snapped free. “Make another bolt!” she yelled. “We’re going to kill this fucker!”

“Fuck yeah!” Cerberus shouted, grabbing a chunk of metal and throwing it to a Chicago Ward in a flowing white robe.

The ground rumbled violently. Victoria rose up into the air, peering through the haze of energy and dust. Behemoth was striking downward with his one arm and his horned head, sinking lower into the churning and smoking earth. “He’s burrowing,” she called down. “I think he’s retreating.”

“Oh for fuck’s sake!” Elpis shouted back. She reattached the cable and stormed back to the controls, snatching up the next bolt. “Think we can get him?”

Victoria made to answer, when something caught her eye. Not down on the ground, but up in the air.

Scion had arrived.

 

 

Kudzu jolted upright, consciousness slamming into her like a battering ram. She tripped over her words, stammered incoherently- which might have been a good thing, given that all she could think to say were the filthiest swear words she was capable of.

“Damn, that was quick,” someone said. She turned her head and saw Legend and a boy she didn’t recognise, wearing a white robe and a golden sheep mask. “You took one hell of a hit there.”

Kudzu instinctively reached for her head- the building had come down, she’d thrown that little kid out the window to give him a chance. “There was a boy-”

“He’s alright,” Legend said. “A villain called Drift caught him, got him out, told others where to dig you out. You did great.”

“The fight?”

Legend managed a smile. “Scion turned up. He didn’t let Behemoth go.”

Kudzu blinked. “So what happened to Behemoth?” she said dumbly. She thought she understood what Legend meant, but the thought was too big to fit in her head. She had to twist it around and push from a weird angle, like when it had taken four of her to move her old couch into her new apartment.

“Scion killed him,” the goat kid said. “Dragged him out of the ground, disintegrated him until there was nothing left. There’s a load of videos people can show you if you want.”

“It’s true,” Legend said. “This is,” her boss shook his head, “amazing.”

Kudzu slowly sat up, expecting pain. There was nothing at all. “So you’re a healer?” she asked the goat boy. It was a stupid detail, but she still couldn’t quite parse a dead Endbringer.

“Sort of. Name’s Scapegoat. I can take people’s injuries onto myself, dump them onto other people.”

Kudzu thought for a minute. “Sounds like you must need one hell of a pain tolerance,” she said finally.

“Yyyyyyup,” Scapegoat drawled.

“Wait,” Kudzu said, “Who got the injuries?”

Legend shifted in his seat. “That’s actually part of why I’m here. Not that I wouldn’t come to visit you, but we needed someone to stand guard.” He nodded past Kudzu, and she turned her head to the other side of her bed.

A woman was slumped in a chair, fully armoured and heavily armed. Weapons hung from her belt, guns were mounted on her forearms, and insects crawled restlessly over her grey and blue armour. She managed a nod and a clumsy wave to Kudzu.

“Holy shit,” Kudzu said.

“Ish no bag dull,” Elpis slurred, waving her hand back the other way. “I’ve go’ rugen’rashun, I’m already ge’ing better.” She sat up in her chair, rolling her head from side to side. “Plus I figure I owe yuh- you, for all th’ crap the Butchers did to your clones back in the day.” Her helmet opened, and she smacked her lips. “Feels like I’ve got peanut butter in my mouth.”

“Must have been something to the taste centre,” Scapegoat suggested. “First time I managed to swap from one to me to another too fast to really feel the symptoms, so I wouldn’t know.” He sounded very pleased about that.

Elpis shook her head. “No, it’s not the taste of peanut butter, just the consistency. It’s going though.” She stood from her chair, weapons clinking. “I’m going to go see what else needs doing. Kudzu, Legend.” She nodded and left, Scapegoat trailing after her.

“Dead Endbringer,” Kudzu said. She felt the smile growing on her face, wide enough to hurt.

Legend smiled back. “Dead Endbringer.” The smile didn’t quite reach his eyes.

“Are you okay, sir?”

Legend sighed. “I’ve just… got a lot on my mind. I need to talk with Alexandria and Eidolon about some of the losses today.” His fingers curled into fists in his lap.

Chapter 150: 15.4

Wednesday September 7th, Amy Dallon’s apartment, Brockton Bay

Dad had insisted on helping to clear away the boxes and wrapping paper, which had got him and Flashbang talking about their kids, and from there, talking about the changes to the city.

“We’re way ahead of schedule in clearing the boats,” Dad said, stuffing another crumpled ball of paper into a trash bag. “And a lot of the stuff that got transmuted is selling well. The real problem is what to do with all the remaining scrap. A lot of it’s so rusted it’s barely worth reclaiming.”

Flashbanng hummed. “I can see how that’d be a problem.” He tossed another paper ball into the bag from ten feet away- nothing but net.

“Guess he’s got a lot of practice from throwing his grenades around,” Anchorage said.

“There’s some kind of joke about him handling his balls, but I can’t be bothered,” Quarrel snorted.

“Boo,” Rotter jeered, “Put in the effort.”

I popped another forkful of cake into my mouth, chewing slowly to savour the taste. It had been a bit awkward when all three groups had brought one- New Wave, the Wards, and the Undersiders. I’d quickly suggested we use the chocolate sponge New Wave had brought as the official birthday cake and use the others as spares, which had got Brandish to stop giving me the side eye. Lady Photon had lit the candles with a laser, Amy had blown them out, and people had relaxed, even unmasking to each other.

Brandish herself was now talking with Amy over by the couch, Victoria and Gallant curled up together, all of them talking about Amy’s new responsibilities now that she’d joined the Protectorate proper. I could hear Glory Girl teasingly asking Amy if she’d be collecting autographs from all the famous heroes she’d be meeting, Brandish interjecting with advice about building professional relationships. Gallant mostly listened, letting Glory Girl do most of the talking. It made a lot of sense that he was actually Dean Stansfield under the mask, now that I knew- the polite bearing and thoughtful tone was easy to pick up on.

“Makes you wonder how that relationship’s going to work out,” Flinch mused. “She’s unmasked, he’s not; she’s a hero all the way, he’s Protectorate plus the family business.”

“Ah, they’ll be alright,” Bearskin said bracingly.

Despite the initial awkwardness, I was glad that Amy had patched things up enough with her family to invite them to her housewarming slash birthday party. Talks over the phone had led to lunches out, which had led to family dinners. There was still some distance, but a healthy amount. They’d brought over her things from her old room, helped set her apartment up, and made an effort to avoid crowding her and talk to everyone else in the room.

They’d also subtly checked out the security of the place. The PRT had arranged it from one of several secure residences they kept around the city, which meant it was close to their headquarters, the door was on reinforced hinges with thick deadbolts, and the windows were made of tempered glass. Victoria had declared it ‘good enough’.

The Wards had come over with more typically teenager stuff- soda and chips and stuff to make it more of a party. Vista had expanded the room to give us more space, and was now carefully petting Rachel’s dogs off in one corner, with Parian looking like she was working up the nerve to ask as well. Chariot had looked awkward until Lisa had taken him aside for a conversation I couldn’t make out, after which he’d loosened up- probably nervous about being the new guy in the room.

“Good of her to do that,” Tock Tick said. “He seems like a good kid.”

Weld, who was actually the newest guy in the room, seemed perfectly at ease. He’d brought his own plastic fork to eat the cake with, chatting with Aegis, Tarquin and Isabella, mostly about art. Apparently it was a minor hobby of Weld’s, since he could work metal like putty. Isabella had picked up some stuff from all the figurines she collected, Tarquin had some ideas about using his own power, and Aegis was occasionally chiming in, sometimes with a Spanish comment that Isabella grinned at.

Laserdream and Shielder had wound up talking with Brian and Aisha, two pairs of siblings. Aisha was shamelessly flirting with Shielder, whose reddening face was contrasting marvellously with his blue hair. Laserdream was treating the whole thing like it was a comedy show, while Brian just seemed fed up.

That left me, Lady Photon, Clockblocker, Spitfire and Flechette in a weird little group of leftovers, discussing the current state of the city.

“Lost Garden’s apparently making their way towards Brockton,” Lady Photon said, finishing her piece of cake and folding the paper plate up.

“I’m guessing that’s a creepy villain group?” Emily asked, refilling her soda.

“Yeah, I’ve heard of them,” Flechette said. It turned out her name was Lily out of costume, and without her visor I could see how she glanced over at Parian every so often. “They’re led by a guy called Barrow- he creates a kind of weird forest around himself. Apparently the group mostly lives off the stuff in the forest- fruits and vegetables and stuff.”

“Sounds like some kind of hippy commune,” Stoneknapper said. “I wonder if they have any fun mushrooms in that forest.”

“Sounds like a nature cult with powers,” Clockblocker said. He’d said to call him Dennis, but even with the ginger hair, I just couldn’t manage it. “I bet they have a bunch of weird rituals to get in touch with Mother Earth or some crap.”

“See, he gets it,” Stoneknapper said.

“It seems kind of stupid for them to be coming towards here,” Emily said. “I mean, if they’re self-sufficient. They could just wander off somewhere and not have to deal with people.”

“Yeah, but I’ll bet that Barrow’s forest can’t make a TV, or books,” I pointed out.

“Or chocolate,” Needler said.

“Or chocolate,” I parroted.

“Oh damn, yeah. That’s gotta suck, actually,” Emily said.

“Well, we can plan on how to push them away,” Lady Photon said. I just could not wrap my head around calling her Sarah, or Mrs Pelham, and the Butchers agreed with me.

“Keeping Brockton Bay villain-free,” Flinch said. “Hell of a thing.”

“Yeah.” We’d had groups drifting in the direction of Brockton, a few probing motions and feints in our direction, but we’d been able to push them away without trouble. It helped that online chatter indicated the Undersiders had a solid reputation now, after multiple S-Class events, and Flechette was being credited as the one who’d made it possible for us to take Behemoth’s arm off.

It was also likely that Accord was doing some work behind the scenes, and I still had no idea how much interference Cauldron might be doing. Of the two, I was more inclined to work with Accord- his plans were helping to rebuild the city at a fantastic rate, and I was considering allowing him to establish a small foothold. The Thinker had several legitimate businesses under his umbrella- it would be easy for him to expand, creating jobs and pulling more people over the poverty line.

I suspected that eventually there would be some fresh Triggers even as the city continued to stabilise, or some low-key villains who could evade us- Movers and Thinkers and Strangers, people who could get out fast, or never even be seen at all. Eventually there would be a cape scene in Brockton Bay again, not just heroes. But for now, the city was at peace.

“I want to think about what comes after that. Beyond that.”

“Yes, you mentioned,” Photon said. “An alliance of heroes.”

“Say what now?” Clockblocker asked.

“I want to try and link up with other hero groups along the East Coast,” I explained. “We’ve got the city on the rise, we’ve got a crapload of cash, we’ve got ironclad reputation- we need to capitalise on that. There’s enough heroes in town that we can afford to have at least a few of us away. We reach out to other heroes, add our strength to take out the more problematic villains, lighten their load- we’ve already got positive responses from Boilerplate, Clean-Cut and Rabbit Punch down in Boston, and a few more are interested. That frees up more heroes to help out, push on the other villains. A lot of the heroes will be too entrenched in their hometowns to move around easily, but I figure we can get a few teams worth of floating heroes to crack down on the worst.”

I could see the thought unfolding in their heads, the expressions spreading across their faces.

“Holy shit, that could work,” Flechette said.

“Such a glowing approval,” Muramasa snorted.

“That’s the hope,” I said instead of voicing Muramasa’s comment.

“Well, I’m all for it,” Clockblocker said. “I mean, I don’t want to get cocky, but things are going pretty well. The Nine’s dead, Behemoth’s dead, and villains everywhere are afraid Eidolon’s gonna come knocking if they go too far.”

“Still freaks me the fuck out,” Butcher said. “Removing somebody’s powers? I’d rather die all over again.”

I agreed with both statements. I’d seen for myself as Eidolon’s power-copying protégé Echo had permanently removed the powers of the Yangban squad who’d attended the New Delhi battle, and it still scared the crap out of me. It scared a lot of other people too- no parahuman had ever had to choose between their power and their life before, but since the powers were the only good thing that came out of whatever horrible trauma they suffered, I was pretty sure most people would rather die than go back to being a powerless normal.

The Protectorate had admitted the truth about Echo after the battle- it turned out she’d been a former villain who’d joined the Protectorate out of guilt for her former actions. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts to rehabilitate her, she’d suffered a breakdown and chosen to sacrifice herself to try and stop Behemoth.

The Chinese Union-Imperial were obviously furious that they’d lost a couple dozen capes to a violation of the Truce, but Dragon had provided evidence of multiple capes being teleported to China when the Yangban were around, and not coming back. There was a lot of talk on the news of diplomatic talks to get the capes returned to their home countries and whether the Yangban’s actions counted as a prior violation of the Truce, and on and on.

“I might be more for holding the fort here, at least for now,” Emily said. “They’ve got me helping with melting down the boats, so-”

“Fair enough. It’s your choice.”

“I’ll talk to the rest of the team,” Photon said, glancing over at her kids, “But I’m pretty sure they’ll be willing to help. New Wave’s been losing momentum for years- it’s time we get back into business.”

“Having Parian join certainly gave them a boost,” Tactical mused. “Disposable Brutes that can be remade on the fly? She’s invaluable.”

“Not to mention they can actually fly,” Firecracker added. “One of these days we need to ride one of those things into battle.”

“There’s no way she can make a puppet that looks more badass than one of Rachel’s dogs,” Nemean pointed out.

“Yeah, and she’d probably have us riding a giant butterfly or some crap,” Rotter snorted, forming a mental image of me standing on top of a giant plush blue butterfly, arms folded, flying to the tune of Ride of the Valkyries.

It took me a moment to stop giggling, and a moment more for me to explain to the others why I’d started laughing in the first place.

 

 

“Stay in touch,” Victoria insisted, finally ending the hug Amy had allowed once the party finally wrapped up. The Wards had already said their goodbyes, needing to get ready for school tomorrow, and the Undersiders had left not long after. I was mostly lingering because I had some ideas for Tinker security mechanisms I wanted to run past Amy, and because I was the only person who didn’t have to sleep or have anything to do tomorrow.

“I promise,” Amy said with a small smile.

“And let us know if you need anything,” Flashbang added.

“Got it.”

Brandish quietly cleared her throat. “We’re very proud of you, Amy.”

That one seemed to throw Amy for a second. “Thanks, Mom.”

“Well, we should leave you to it,” Dad said. “First night in your own place, it’s a big milestone. You’re doing better than when I first moved out- it was typical bachelor squalor.”

I tried to imagine my dad as being a young bachelor in a crappy little apartment, and just couldn’t form the image.

“Plus she doesn’t have a bunch of moron roommates and a creepy landlord,” Quarrel noted.

“Yeah, I think I’m just going to sort all my presents and turn in,” Amy said. “Thanks for all the food, Mr Hebert.”

“No problem.”

Finally, after many lingering goodbyes, Dad headed off to his car, and New Wave took off into the air, Parian creating a pair of bird puppets, one for her and one for Brandish and Flashbang. Amy shut the door and ran a hand through her hair with a sigh.

“Not that I’m not happy about the party, but I’m glad it’s over. I think I’m all peopled out for today.”

“I can leave too if you want-”

“Not you,” Amy said, poking me with a finger. “I don’t mean you. You’re not ‘people’, you’re Taylor. That’s a whole other category just for you.”

“Ooooh!” Anchorage cooed childishly.

“When the moon hits your eye, like a big pizza-pie, that’s amoreeeeeee!” Stoneknapper sang, deliberately badly.

I blushed at the praise and the teasing. “Okay. Uh, sure.”

“Plus, it’s the whole ‘Surprise, you’re 18’ thing,” Amy continued. “Like I just skipped over my 17th and we’re all just not talking about it.”

“Right.” That was something I’d noticed everybody carefully avoiding throughout the party. Amy had mentioned a while ago that she was still processing it.

Brandish had apparently provided some good arguments- that Amy was small for her age when they took her in, and had a spotty education record, mostly kept home by Marquis. It was safer to change the details, and made it easier for Amy to start school fresh, at a level she could handle.

All very good points- but Carol Dallon was a lawyer after all. Amy was still processing it.

“So, do you want help moving stuff?” I asked, gesturing to the pile of presents.

Amy gave me a quick look. “Yeah, if you could move the big bags into the cupboards, that’d be great.”

“Can do,” I said, hefting the big sacks of rice and pasta Dad had bought. His idea had been to give Amy a bunch of essentials for living and cooking alone, and Amy had appreciated the gesture. There was also a lot of canned stuff, beans and tuna and pasta sauce, plus a couple of little bottles of herbs and spices.

Amy got to sorting the rest by herself; Victoria had got her a boxset of gory horror movies, Brandish had got her a nice coffee maker, and Flashbang got her a bunch of recipe books focused on easy recipes for beginners.

“I guess dads have a similar mindset,” Bearskin pointed out.

Parian had brought a very soft bedspread she’d woven herself. It had all the symbols of New Wave worked into the pattern, which I thought was a nice touch. Amy disappeared into her bedroom with it bundled in her arms, while I got the coffee machine plugged in for her. I vaguely heard the rustle of fabric from her open door.

A pack of funny mugs from Isa and Tarquin, a poster from Aegis, bags of chocolate from Vista and Rachel. Laserdream and Shielder had got her a comfy bathrobe and extra fuzzy socks respectively, perfect for relaxing. Gallant had bought her a nice-looking painting in a frame- I figured I’d leave that for Amy to decide where to put it. Brian had got her some good quality pots and pans, Aisha had got her a t-shirt that said “Brockton Bay Babe”, which Amy had bemusedly thanked her for. Weld had made her a little statue of a snake like her necklace, Emily had got her some fantasy books, Chariot got her some CDs.

As for myself, I’d got her the fanciest chocolates I could find, and several sets of reinforced silk clothes fit for civvies or costume. I’d worried that she might not like them, but Amy had positively glowed when she’d unwrapped them, so I was counting that as a win.

I caught the scent of something from Amy’s bedroom- lavender and lilac, mixed with smoke. “Is that incense?” I asked.

“Scented candles,” Amy answered. “Lisa’s present, remember? Good for relieving stress, she said.”

“Oh yeah.”

Amy was silent for a moment. “Are you done with the big stuff?” She asked at last.

“Yep. Do you want me to help hang the painting or anything?”

“That can wait. Just… come here.”

I crossed from the kitchen table to her bedroom at the back of the apartment. “Do you need-”

I stopped. I could have sworn I heard my brain snap.

Amy was perched on the bed, hands on her knees, wearing something white and lacy and gauzy. Her regular clothes were dumped on a chair in the corner. The lights were off, and the scented candles cast flickering light across her from the dresser and the side table, shadows dancing over bare freckled skin.

The Butchers burst into lewd whistles and cheers and encouragement to me. I reflexively shoved the loudest into the dark as my face burned red.

“How did you not see this coming?” Needler said with fond exasperation.

“I’m 18 now,” Amy said quietly. “I know you said you don’t always feel the same age, but I figured…” she trailed off, rubbing her thighs with her hands. The movement drew my attention, and I swallowed before I could drool.

“Um. I mean. Um. You don’t- I mean if you’re not comfortable-”

“Taylor.” Amy stood up, and I made an embarrassing sound as I saw just how little that outfit covered. “I want this. I want you.” She took a step towards me, staring up at me with those big brown eyes that turned gold in the candlelight.

“The Butchers-”

“Can shut the fuck up,” Amy said firmly, taking another step forward. “They’re no part in this.”

I braced myself for one of them to interrupt, to make some horrible joke, to jeer about how Marquis’s daughter was standing in front of them in lingerie.

None of them said a word. I could feel their breathless anticipation pressing against the inside of my head, but none of them made a sound.

I swallowed again, took a deep breath, smelling the floral candles and Amy’s body scent- that impossibly fresh scent of her power keeping her skin clean from bacteria. I could smell her pheromones wafting through the air, and I could feel my body reacting.

“Okay,” I managed, feeling like my brain was dribbling out of my ears.

Amy took two quick steps forward, went up on tiptoe, wrapped her arms around my shoulders, and crushed her lips against mine.

Oh god, she was so soft- her lips, her hair, her body. I felt her warmth as she made a breathy little noise, and kissed her back with all the force I dared.

I kicked the door shut and stepped the both of us towards the bed.

The Butchers held their silence until sunrise the next morning.

Chapter 151: 15.5

Saturday 10th September, Brockton Bay Cemetery

It had been just over a week since Behemoth’s death at New Delhi, and there was a lot to do- the world was buzzing with the news of a dead Endbringer, capes were all trying to figure out what this would mean going forward. Reconstruction efforts in Brockton Bay were ongoing, and going faster with the rush of hope flowing through the people. Accord’s last message had claimed a cynical belief that the other Endbringers would react to this, but he was still willing to up the pace of his support for the Bay’s revival.

I had about a hundred different things I needed to be doing. But right now, I needed to do this. There hadn’t been an opportunity in years.

I walked down the rows, holding a bunch of flowers in my hands- Lilies and baby’s breath. Despite the years since any of the Butchers had visited, I knew exactly where to go.

Butcher finally stirred as I reached his mother’s grave. Wordlessly, he directed me to set the flowers down carefully, pick a leaf off the headstone, and give the top a gentle touch.

Butcher had always been bad-tempered, foul-mouthed, violent and mean. He’d had very few friends and plenty of enemies. But the one person who he’d genuinely loved, and who’d loved him no matter what he’d done, was his mother.

I stayed kneeling on the grass for a few more minutes, neither the Butchers nor me saying anything, before Butcher finally sighed. “I’m done,” he rumbled.

After another second, I got to my feet and walked away.

 

 

Tuesday 13th September, Philadelphia

Angie twisted her fingers together. She was middle-aged now, a few grey hairs amongst the brown at the temples, lines on her face. Her clothes were comfortably nice, and she wore a pearl necklace around her throat. She didn’t have a wedding ring, which pained Flinch to see.

“I… I don’t know where to begin,” she admitted.

I opened my mouth, and Flinch’s words came out. “Me either,” he admitted.  I’d come in casual clothes, just a mask to cover my face- I didn’t think it’d be easier for Flinch’s family to have to talk to me in full armour.

Carmen and Tina sat on either side of their mother, looking similarly stricken. The last time Flinch had seen them, they’d been three and one years old. Now they were grown young women; Carmen aged 23 with her black hair in a straight bob instead of the curls Angie had cooed over; Tina fresh out of college at 21 with shoulder-length hair and a bar in her left eyebrow. Technically speaking, they were both older than their father now, depending on whether you counted Flinch’s 20 years with the Butchers.

It had been a long time since the Protectorate had passed along Flinch’s letter to his family, and a long time for them to reply. I imagined that the shock of getting a letter from someone who’d been dead for twenty years would take a while to process.

But, after the New Delhi battle, I’d finally received a response, haltingly asking if I’d be willing to come and see them in person, so Angie Juarez could speak to her late husband, and so Flinch’s daughters could finally talk to their dad.

I’d been considering a trip to Philadelphia for a while now anyway. Besides a few indie heroes to reach out to and some nastier villains to take down, there was also the Parahuman Asylum, where capes with powers or mental problems too dangerous to be allowed out in public were usually sent. I knew Labyrinth had been a resident there for a time- so had Burnscar. Amy was checking with the PRT to see if there was anything she could do for some of the residents.

But that was all secondary- right now, it was about Flinch reconnecting with his family.

“I missed you,” Flinch said at last.

Angie clamped her hands around each other to stop fidgeting and took a deep breath. “I missed you too, Miguel,” she said in a rush. “How… I mean, are you always attached to the Butcher, or… I don’t know if you can ghost about wherever you want.”

“No,” Flinch said, “I’m always stuck with whoever the Butcher is. See what they see, hear what they hear. If I could have left, I’d have stayed with you as much as I could.”

Angie nodded, looking crestfallen. “Right.”

“Are you okay?” Carmen asked, shifting in her seat. “I mean, I read the files on Butcher- the things they did. If you had to see all that-”

“That was… It’s been rough,” Flinch admitted. “But having Elpis in charge, being a hero- it helped me come back to myself. They’ve got easier to live with.”

“But if you’re stuck in Elpis’s body, does that mean you feel it when-”

“Yes,” Flinch said quickly. “Trust me, it’s better if you don’t think about it too hard.”

Carmen looked vaguely disgusted. Tina looked very disgusted.

“I think they’re thinking about it,” Firecracker said, not unkindly.

“Can we talk about you?” Flinch asked gently. “I mean, this is a nice house. I’m glad to see you’re doing well.”

Angie nodded. “Yeah. Mom and Dad helped me get settled, and your parents left me some money- I’m sorry, I don’t know if you heard-”

“It’s fine.”

“Right. Well, I took a few courses before we moved out here, got a job as a clerk in an accounting firm. Things are quieter here, compared to Brockton Bay. I wanted to get away from the gangs, keep the girls safe…” She trailed off again and I noticed how her eyes briefly flickered to Carmen.

Carmen nudged Angie with her elbow. When Angie turned her face to look, Carmen jerked her head towards me in a ‘Can I?’ sort of gesture. Angie hesitated, then nodded.

Carmen turned towards me. “I got powers halfway through freshman year,” she admitted. “I joined the Wards, now I’m in the Protectorate.”

“Oh damn,” Anchorage said.

Flinch stared at his eldest daughter with a heavy heart. “Baby girl,” he said softly. “I’m so sorry you had to go through that.”

Carmen shrugged uncomfortably. “Yeah, it sucked when it happened. But I got to help a lot of people- it kind of felt like following in your footsteps. I wanted to try and have my costume look like yours, but Image wouldn’t let me.”

“Really?” Flinch’s smile stretched across my face. “That’s so sweet, Carmen. So what’s your hero name? I mean, obviously you’re not Chevalier.”

Carmen chuckled a little. “No, I’m Southpaw. Super strength, plus I can pick a person and sense any immediate threats coming their way. I get a lot of protection details, obviously.”

“Hey, her power’s like yours,” Stoneknapper pointed out warmly.

Flinch smiled even harder. "That’s a real heroic power.” Tactical sent over a thought. “Hey, if you target a villain, does that mean you can tell what attacks are going to work on them and what won’t?”

“Actually, yeah,” Carmen said, pointing a finger. “It’s great for getting through people’s defences, or just figuring out their weaknesses.”

“Fantastic,” Flinch said proudly. “Tina, how about you? Now that you’re done with college?”

Tina tilted her hand from side to side in a so-so gesture. “I mean, I’m looking at jobs, but I also kind of want to travel with friends for a while. Maybe head to New York or something, do some sightseeing.”

“I can recommend some spots if you like- I’ve seen a lot of New York. Although mostly it’d be places to avoid,” Flinch admitted.

I could see Tina thinking it through, before tentatively asking “If we wanted to come to Brockton Bay, would that be alright?”

“Of course,” Flinch said at once. “I’d love to have you come down. We could do some more catching up- you girls might not remember a lot, but I could show you around.”

“I think we could do that, Miguel,” Angie said with a small smile.

 

 

Thursday 22nd September, Boston

Tactical dropped to my knees with a thump that made his brother and sisters wince. He didn’t notice, too preoccupied with the little red-headed girl before us.

“Holy crap,” Quarrel said.

“Nora,” said Elaine, Tactical’s old ex-girlfriend, who was standing behind Nora with her hands on the little girl’s shoulders, “This is Elpis. You remember what we talked about?”

Nora’s eyes were big and blue, staring back at us as wide as they could go. “Is my dad really in your head?”

“For god’s sake, answer her,” Nemean prodded me when I failed to immediately respond.

“Yes… Yes, answer her, let me talk to her, quick,” Tactical gabbled.

“Yes, he’s in here,” I said, opening my helmet. “I can let him talk through me, if you like?”

Nora’s little face frowned. “Is he going to make weird groaning noises like ghosts on TV?”

Rotter barely choked back a laugh- if he hadn’t held back, I’d have rammed him into the dark for interrupting this moment.

“No, it’s nothing like that. I just relay what he wants to say.”

Nora glanced up at her mom, then nodded hard, sending her ginger hair flicking about. “Okay.”

I pulled Tactical up and focused carefully on his thoughts. It was as close as I could get to letting one of the Butchers into the driver’s seat. As soon as he’d settled in, he reached one hand out to gently touch Nora’s cheek, light as a feather.

“Look at you,” Tactical said in his Southie accent, full of wonder.

“Is that dad talking?” Nora asked.

“Yes. Yes, this is me. I’m Frank, I’m your- I’m your dad,” Tactical managed. In the privacy of my head he added “Holy fuck, I’m a father.”

Nora grinned, showing a gap where an adult tooth was growing in. “Ghost dad,” she said, like it was the coolest thing ever.

Tactical laughed in surprise. “Yeah, pretty much. Oh, look at you, you’re wonderful. I’m so sorry I couldn’t be around for you.”

Nora shook her head, hair flicking about again. “S’okay. Mom and Uncle Billy and Auntie Maddy and Auntie Grace told me a bunch of stuff about you.”

“That’s good. But I still owe you a lot of time- and I guess I owe you a bunch of birthday presents too.”

“You don’t have to-”

“Yes please!” Nora said over Elaine’s objections.

“Well, what sort of stuff do you like?” Tactical asked, grinning back at Nora.

Billy cleared his throat. “How about we all sit down first?”

“Right, yeah,” Tactical agreed, hauling my body off the carpet and onto the end of the sofa. Elaine took the other end, and Nora hauled herself up to sit between us, bouncing in place. Billy, Madolyn and Grace settled into the remaining chairs.

“I like wizard stuff,” Nora said as soon as everyone was sat down. “The Maggie Holt Books are cool, especially the stuff with the vampires, but I like the stuff that’s more magicky- like when there’s dragons and monsters and stuff.”

“Ah, right, proper high fantasy,” Tactical said. “Although, I’ve met a couple of people you’d call dragons and monsters.”

“Wouldn’t dragons count as monsters?” Vladimir wondered.

“Not the time,” Needler said.

“Really?” Nora said.

“Yep. I met Dragon, the Tinker- and I fought Lung, who could turn into a dragon.”

Nora scrunched up her face. “But Dragon’s not really a dragon, she just makes robots shaped like dragons. That doesn’t count.”

“A robot dragon is still pretty close to a dragon,” Tactical said. “Do we agree that Lung counts?”

Nora thought for a second. “Did he have wings?”

“Yeah, if he kept going long enough.”

“Cool,” Nora grinned.

“And as for monsters, just for starters, maybe you’ve heard of a girl called Cerberus? She makes dogs grow enormous- big as pickup trucks.”

“I saw them on TV,” Nora said. “They didn’t really look like dogs though- more like spiky lizards.”

Tactical chuckled. “Yeah, I guess they do.”

“I’m just glad we weren’t anywhere near all that,” Billy said. “They were cleaning up after Blasto’s mess for days.”

Tactical shrugged. “Yeah, sorry about that. Good news is he’s gone- and I’m planning on checking up on Boston pretty regularly.”

“I was just going to ask if this was a one-time thing,” Grace admitted.

“Not a chance,” Tactical said. “I’ll be passing through Boston fairly regularly, and I’ll try to catch up whenever I can. Especially since I need to make up for lost time with this little munchkin,” he added, giving a nod in Nora’s direction.

“I’m not a munchkin,” Nora said, folding her arms.

“Ah, sorry,” Tactical apologised. “When I was your age, I used to get mad if someone called me a leprechaun.”

“Really?”

“Yeah. It was a real sore spot for me. I mean, yeah, I’m short and Irish, but they couldn’t think of anything better?”

“It was kinda dumb,” Maddy admitted. “Even dumber after you beat up the first couple of guys.”

“Can you teach me to fight?” Nora asked eagerly.

“Is someone picking on you at school?” Tactical asked at once, mind already whirring away with plans on how to stop it.

“Nah,” Nora said, shaking her head again. “I just wanna learn.”

Elaine gave Tactical a hard look and a chopping gesture behind Nora’s back.

“Probably not,” Tactical said carefully. “Maybe you could talk to your ma about karate classes or something.”

Nora immediately whipped her head around to look to her mom. I couldn’t see, but I imagined she was making her eyes all big and innocent again.

“We’ll see,” Elaine said noncommittally, giving Tactical a look.

 

 

Friday 30th September, New York

“Oh my god,” Annie said. “You’re so fucking white!” She broke down laughing, pointing at my exposed pale skin. “Oh god, look at you!”

“Yeah, yeah, laugh it up,” Anchorage said, rolling my eyes.

Annie clutched her stomach.  “Oh shit! When you need an x-ray, I bet they just hold you up to the window!” She laughed even harder.

Anchorage’s dad put a hand on her shoulder. “Come on Annie, that’s enough.”

“There’s no need to make fun of your sister,” said her mom, although I could see her fighting back a smile.

“Don’t blame me, I would’ve chosen a better meatbag if I could,” Anchorage said, gesturing to my body. “I mean, look at this. No tits, no ass.”

I made the bugs in the glass box buzz “Alright, that’s enough of that.” I could handle some light ribbing, but I didn’t have to stand for cracks about my figure.

“Okay, okay,” Anchorage said. “Enough about the body, more about the stomach.”

“Damn right!” said Grandmaw, thumping her cane on the carpet. The cane was new, and her hair had passed from grey to white, but she still looked as feisty as ever. “Elpis, you’re too damn skinny- we’re going to put some meat on ya!”

“We keep trying to get her to eat more, but her metabolism’s like one of those grills,” Anchorage said as she offered Grandmaw her arm to help her into the next room. “The fat just drains right off.”

“Phooey,” Grandmaw said, taking my arm and leaning on me with a huff. “I’m still going to try- gonna need a full stomach to deal with those sons of bitches. I heard about those guys in Boston- nasty stuff.”

“You mean Orchard? Yeah, those guys were goddamn freaks.” Mr Bough and Mr Drowsing were a pair of human traffickers who used their powers to do ‘custom orders’- altering people’s bodies and minds for whatever purposes. That ranged from turning three women into identical copies, creating a copy of Legend for some obscure scheme, or giving a boy the head and legs of a dog. They only pulled a few jobs a year, but tracking them down and beating them senseless had been a good use of my trip to Boston.

“Plus it keeps the Boston gangs afraid you’ll swing by and stomp on their heads if they cross a line,” Tock Tick added.

“That too,” I agreed.

The table was set for dinner, and Anchorage’s parents started laying out the dishes- roast pork with roast potatoes, plus collard greens and mac and cheese on the side.

Anchorage took a deep breath, concentrating on the smell of the herb rub Grandmaw had invented years ago for roast pork. “God I missed this.”

 

 

Tuesday 18th October, Little Tokyo, New York

I tweaked the focus on the scope I’d made. I had to hang off the side of a neighbouring building to have the right angle to see through the window, but the grappling hook made it easy enough. I wasn’t too worried about anyone spotting me either- one thing that you learned as a cape was that normal people rarely looked up.

Through the window, I could see Quarrel’s parents going about their afternoon. Her father was sat at the kitchen table, reading a thick book, while her mother was doing the dishes.

That was how they’d spent most of their afternoons, for as far back as Quarrel could remember. Father would come from work and sit down to relax, Mother would handle the housework. Very cozy, very traditional, very repetitive. To a teenager who’d come to America young enough to have no real memories, who’d happily adopted American culture, it was stifling.

They’d never grasped that Yuki had wanted something different- they’d pushed her to get good grades and take up some traditional Japanese hobby, and it had taken a lot of debates and arguments before they’d allowed her to pick archery instead of flower arranging. They’d disapproved of her dressing tomboyish, of not speaking Japanese at home, of her wanting to go out with her friends instead of going to study sessions. For a while, Yuki had been able to think of it as her parents wanting her to succeed, get out of the cramped and crime-ridden district of Japanese refugees, and that took the sting out of things.

Yuki had seen the path they were really trying to set her on when they’d started talking about their friends and their nice sons, good grades, doing well in school clubs, Japanese of course. She’d felt the life of a demure little housewife closing in around her like the jaws of a beartrap, and that had only made her fight harder. Chop her hair short with kitchen scissors, date bad boys that she didn’t even like, stay out late, fight to make it clear that she would live her life on her own terms.

That had led to more arguments, the kind where the neighbours knocked on the door and uncomfortably ask if everything was alright. Things had settled into a sullen resentful standoff.

And then one day one of her ex-boyfriends had cornered her after school, wanting to get back together. Except it turned out that he just wanted access to her study notes again to bring his grades up, and Yuki was tired and stressed from a week of shouting at her parents every day, and he just wasn’t taking no for an answer.

She’d hit him, he’d hit her back, and things had turned into a brawl in the empty hallways until he pulled a pistol out of his bag. She’d known he was a piece of crap, and he’d joked about ties to the Yakuza, but she hadn’t thought he was that nuts.

Yuki had run, and he’d chased her through the halls, yelling for her to stop, to listen, to stop being a bitch. He’d cornered her in a science lab, the chairs stacked on the tables for the cleaners to come in and mop the floors. That was why, when she’d started throwing stuff in a desperate attempt to keep him back, she hadn’t been able to hit him. She’d seen him lining up a shot.

And then she’d triggered. She’d landed her sharpest pencil right in his eye, and ran out of the room, out of the school, and all the way home, while he’d screamed in pain as a teacher tackled him to the floor and tore the gun from his hands.

Her parents had barely noticed how she’d been quieter, shaken. When they’d heard about a shooter at her school, they’d been concerned, but it hadn’t lasted long. They’d mostly been concerned about her grades slipping.

That had been the final straw for Yuki. She packed a bag, left a note, and ran. For a while she worked some menial jobs as she put together a costume, then went out as a cape. A few fights gone wrong got her labelled as a villain, and she had to get more and more brutal to survive, until she finally caught the attention of the Teeth.

A gust of cold wind hard enough to make me sway on the grappling line shook me out of my thoughts. I was still looking through the scope at Quarrel’s parents through the window.

“Quarrel?” I asked gently.

For a long moment, she said nothing. I hung from the wall and waited patiently.

“No,” she said at last. “I’m not ready for that.”

“Okay,” I said, putting the scope away and reeling the grappler in to get back to the roof. “You want to do something else?”

Quarrel sighed. “Fighting someone sounds really good right about now.”

Muramasa cleared this throat. “If we’re continuing our theme of targeting biotinkers and such,” he said, “There’s the Chopshop.” A group of Tinkers who dealt in cybernetics and wetware body upgrades- very cyberpunk. They also had a line in combat servitors, often using human components.

“Worth a shot,” Quarrel grunted. “Means I can shoot bits off them without Taylor whining about drawing blood.”

“That would help,” I said, clambering back onto the ledge.

“If we’re staying for longer, we could always take a crack at the Adepts,” Bearskin suggested. “It’s not like those morons are hard to find, with the robes and symbols everywhere.”

“Also a good idea,” I said. “How about Chopshop first, Adepts if we have time? Sound good?”

A scattered chorus of agreement came from the Butchers.

“The ayes have it,” I said, readying my weapons.

Chapter 152: 15.6

Thursday 24th November, Thanksgiving, Hebert Residence

I had the door open before Tarquin could knock. “Come on in,” I said, stepping aside.

“God it’s cold out there,” Tarquin groaned, hustling inside without hesitation. His parents followed a little behind, glancing at me.

“Hello, Mr and Mrs Gleed,” I said politely. “Was the drive here okay?”

“Yeah, no problems,” Mr Gleed said- a heavyset man with the same dark hair as T, going grey at the temples. He looked a lot more at ease with me than when we’d met up to introduce the Gleeds to the Undersiders. Then again, this conversation wasn’t taking place in the Lair.

“Except for a few of the drivers,” Mrs Gleed remarked. She was shorter than her husband or son, with brown hair and little pearl earrings. She was also holding a pie in one hand as she tried to take her coat off with the other. “Honestly, don’t people know how to use their indicators?”

I gently took the pie from her hands so she could stop struggling with her outer layers. “I’ll stick this in the kitchen. Anybody want a drink?”

“I’d love a beer,” Mr Gleed said. “Just the one though.”

“Wine for me, please,” Mrs Gleed said, finally shedding her coat and hanging it on a hook.

“Beer,” T said with a mocking grin.

“Nice try, T,” I said with an eyeroll.

“Can’t blame the man for trying,” Dirty Rotter noted.

“Everyone else is in the living room if you want to sit down,” I said over my shoulder as I took the pie into the kitchen.

The combination of smells was incredible- each of the Undersiders had brought along a different dish, now waiting on the counter to be warmed or dished up as needed. The turkey was cooking nicely in the oven, basted to within an inch of its life, and Dad was cracking open the cans of cranberry sauce.

Anchorage pulled a face. “Out of a can,” she grumbled. “Savages.”

“Hey, canned cranberry sauce is a fine tradition,” Vladimir defended. “Nothing like having a slice to make the meal complete.”

“Slice?” Anchorage demanded as Dad slid the contents of one can out and onto a dish, a perfect translucent cylinder. “Oh, that is wrong.”

“Far as I’m concerned, most Thanksgiving stuff is weird,” said Dirty Rotter.

“Shut it, Limey,” Anchorage jeered.

“Need any help?” I asked Dad, managing to clear an empty space on the counter to set the pie down.

“I think I’ve got it from here,” Dad said, sliding a second can out to join the first. “All that’s left right now is waiting for the turkey.”

“And warming the dinner rolls,” I pointed out.

“Yeah, that too.” Dad arranged the third can of cranberry sauce and finally glanced up. “So what kind of pie is that?”

“Pecan. Looks like a good one too. Anyway, I’m going to bring some drinks out.”

“I’ll join you in a second,” Dad said with a smile.

I made it to the living room with a tray of fresh drinks to find Tarquin on the sofa next to his mom, who was complimenting the kitschy dangly earrings Isabella had in. “Where on earth did you get these?” Mrs Gleed cooed, touching one tiny cornucopia with a fingertip.

“Found them on the internet,” Isa admitted with a shrug. “They’ve got all kinds of junk, and I thought they’d be fun.”

Rachel was on the floor with her dogs, Brian was talking with Mr Gleed, Aisha had claimed an armchair for herself, and Lisa was flicking through TV channels.  “Hey boss,” she said, glancing up from the remote.

“Hey. Drinks all around.”

“Sweet,” Aisha said, hopping out of her chair and making a beeline for me. I plucked a glass of soda off the tray and held it out for her. “Brian said I could have beer,” she said with a straight face.

“No he didn’t,” I said.

“No I didn’t,” Brian said.

“And you’re the second person today to try that crap.”

Aisha pouted. “Fine. How long until turkey time?”

“About 20 minutes. Nice job on the mac and cheese, by the way. Looks great.”

Aisha shrugged. “I got lots of experience making it. Dad’s not much of a cook, so I learned some basic crap.”

“Ah, the life of a latchkey kid,” Stoneknapper said. “Can’t say I miss that crap.”

I handed out the other drinks- Mr Gleed’s beer, Mrs Gleed’s red wine, and soda for the rest. Dad had caved and allowed me to have alcohol, on the grounds that it didn’t do a damn thing to me, so I’d poured myself a glass of red as well.

“Is Panacea not coming?” Mr Gleed asked. “Tarquin said you two were dating, I thought maybe…”

“No, she’s with New Wave. They are her family after all.”

“And god help her,” Bearskin noted. “Nothing like extended family at Thanksgiving to raise the blood pressure.” He spoke from experience- his family had plenty of arguments, and one cousin had almost lost a finger trying to carve the turkey one year.

“Eh, my family did alright,” Flinch said with a shrug. “You guys should try pepper turkey some time- it’s so good.”

“Ooh, we could make it with the leftovers tomorrow,” Firecracker enthused.

“I think Amy will be fine,” Needler said. “After all,” she added slyly, “She was very relaxed last night.”

“Woo!” Quarrel cheered.

I quickly swigged my wine to cover the rush of blood to my face. “Knock it off.”

“Oh come on,” Butcher snorted. “Don’t pretend you weren’t living it up. Especially that thing with the tongue,” he leered.

I gave Butcher a shove, even as I grinned a little. As it turned out, there were many possible benefits to dating a biokinetic.

“Is it okay for two whole superhero teams to take the day off?” Mrs Gleed asked. “I assumed there’d be someone on call for a day like this.”

I swallowed and answered, “Yeah, I asked them about that, and they’re usually at least on standby for the big holidays- the Protectorate are too, and to a lesser extent the Wards. But since there’s basically no villains in town right now, everyone’s relaxing a little.”

Lady Photon had certainly seemed happy to have a Thanksgiving with little to no chance of villain bullshit. I’d bought a nice bottle of wine for Amy to take along as a present.

“The big holidays are rarely a time for villain activity anyway,” Lisa pointed out. “For one, villains like to celebrate too.”

“That’s true,” I said, remembering some of the Teeth Thanksgivings. Multiple turkeys spit-roasted over an open fire, carved with a sword; and the side dishes were done in such big portions that they often used steel drums, like they shipped oil in. After the booze had been flowing for a while, people would often just stick their whole heads into a barrel of sweet potato mash and chow down.

“Gotta be really careful to clean those out right,” Tock Tick noted.

“And for another, the authorities will be preparing for villain activity,” Lisa continued. “So that means heroes drawing the short straw to be on duty, the rest on call, troopers on standby.”

“Plus the heroes’ll be ticked off from getting pulled away from dinner,” Brian pointed out.

“Another good reason. And all the crowds and traffic will clog up the escape route, unless you plan on flying or teleporting out or something. Really, the best time for villains is right after a holiday. Everybody’s tired or hungover or working off the food, all the stores will have taken in a bunch of money but haven’t banked it yet- that’s the sweet spot.”

“It doesn’t even have to be a big heist,” I said. “Back before buying online made things easier, the Butchers used to go along to Black Friday sales, blend with the crowd, and just walk out with whatever they wanted.”

“Good grief, really?” Mr Gleed asked.

“Yup. Firecracker got a bunch of consoles and video games one year, just tucked under her arm. Although to be fair, she did teleport out.”

“Man, I would’ve been great at that,” Aisha said. “Just turn my power on and fill my pockets with jewellery.”

“Yeah, until you set off the detectors at the door,” Lisa pointed out.

“Or get trampled by angry shoppers who don’t know you’re there,” Tarquin pointed out.

“Or get picked up on security cameras,” Brian said.

“Yeah yeah, bust a girl’s dream,” Aisha grumbled into her cup.

 

 

The dining room wasn’t really built for nine people- even with the extra leaf in the table, things were crowded. At least the dogs were out in the living room, happily digging into bowls of kibble, plus a piece of turkey as a treat, prepared in a way that Rachel had confirmed was healthy for them to eat.

The turkey was pride of place, still massive even after being carved. There was sweet potato mash from Isa, without marshmallows, which had set off an argument amongst the Butchers; green bean casserole from Lisa; stuffing from Rachel; Brian and Aisha’s mac and cheese; roast potatoes, cranberry sauce, gravy, dinner rolls.

“Okay,” Dad said, settling into his seat. “So, what’s everyone thankful for this year? I’m thankful for my daughter being so successful and happy.”

“Thanks Dad. I’m thankful for the city being villain-free and peaceful for once.”

Lisa shrugged. “I’m thankful for the surprising job satisfaction of being a hero.”

“I’m thankful that my sister’s finally behaving herself,” Brian said with a smirk.

Aisha punched him in the shoulder doing absolutely nothing. “Ha freaking ha. I’m thankful that I’m on the coolest hero team in the world- even if Brian’s on it too.”

While the siblings glared at each other, Isa went next. “I’m thankful that I’ve found friends who’ll stick with me through anything. And love,” she added shyly, brushing her hair back behind her ear.

“Ah, to be young again,” Tactical said.

“I’m thankful for the food,” Rachel said simply.

Mr Gleed chuckled. “Well, you beat me to it, so I guess I’ll say I’m thankful for getting to meet heroes in person.”

“I’m thankful for my son finding his place in the world,” Mrs Gleed said. “Even if he worries me sick with it.”

“I’m thankful that you’re letting me be a hero,” Tarquin answered, patting his mom’s hand fondly.

“Alright then,” Dad said. “Dig in, everyone.”

“Hear hear!” Nemean shouted as I picked up my fork.

 

 

Friday 25th November, Black Friday, Hebert Residence

“Feeling any better?” I asked Aisha.

“Feel like a bowling ball,” Aisha grunted from her little blanket nest on the couch.

“Eyes bigger than her stomach,” Muramasa scoffed.

“So that’s a no to breakfast then. Glass of water?”

“Please,” Aisha said, burrowing back down.

Everybody had been so stuffed from Thanksgiving dinner, including slices of multiple pies, that there’d only been enough collective energy to watch the football game on TV and talk a little. Eventually we’d decided that the Undersiders could just stay over for the night. Brian and Isabella got the guest room, Lisa slept in mine, Aisha took the couch and Rachel slept on the floor with her dogs sprawled around and partially on top of her, which frankly looked very comfortable. The Gleeds had managed to drive home, with several boxes of leftovers and many thanks for that pecan pie- it was damn good.

As for me, the metabolism of multiple Brute powersets meant that I felt perfectly at ease, even after eating more than anybody else. Hell, I’d cracked open a couple of turkey bones and sucked out the marrow without trouble. I’d spent the night doing a solo patrol in case anybody decided to cause any trouble. We’d had unconfirmed rumours of a group of thieves called the Red Hand eying Brockton Bay, and I wanted to keep an eye out. By all accounts they were relatively non-violent, but I still didn’t want them in town.

“So I guess once everyone’s woken up and cleared their systems a bit, we see if anyone’s trying some Black Friday looting in daylight hours?” Firecracker asked.

“Yeah, probably,” I said, filling a glass of water for Aisha before fixing myself a bowl of cereal. Another thing that had been complicated by the Butchers- we now had multiple different brands of cereal to satisfy all their cravings. Today was Anchorage’s turn, which meant Frute Brute with milk. I idly munched on the bowl as I stepped back into the living room and sat down, turning the TV on and lowering the volume. Aisha poked her head out to sip her water while I watched the news.

No mention of me specifically, but there was talk of how the various cape groups around were reacting to the various arrests I’d made. Orchard being taken out of Boston meant that Mass and Cass was being cleaned up- which might take a while, since another name for that neighourhood was Methadone Mile. A few Adepts knocked down, the Chop Shop raided, and I’d swung through Boston again to hunt down a particular troublemaker from Mystic Mass. The end result was that the villain groups were staying quiet to avoid attention while the heroes were capitalising on the lull to push forward.

Turning to local stuff, the Boat Graveyard was almost completely cleared out, what with the valuable materials littered throughout, and multiple hero teams volunteering to help clear stuff. No mention of the cutting tools I’d Tinkered up for the Dockworkers Association, which was a relief. There was a brief segment about Armsmaster, who was now with the Guild fulltime, doing some important missions with Dragon- very far from Brockton Bay, but I guessed that he got a mention due to being stationed in Brockton for so long that he still counted as one of ‘our’ heroes.

I had to stifle a laugh at the next segment- the Butchers didn’t have that problem.

“HAHAHAHA!” Stoneknapper cackled at the sight of Bakuda in handcuffs, being frog-marched into the back of a PRT van. Apparently she’d finally resurfaced, and as promised she’d tried to do something big. There was a containment zone around a town called Eagleton in Tennessee, and Bakuda had apparently travelled all the way there to try and drop an enormous bomb on it.

“Would that have even worked?” Muramasa wondered. “I would think that the PRT would have attempted to bomb their quarantine sites if they thought it would work.”

“Perhaps?” Vladimir said. “I know they didn’t just nuke Nilbog because his creations would give off spores and spread, but that’s not a problem you’d have with machines.”

“Yes, but these are tinker machines we’re talking about,” Tock Tick countered. “For all we know the damn things might reproduce with spores.”

“Hang on,” I said as the segment switched to a Protectorate hero who manned the Eagleton quarantine, a guy in bonze armour called Brazen. Apparently he was a Tinker who specialised in alloys and metallurgy, and he was explaining how the Machine Army did indeed plant metal seeds to grow new machines from. These seeds were also partially extradimensional, so the bomb probably wouldn’t have got them all.

“Well fuck, that’s a waste of a good bomb,” Anchorage grumbled.

“Hey, if it works on biological stuff, maybe they can use it to kill Nilbog,” Bearskin said.

“Now there’s a thought,” Needler said appreciatively.

“If they can get Bakuda to work for them, the Protectorate’s going to have it a lot easier taking down the worst of the worst,” Quarrel noted. “Drop a big-ass bomb on whatever fucker’s busy eating babies and call it a day.”

“Big if,” Butcher retorted. “Bitch is crazy.”

“True,” I acknowledged.

The rest of the Undersiders gradually woke up and got in order more easily than Aisha. “She’s always like this at Thanksgiving,” Brian said. “I always tell her to take it easy, she always eats too much.”

“Bite me,” Aisha said, serving herself a leftover slice of pumpkin pie for breakfast.

“Well, at least we’re all nice and carb-loaded to handle Black Friday,” Isabella noted, running a steel comb through her hair. I’d made her that- apparently plastic ones had a tendency to break trying to handle her hair.

“Breaking up brawling shoppers, yippee,” Lisa droned.

“Oh, hush,” I said. “It’ll mostly be meet and greet stuff, probably. And you’ll be last to do anything physical- just spot any shoplifters.”

Lisa nodded with a grin. “Now that I can do.”

“Is anyone going to be dumb enough to fight or shoplift when the Butcher’s in the area?” Brian asked, finishing his coffee.

“People are stupid,” Rachel said.

“True,” Brian conceded.

“Taylor?” Dad called from the living room. He sounded worried.

I saw what he meant as I walked in. The TV was turned to the news, showing clouds with a horrible silhouette barely visible in the midst. The Simurgh.

“Well, we’re not going,” Dirty Rotter said. “Don’t even think about it.”

“I wasn’t,” I said truthfully. I checked my phone- a notification came through just as I opened the home screen. Simurgh attacking passenger plane over Pacific Ocean. Natural fliers required to respond.

This was different from usual Endbringer attacks. They went after cities, population centres, large structures. A passenger plane in midair was way out of left field- a small moving target, too far away from land for most people to fight.

It felt like a direct response- we’d killed Behemoth with record attendance and the terrain to set up defences, evacuate civilians, prepare weapons that could actually hurt it. Legend, Alexandria and Eidolon were engaging the Simurgh, but they didn’t have the Dragonflight and groundbound forces to back them up.

We all watched in silence as the Simurgh and heroes battled, using the plane as cover. At some point, the heroes switched to trying to destroy the plane, the Simurgh trying to defend it, moving it around with her telekinesis, occasionally intercepting shots with her wings.

Finally Eidolon tore into her with some reality warping power, complete with lightning, fire, ice, and distorted light. The Simurgh let the plane go in the next second, letting it flip, burn and tumble before crashing into the water below, virtually disintegrating on impact.

That done, the Simurgh ascended, rising into the clouds. A few capes tried to follow her, but Scion was not among them.

I checked my watch. Forty minutes from start to finish for the Simurgh to come and go. Too fast for Scion to get there and attack her. There would be fallout from this- maybe one of the passengers was politically important, maybe many of them. Maybe they were related to someone powerful who’d go mad with grief. It was impossible to predict until it was happening.

This was minimal by Endbringer standards. I’d counted barely forty capes out there, and I hadn’t seen anyone die. No deaths besides the plane’s passengers. But it was a new tactic, a hit and run, avoiding the risk of us destroying another Endbringer, denying people even the chance to participate.

“Well,” Aisha said finally. “That was a fucking letdown.”

 

 

Saturday 26th November, PRT Headquarters, Downtown

“Lost Garden is definitely turned away from Brockton Bay,” Director Piggot said. She looked better than ever, with the fat gone and a noticeable amount of muscle gained. Apparently she’d once been a field agent, and now I could see how. “That’s one less problem to deal with at least.”

“Good to hear,” Lady Photon said. She and Glory Girl were representing New Wave for this talk, although I wasn’t sure why they wouldn’t send two adults. They’d both been giving me weird glances since they’d walked in.

Miss Militia and Dauntless were representing the Protectorate. With Armsmaster gone, Miss Militia was technically the leader of ENE, but apparently Dauntless was being groomed to step up and take the lead soon. Possibly Militia just didn’t like the responsibility.

Regardless, the mood was tense after the Simurgh’s attack yesterday. Villain activity often saw an overall uptick after Endbringers, partly due to heroes being dead or injured, and partly due to having a long window for crime until the next Truce. Even with no fatalities that time, there was still a worry that someone would get cocky.

“The bad news,” Director Piggot continued fatalistically, “Is that we’ve got intel of Heartbreaker looking our way. Possibly because one of his brood is based here, possibly because another of them died here, or maybe he likes the look of the local girls. Either way, we need to prepare for that.”

Flinch shuddered. “God, I hope someone kills him soon.”

“Amen to that,” Tactical agreed. Heartbreaker was someone the world could do without- and frankly the man was a really bad match up for us. On the one hand, no Brute powers or physically damaging powers for him or any of his children, as far as I was aware. On the other hand, they all had some kind of Master power. Cherish had been bad enough, but at least the effects of her powers eventually wore off- everyone she’d enthralled had made a full recovery. If Heartbreaker got someone, it was permanent.

I was reasonably confident that the range of my insects would beat the range of his emotional control, but I really didn’t want to test that. If he managed to get his hooks in me, he might be able to turn me into one of his toys, and frankly that felt like a fate worse than death.

There was also the matter of his thralls- fanatically devoted soldiers, double agents, and there was a solid theory that Heartbreaker had conditioned all his thralls so that they’d commit suicide if he died. Taking him out would mean having to catch dozens of innocent people before they slit their wrists.

“The good news is that Armsmaster’s sent us something he and Dragon worked on,” Piggot said. “It’s a lie-detector program- works through audio or visual, preferably both, but he’s confident we can use it to check and catch any double agents Heartbreaker might try to send at us.”

“That’ll definitely help,” Vladimir said through the bug box. “You’ll want to check for secondary agents though. It’s possible Heartbreaker might have a particularly rich thrall hire mercenaries for another degree of separation.”

“True,” Piggot sighed.

Miss Militia raised a hand. “If he sends his children, how do you want us to engage?”

“Carefully,” Piggot said. “They’re all ruthless little bastards with a lot of experience, and they’ll undoubtedly be more afraid of their father than you. Try to take them alive if possible, but some injuries are acceptable. Just nothing we’d need Panacea to heal- we don’t want her anywhere near them.”

“Damn right,” Glory Girl muttered.

“They’re still children,” Nemean pointed out. “And they were raised by probably the worst father in history. Is there anything we can do for them?”

“It’s unlikely,” Miss Militia said. “Heartbreaker’s children all have extensive criminal records, all including at least some form of sexual assault. That’s not the kind of people we can trust to switch sides. Not to mention human Master powers are much more difficult for us to contain.”

Nemean sighed. “That’s about what I expected.”

“As for Heartbreaker, is it kill on sight, or do we try to keep him contained until we can disarm his human dead man switches?” I asked.

“Ideally we’d have him drugged to the gills long enough to dismantle his network, then execute him,” Piggot said, “But frankly speaking, we don’t want him alive any longer than necessary. Take the shot at earliest convenience, and we’ll handle the fallout. Can we borrow Tattletale to help find his thralls?”

“I’ll talk to her, but I’m pretty sure she’ll say yes,” I said. “Grue’s darkness can help block line of sight stuff, the dogs will obviously be immune to human-only effects- and I assume Gallant and Glory Girl will be first pick if things go hot, since they’re resistant to Master powers?”

“Correct.”

“Ohhhh, that’s why Glory Girl’s here,” Firecracker said with dawning understanding.

“Well, I guess I’ll figure out some long-range options,” I said. “Net arrows for the kids, and a really long rifle for Daddy Worst.”

“Daddy Worst?” Dauntless asked.

“I was trying to do the opposite of Daddy Dearest,” I admitted. “I guess it doesn’t work.”

“Father of Never? Instead of Father of the Year?” Tock Tick suggested.

“If we’re finished discussing nicknames for the rapist supervillain,” Piggot said heavily, “That concludes everything for this meeting. I have paperwork, so I’ll let you see yourselves out.” She gave a single nod and then hustled out the room.

“No sense of humour on that woman,” Stoneknapper noted.

The name plate and resonator plates of the bug box clicked into a new position, and Muramasa said “I admire it. Very no-nonsense.”

“Well, I’m going to head out,” Dauntless said. “Ladies.” He gave us a more friendly nod and left.

“Before you leave as well,” Lady Photon said to me, “I wanted to confirm the fitting. Thursday works for us, if that’s alright.”

“Yeah, I’ll bring the silk. Also some steel- I can shape it into armour inserts for whatever you go with.”

“I’m sorry, I must have missed something,” Miss Militia said. “What about a fitting?”

“I’ve got a lot of spider silk besides what I’m selling to the PRT, and I offered some to New Wave to reinforce their costumes,” I explained. “With Parian being able to weave the stuff even better than me, it’ll be a lot faster to just bring it with me and let her make the costumes.”

Miss Militia frowned. “We should have thought of that. Could we consult with Parian for getting our own people fitted?”

“We’ll figure something out,” Lady Photon said.

The four of us made our way down to the lobby. I noticed some new merchandise in the gift shop- t-shirts proclaiming Brockton Bay to be the final resting place of Jack Slash, or the entire Slaughterhouse Nine. I grinned a little to myself.

“There was one more thing,” Glory Girl said, giving me a hard look as we exited the front door. “Amy brought something up at Thanksgiving.”

“Oh boy, here we go,” Anchorage said.

“Oh?” I said in a light tone of voice.

“Yeah.” Glory Girl leaned in closer, lowering her voice. “She said you two are ‘going steady.’ Have been for a while.”

“…Yeah, that’s true,” I admitted. “I’m not sure where you’re going with this though.”

“Easy, Victoria,” Lady Photon said.

“It does make a bunch of things make sense,” Glory Girl admitted, “And Amy’s happy and fulfilled, and that’s the important thing. But.” She stuck a finger under my nose. “I know you don’t feel pain, and I know you regenerate, so this is technically kind of meaningless. But. If you, or your predecessors hurt my sister, physically or emotionally- I will feed you your own teeth.”

“Honestly, that’s not a bad threat,” Bearskin admitted.

“Message received,” I said.  

Chapter 153: 15.7

Chapter Notes

This one is a short bonus joke chapter I wrote on a whim while I was off work.

If you haven't seen Jaypierlis's videos, I highly recommend you check them out. It'll both give context for this and tickle your funny bone!

Saturday 10th December, Undersiders Lair, The Docks

I pushed open the door to the teleportation booth. “I’m back. Please tell me there’s coffee.”

“Pot’s still warm,” Lisa said from the couch. She had her laptop with her, and Isabella and Aisha were leaning in on either side of her to see.

“Thanks.” I released all the bugs from my armour to go warm up and eat in the terrariums downstairs- meanwhile, I needed to warm up and eat something myself. Running around in full armour and thermals did help me stay warm on a midwinter patrol, but in a way that still left you very aware of the cold. Plus I was sweaty as hell- I’d need a shower after this.

“Hey, do you want to see this?” Aisha asked as I pulled off my helmet and poured myself a mug.

“See what?” I asked. “Do we have an update on anything?”

“No, but it’s funny,” Aisha said.

“There’s this guy who does web videos- stuff like How Villains React To X Hero, and so on. He just did one on you,” Lisa elaborated.

“That actually sounds hilarious,” Firecracker said.

“Yeah, okay,” I said, crossing over and leaning over the back of the couch. Lisa rewound the video to the beginning, showing the title ‘How Villains Talk About Elpis’. There was a picture of me from a news story two weeks ago- I had a sword in one hand and an axe in the other. I thought I looked good.

There was a bass chord, and then a black guy in a hair bonnet was sitting in front of the camera. “They say she’s the first Butcher that ain’t crazy,” he said slowly. “I say she’s a different kind of crazy.”

The girls all glanced at me, visibly suppressing smiles. I snorted and gestured for them to continue.

“Can’t argue with that,” Quarrel snickered.

“Hush,” I said.

The chord played again- quick flash of my picture, then back to the host.

“How do you prepare for Elpis?” asked a voice from offscreen.

“Oh, that’s easy,” said the host, holding up a glass and a bottle of Hennessy, which he started pouring- and pouring, and pouring. Then he drank straight from the bottle. Aisha made a spluttering noise.

“Okay, that one’s pretty good,” Anchorage said.

“Personally I think Hennesy’s overrated,” Stoneknapper said.

Chord, picture.

“You ever been bitchslapped by someone with steel gloves and six kinds of super strength?” I noticed Isabella was mouthing along to the words.

“No?” said the offscreen voice.

“It don’t feel good.”

Tock Tick snickered. “Okay, that’s kind of good.”

Chord, picture.

“She didn’t even touch him, she just looked at the guy and he dropped and started screaming! I almost called my mom!”

“Hah!” Butcher laughed. A couple others did too. My lips twitched.

Chord, picture.

“She just walked up and pulled a sword out of the wall! I lost my will to fight that day!”

That one got a proper laugh from me.

“Damn right!” Muramasa chuckled.

Chord, picture.

I noticed some ominous music playing in the background, gradually getting louder. “The insects all over the walls was bad enough, but when they started talking? My pal Lenny had a stroke off pure fear.”

Dirty Rotter just cackled horribly.

Chord, picture.

“So how many powers does she have?” asked the offscreen voice.

“Mm-hm.”

“The fuck you mean mm-hm?”

“I mean yes!”

Chord, picture.

“She’s a nightmare… She’s like if-”

“-if Doom Guy was wearing a cape?”

“Yeah, but how the fuck you know that?!”

“Oh my god, that’s exactly right,” Vladimir realised.

“Rip and tear!” Bearskin roared

Chord, picture.

“She killed Jack Slash in a knife fight! Why the fuck am I here?!”

Chord, picture. I noticed the background music had stopped.

“You know what? There’s not enough Raid in the goddamn world, I’m out.” The guy got up and just walked away.

“And that’s it,” Aisha said with a giggle. “So what did you think, boss?”

“That’s fantastic,” I agreed, grinning broadly. “Does he have other videos?”

“Tons.”

Chapter 154: 15.8

Friday 20th January, Philadelphia

Faultline flicked through the second half of the payment and nodded. “All right, we’re done. Thank you for your business.”

“No, thank you,” March said with a genuine smile. “This is definitely going to come in handy.” She ran a finger down the folder of top-level parahuman power research files lovingly.

“If that’s all, we’ll be leaving now,” Faultline continued.

“Right, right, have a safe trip,” March said with a careless wave.

Faultline nodded, and she and her crew trooped out through the back door of the underground bar that catered to villains, Trainwreck bringing up the rear.

March waited until the door was closed behind them, counted to five, then got up and walked over to the bar. The man behind the counter was wearing a mask- she wasn’t sure whether he had powers, but he was good at what he did.

“They’re leaving,” he said, glancing down below the bar. She’d peeked just enough to confirm that there were little screens down there that showed the feeds of various security cameras around the establishment.

“And the tracker?”

The bartender held up a cheap plastic keychain of a baseball. It swung slightly on its chain, pulling to the left in defiance of gravity.

“Planted on their car. This is the paired object. Polestar said it’ll last for three days before the effect wears off. The greater the pull, the further they are.”

March took the keychain with a nod. “Got it.” She handed over his payment and left without a word.

Another car was pulling into the parking lot as she made it up the stairs and out the door. Right on schedule. She slipped into the passenger seat and held up the keychain. “Drive.”

The driver set off without a word.

 

 

While the driver drove, occasionally consulting the keychain to make sure they were following the same route as Faultline’s crew without being close enough to be spotted, March paged through the files.

She knew plenty about powers. Homer, her other clustermate, had filled her in on some stuff he’d learned, and she’d acted as bodyguard for an independent researcher. That was what had led her to the six-person cluster from White Rock, who’d triggered next to the portal someone had made between worlds. And that had led to her being kidnapped and drained of blood by Bill, who’d thought he could take her powers like he tried to take the rest of his clustermates.

It hadn’t worked- he couldn’t take her powers, and he couldn’t get them all. Bianca had finished him off, had rescued her clustermates and March. But in that one shining moment, when she’d lost just enough blood for the darkness to wash over her, she’d seen the black-and-red crystals, the power running through them, the patterns that resembled events and ideas and people.

She’d seen Homer, poor dead Homer, and communicated with him in a way that exceeded anything flesh could produce, felt his sadness that he’d been swallowed up by the villains he hadn’t known to avoid and beware until it was far too late. But he was there, in the endless after that awaited everyone else with powers.

And she’d remembered it- not everything, the particulars blurred when the doctors had managed to revive her- but the deep impression, fuelled by the energy of that portal? That lingered, and she knew what she had to do.

Flechette was in Brockton Bay now, which was a problem. Elpis ruled the city like a spider in its web, repelling all attempts by other villains to move in and start doing business. March had no intention of fighting the Butcher- the last time she’d tried to fight someone with multiple strong powers, she’d ended up strapped to a chair being drained of her blood.

However, Elpis also ventured out of the city on little trips, often with a few of her teammates or allied heroes, up and down the East Coast to flatten whatever villain groups had managed to overstep and get themselves in the news. The fools down in Connecticut who’d kidnapped a Ward had become more famous for the way Elpis had dragged their broken bodies to the PRT than for anything they’d done before.

So, Elpis would not always be in the city, and would usually take a few other heroes with her. March would slip in just behind Faultline’s crew as they returned to Brockton Bay to help throw off any Thinker powers trying to detect incoming capes, and bide her time until Elpis’s next outing. That still left the reduced Protectorate team, the Wards, the unmasked heroes New Wave, and the Undersiders themselves. It would take careful planning, painstaking reconnaissance, and perfect timing.

March smiled to herself. She was all about timing.

 

 

Wednesday 1st February, Brockton Bay
