I made some sculptures out of it- they just sold at auction.” Not the first time I’d done that either- the victory sculptures I did were a pretty minor sideline compared to the businesses I owned, the silk I sold and the various bounties I’d pulled in over the years, but every little helped.

“Plus it gives us an in with the rich bastards who want to look good donating to charity,” Stoneknapper snorted.

“Well, I hope you got a good price.”

“Oh yeah, pretty good. We donated the money to charity- there’s a foundation helping homeless people get back on their feet right here in New York. They do good work.” Admittedly, part of the reason I’d chosen it was because homeless people were often the first pick for villain’s henchmen, but it was still a good cause.

“And that’s just the most recent victory we’ve seen from you. What was it last month, the Adepts?”

“Oh yeah- although that was a group effort. The New York Protectorate really did most of the legwork, we just added extra muscle.”

“Still, I think we can say New York appreciates it,” Kevin said, turning towards the audience. “What do you say folks, do you appreciate it?”

There was another round of whistling and whooping. I smiled and waved it off again.

“Woo! Noo Yawk, bay-bee!” Anchorage hollered.

“Bada-bing, bada-boom!” Quarrel added.

“I guess the next question is, what villains are you going after next?”

I shook my head playfully. “Now, I can’t really say that. After all, I have to keep the element of surprise. Plus, if they don’t know who I’m going to hit, it makes all the villains hunker down to try and avoid attention.”

Kevin nodded. “You’ve certainly developed a reputation as a figure to be feared by villains. What are your thoughts on that, does that ever hurt more than it helps?”

“Fear always works,” Nemean said with a snort.

“You know what he means,” I countered, putting a hand to my chin. “Usually no. I mean, when I’m taking out a villain group, I want them to be afraid of me- they know I’m there to take them down, they know they’re facing consequences, and they should be afraid of that. And after the dust has settled, I’m usually playing the bad cop, y’know? Which is kind of fun.” I sharpened my teeth to grin nastily.

Kevin jerked theatrically in his seat. “Jesus,” he said, clutching his chest. I had to admit, he wasn’t a bad actor. If I hadn’t known we’d rehearsed this hours before, I might have been fooled.

I retracted the fangs and spoke more soberly. “I won’t lie, there are moments when it’s a drawback. If I’m trying to convince some minor offender to turn to the heroes, they might be too scared to really listen, and that’s a problem.”

“What do you do when that happens?” Kevin asked.

“I usually hand them over to the local heroes, let them make the recruitment pitch instead. I can’t do everything myself.”

Kevin nodded. “Openly recruiting former villains is one of your most well-known tactics- and we’ve seen how that opened the door for other groups to follow. The Protectorate and Wards have a few people in their ranks now who admit to having a checkered past. I’m guessing you’re proud of that.”

“Oh, absolutely,” I said with a nod. “Part of the reason that there’s such a high villain population was because people believed that even a single crime would bar them from heroics forever- even something like accidental damage or fighting in self-defence. I think being able to create opportunities for capes to openly redeem themselves is one of my greatest achievements. I mean,” I gestured, “I understand very well how easy it can be to slip into crime when you’re desperate or backed into a corner.”

Kevin nodded, fiddling with the mug on his desk. “I think we all feel better knowing it’s possible to start again.”

“Amen to that.”

“Which brings me to another topic- Brockton Bay. If there’s anything you’ve had a hand in turning around, it’s your hometown.” The screen behind us switched to pictures again- satellite photos of Brockton Bay, just after Leviathan’s attack on the left, and a few weeks ago on the right. The difference was easy to see- waterlogged streets and ruined buildings replaced by clear avenues and new construction, wrecked ships removed to leave the Docks clear and open. I could just make out the crater where Jack had died, and the intersection we’d widened to let people get around the time bubble still holding Lung and Crawler.

“Everybody’s heard of Brockton rising from the ashes- or I guess I should say the waters,” Kevin said with a grin. “Low crime rates, a growing job market, massive reconstruction efforts- I heard you turned down an offer to build a statue in your honour.”

“I still say you should have taken it,” Muramasa grumbled.

“Well, it would have felt arrogant to accept,” I said to both of them. “As proud as I am of my achievements, I had good people supporting me every step of the way. The Undersiders, the Protectorate, the Wards, New Wave- not to mention the people of Brockton Bay. We all came together to rebuild our city into something great. And there’s still work to be done, it’s a constant effort.”

“Right,” Kevin said, taking a sip from his mug. “There’s a few villains that have managed to slip into Brockton, aren’t there?”

I grimaced, the eyebrows on my helmet bumping together. “Urgh. Unfortunately.”

“As a matter of fact, we have a clip from your encounter with one of them- a woman called Multitude?”

I sat forward in my chair, pointing a finger. “Kevin, don’t you dare-”

“Let’s take a look!” Kevin crowed as the screen switched to a clip I knew very well.

Phone camera footage shot from an upstairs window showed a woman in a blue suit covered in black stick figures, backed up against a wall on the street below. I was approaching her with an arrow nocked in my bow, Grue and Whirlygig on either side of me. “It’s over, Multitude!” I heard myself shout. “Surrender!” Insects whipped around me, approaching Multitude from every angle.

Multitude reached for a shoulder holster, whipped out a snub-nose revolver, and put it to her own head. “Hold it!” she shrieked. “You let me go or I blow this bitch’s head off!”

“What the fuck?” muttered the person behind the camera.

Then the me on screen lowered her bow, pulling back the insects. “Hold it guys,” I said grimly. “She’s not bluffing.”

The audience burst out laughing. I clapped a hand to my face with a groan.

“Get back!” Multitude snarled at Whirlygig. “Or I swear to God I’ll paint the walls with her brains!” She changed from a snarl to a terrified whimper, saying “Oh god, do what she says! I don’t want to die!”

Slowly, Whirlygig let her storm die down, and Multitude began to edge away, still holding the gun to her temple. “Help me!” she screamed. “Please help me- Shut up!”

Multitude threw herself around the corner, and the clip ended.

The audience was roaring, and Kevin was laughing hysterically, slapping the table with his palm. I just put my face in my hands and groaned.

“Oh, oh man,” Kevin said, catching his breath. “I’m sorry, but that was hilarious. How did that even happen?”

I dragged my hands up and off my face with a sigh. “Well, we thought Multitude was what you’d call a Master- a cape who fights through minions, in this case by duplicating herself. Turns out she was a Stranger- a cape with stealth powers. She wasn’t actually duplicating herself, she was creating the illusion of being multiple people. So when she put her gun to her head…”

“You thought she was taking a hostage,” Kevin finished, still snickering a little. “Okay, that- that makes sense.”

“Can’t believe you fell for the Blazing Saddles gag,” Firecracker snorted.

“Bitch, you fell for it too!” I snapped. “You all did!”

“We got her in the end at least,” I said out loud, raising a finger. “Once we got hold of the footage we realised what was going on.” That and Imp’s own power once again coming out on top. She was getting really smug about out-Stranger-ing Strangers.

“You’ve had problems with the sneakier sort of villains before, right?” Kevin said, sounding a little more serious. “There was that guy who snuck through the Gimel portal to go hunting buffalo?”

“Well, that was multiple guys. Trespasser was the one who got them through the portal, but Big Game, Backwoods and Trophy Wife were the ones doing the poaching.”

“You caught them a lot faster though, right?”

“Oh, absolutely. Security’s tight around the portal, on both sides.” Part of that was Protectorate Tinkertech, part of that was my own booby-traps, and part of that was Accord’s off-the-books security measures in exchange for permission to expand legitimate businesses into Brockton. “We pinged them fast- the only real delay was in Cerberus tracking them through the wild and dragging them back. She did a great job there.”

“That’s another bit of construction you’re famous for,” Kevin pointed out. “You guys had the first portal to Gimel, and you’re still in the top five spots for most developed Gimel settlements.”

I shrugged. “Well, it was an unprecedented opportunity to expand and revitalise the city- and a lot of people were happy to make the move. Get out to the unspoilt countryside while still staying within walking distance of all the good shops? Heck, if I weren’t busy I might have given it a shot.”

“Yeah, all the pictures I’ve seen of it look amazing,” Kevin said. More pictures flashed up on screen- the rapidly expanding Gimel Brockton, or New Brockton, starting simple lumberyards and fishing docks, then adding train tracks and stations and warehouses to transport and store the goods, then proper houses and streets. Lots of people were happy to live the frontier lifestyle when they could still pop back into Bet for fast food and movies anytime they wanted. “Is it true you hunted a mammoth out there?”

I snorted. “I wish! Nah, some guys made the trip to do legitimate hunting , but they couldn’t get the skull through Customs, so they gave it to me instead.

“Wow. What did you do with it?”

“Donated it to a museum,” I said with a shrug. “I didn’t have room for it at my place.” The lair had enough trophies as it was- Kaiser’s helmet, March’s sword, a fragment of wood from the Fallen’s barn…

“Besides the bones, is it true you can get mammoth meat in Brockton?”

“That’s pretty rare- Mammoths mostly range up in Canada or Europe. Bison and Buffalo are easier to get- and passenger pigeon. I heard about somebody planning to sail down to Mauritius to get some dodos, but no results so far.”

“I bet they make great omelettes,” Kevin said with a grin.

“I’ll let you know when I try one,” I said. That got a laugh from the audience.

“Personally I want to find out what sea turtle taste like,” Vladimir admitted.

“But besides the portal, there’s plenty going on in Brockton Bay these days, huh?”

“Oh yeah. Lots of tourism for the Jack Slash Crater, for one. There’s also plenty of people coming up to see all the heroes, especially since we got the new cross-training initiative set up.”

“Can you tell us a little more about that?” Kevin asked, leaning forward.

“Of course,” I said. “Basically the Undersiders partnered up with the Protectorate and the various hero groups we’re associated with, and we run training exercises with various new heroes to get them ready for the job. Basics of combat, strategy, coming up with creative uses for their powers, stuff like that.”

“And a lot of those heroes are former villains that you helped flip, right?”

“Yes, that’s true as well. It’s definitely satisfying to watch them grow and change in front of my eyes.”

“Plus it helps them get their names out there by association. A lot of the heroes you’ve mentored have gone up in the world fast.”

“Oh, absolutely. But that’s not just me, that’s because of their hard work and dedication too.”

“Still, you do have a well-deserved reputation for sticking up for the underdog. Your work with Case 53s, for instance.”

“Well, I’ve got the memories of a Case 53- I know what it’s like. I couldn’t just stand by and do nothing to help.”

Kevin nodded. “No arguments here. And then there’s your outreach to the LGBT community. I don’t mean to be rude, but Brockton used to have a reputation, what with the gangs-”

“Oh, you can say it. The Empire Eighty Eight were a bunch of Nazis- being openly queer in Brockton Bay used to be seriously dangerous. But after we drove them out and carved out a few safe spaces, I’m happy to say that things have really turned around.”

“Oh, absolutely. In fact, we’ve got some footage of last year’s Pride Parade.” Kevin gestured, and the screen changed to more cellphone video.

The footage was from the side of the street, lined with people cheering. A lot of them were tourists, but every year more locals had turned up.

I came first, holding a long spear with a rainbow flag hanging from just below the head. I remember I’d thought it would make a good statement- we’re here, we’re queer, we’ll stab you.

A float of civilians came next, gay men waving and blowing kisses in various colourful outfits. Aegis flew overhead, darting back and forth through the air, waving pride flags in either hand.

Parian came after them, riding on a horse puppet with a mane in lesbian pride colours, red-orange-white-pink-purple. She was tossing handfuls of confetti from a basket in her lap, waving and beaming at the crowd. Close behind her was the lesbian pride float, with Amy perched on top in a place of honour, blowing kisses to the crowd. As I remembered, quite a few women had been blowing kisses back. Flechette was stood at the front, waving a little stiffly. Only someone who knew what to look for would have seen she was sneaking glances at Parian half the time.

After that, a march of people on foot, including heroes and civilians. Vortex had visited just for the parade, and was bouncing through the air with her gravity powers, trans pride colours painted on her armour. On the ground, Tattletale was idly waving an ace pride flag, looking supremely unbothered by all the commotion. Smokescreen from Boston was bringing up the rear, shifting into mist and back again, occasionally tipping his hat to people in the crowd.

“Looks like one hell of a party,” Kevin said.

“Oh yeah, it only got wilder after that,” I said.

“Any plans to top it this year?”

I very carefully kept smiling. The countdown was still going, and we checked with Thinkers every week or so to see if anything had changed. The end of the world was set to happen in late June this year.

“Fingers crossed,” I said, instead of admitting that I was worried everything would go to hell before we could throw another parade.

 

 

Saturday March 29th, Brockton Bay

Amy was curled up on the couch when I got in, late in the afternoon. “Hey,” she said, muting the TV and getting up. “Did you get them?”

“Most of them,” I said, kicking the door shut and dropping my bag with a sigh. “The Legionnaires were slippery- a couple managed to escape into the subway tunnels. We got the heavy hitters though- Aquila and Romulus and fucking Colossus.”

“Goddamn stupid,” Tactical muttered. “The Colossus of Rhodes was Greek, not Roman.”

“Yeah, but the Romans pinched everything from the Greeks anyway,” Rotter pointed out.

“You looked good on TV,” Amy said, slipping her arms around my neck. I leaned into her warmth, leaning down to peck her on the lips.

“Thanks. I missed you.”

Amy kissed me back, more insistent. I matched her at first, but she pulled herself in close and clutched at me almost desperately. I broke the kiss to look her in the eyes. “What’s wrong?”

Amy worried at her lower lip with her teeth. “What you said, about Pride this year… I just got to thinking about the end again. We’ve only got a few months left, and we’ve got no idea what sets it off.”

“Hey.” I cupped her face. “We’re going to figure it out, okay? Every group on the planet is looking- they’ll find something. Okay?”

Amy pressed herself to me again. “Just… just hold me.”

I squeezed her gently. “Okay.”

Chapter 158: 15.12

Friday 20th June 2014, PRT Quarantine Zone 5, Flint, Michigan

“We’re approaching the drop site,” Dragon said over the intercom.

“You’ve got this,” Flinch told me. Despite the confidence in his tone, I could feel the nerves radiating off him.

I rose from the hard seat of the Dragoncraft, checking my equipment one last time. I’d made myself a new set of mechanical arms for this- they were attached to the back of my armour, my cape rolled up and out of the way. Moving the insects in special control chambers unfolded the arms, spidery things tipped with bladed claws. Four attachable guns were loaded into slots at my belt- I checked each one before folding the arms back.

On my wrists, two more guns, with plenty of spare magazines. Two swords, my flail, an axe. Knives all over, balanced for throwing or stabbing. My stun batons. Smoke grenades, frag grenades, a couple of Bakuda grenades- the PRT had to be very careful in what she was allowed to make in prison, but the effectiveness of her bombs were worth the risk.

Several crates were lined up along the length of in craft’s interior, all packed with insects modified by Amy. Most of them were based on dragonflies, fast and agile, with a sharp bite. Others had stingers loaded with paralytic and sedative venoms. Some could spin silk thread, some sprayed noxious chemicals, and there were a few that Amy had made after much careful experimentation together; relay bugs that could boost the range of my insect control.

“I’m surprised it took so long, with all the experimenting you two do,” Dirty Rotter leered.

“Yeah, but cat ears ain’t exactly power research,” Firecracker pointed out with a snicker.

I chuckled along with the Butchers. Amy and I had done some weird stuff with her power. And right now I needed a laugh.

“Touching down,” Dragon said. I felt a slight jolt as the craft landed. The cockpit door opened, Armsmaster coming out. I glimpsed Dragon, seated at the pilot’s chair. She still didn’t show up on bloodsight- I’d never questioned her on it.

Armsmaster gave me a nod as I opened the crates. His armour was thicker, heavier, even with his speciality in efficiency and miniaturisation. He had two halberds on his back, folded up, and I knew that this version of his armour had nanothorn projectors in the arms and legs.

The cargo door at the back of the craft opened, lowering into a ramp. I drew the insects out of the crates and headed down, spreading the bugs out to check the area while I looked around with bloodsight. So far, nothing. The streets were empty, the houses worn by time, yards overgrown and pavements cracked.

The PRT had walled the town off years before I got powers, when someone had popped up with the power to force people to develop corona pollentias and trigger with powers. They’d started a villain group, put together from as many of their triggers as they could, and had rapidly taken over the town with sheer force. Then the group mutinied.

Someone in the PRT must have had a morbid sense of humour, because the original cape’s provisional name in the files was Golden Goose. The group had carved them into chunks, taking care to leave the victim alive just in case, and used the bits of flesh to cause more triggers, forcibly inducting people into their gang. Factions had formed, betrayals and backstabs everywhere, and the town was hastily quarantined to prevent the violence from spilling outwards.

After several years, the town was mostly emptied- the civilians had slowly been evacuated after careful checks to make sure they didn’t have powers, and the villains had gradually worn themselves down. Still, I kept my guns cocked and ready.

“Feels like a ghost town,” Stoneknapper muttered.

“Not ghosts,” Vladimir said. “Monsters.”

I clicked my earpiece. “Cassandra, check in. Tell me how many questions you can manage.”

“Thirty one,” Cassandra said quietly. “Maybe more, maybe less, it depends on how I stretch it. Confirm the colours.”

“Red means forward, left, attack, team. Blue means back, right, retreat, solo. Thank you for this.”

“I can’t find where the pieces are for you,” Cassandra warned. “They make the numbers fuzzy. You’ll need to ask Tattletale for that.”

“Got it. Thank you.”

“Go save the world.”

The other Dragoncraft had landed nearby, and the other members of the strike team were emerging. Ironclad’s armour was mostly thick plates now, like a battleship, and I’d added and axe blade to one side of his hammer. Rachel had a dozen dogs, all growing to full size. Grue, Whirlygig, and Imp all had armoured costumes and guns just in case.

Secondary members of the Undersiders were getting ready as well- Clean-Cut with his three swords, Smokescreen in his trenchcoat, Vortex in her roller derby outfit, Wraith with his ragged cape and steel helmet. Boilerplate cracked her knuckles and rolled her shoulders, while Damsel of Distress flicked some of her white hair over her shoulder with a gloved hand- you had to look close to see the hexagonal patterns in the thick fabric that extended to the elbows, Tinkertech designed to help her control and focus her destructive blasts.

“Alright,” I said, now confident that the immediate area was secure. “You all know what’s at stake. Thinkers say this zone affects the odds of the end of the world scenario. We don’t know exactly how, but the popular guess is some runaway power-inducing scenario- liquify some of Golden Goose’s flesh and drop it into the water supply of a major city, cause hundreds of trigger events in one go.”

“Disgusting,” Imp said cheerfully.

“And horrifying,” I agreed. “So we’re going to turn this town upside down if we have to, gather up the pieces and destroy them, then find Golden Goose and extract them. Remember that the villains in this town are ruthless, so don’t pull your punches. Got it?”

“Got it,” Grue said. The others joined in with various affirmatives- Damsel just gave an imperious nod, but I’d expected that. She still had a massive ego- half the reason I’d managed to recruit her was because she respected my reputation, so when I treated her as a peer, it elevated her by proxy.

“Good hunting,” Armsmaster said to me as the ramp closed and the Dragoncrafts lifted off with a roar of engines. They’d keep watch from the air, monitoring the quarantine zone for trouble, especially any escape attempts. There’d been villains trying to break out before, and a few individuals had even succeeded, but a mass breakout now would be the kind of event that might trigger the apocalypse.

I led the way deeper into town, sweeping the area for any traps or people. After a few minutes, I found some- puddles on the ground that looked like water, but killed my bugs on contact. I directed the Undersiders to avoid the acid, and we kept going. I was proud of how alert everyone was- heads on a swivel, hands on their weapons. Even the dogs were periodically sniffing the air.

As we advanced further in, the signs of powers became more and more apparent. Cut off from the rest of the world, with only limited supplies provided from outside, people had got creative to survive. Lawns had been torn up and converted into vegetable patches, cars had been stripped, houses had been gutted of everything down to the wiring in the walls. I picked up on a few people watching us from a distance, hiding in shadows or peering from their homes. I alerted the Undersiders, but otherwise we ignored them.

There was a bang like a cannon going off, and I saw something shoot up into the air from the north. I looked up in time to see one of the Dragoncraft swerve to avoid the shot.

“Elpis, something’s shooting at us from the surface,” Dragon reported. “Armsmaster’s going to drop in to deal with it, but I’ll need to move my suits higher to avoid getting shot down.”

“Got it,” I said, watching the suits gain altitude. A blue object dropped from one- that’d be Armsmaster.

Off in the distance, my bugs brushed up against somebody inside a house, touching all the glass- windows, lightbulbs, picture frames. When he touched it, the glass turned liquid and poured out of the frame, then hardened again. The guy picked the glass up and stuck it in a bag on his back. Another bang sounded as somebody fired at Dragon again, and the guy looked around nervously.

“He must be a scavenger,” Muramasa noted. “Perhaps they’re trying to set up greenhouses for gardening.”

“Or there’s some Tinker who needs it for god knows what,” Tactical added.

“If he can affect it with his power, maybe he’s gathering ammo,” Butcher said.

“Could be all of the above,” I admitted, moving a few more bugs over. I picked up the approach of several people coming down the road the scavenger was working. They had markings on their skin- little glowing cracks or spots, bits that changed colour or moved around. One of them had eyes that glowed slightly. The scavenger seemed to lack them- odd.

“Maybe he’s a natural trigger,” Stoneknapper suggested.

“People moving down the road about three blocks east,” I said to the group. “Let’s keep it quiet.”

One of the group, a woman in a dirty green hoodie, raised a finger and pointed at the house. “Come on out, little rat!” yelled the guy at the front of the group, loud enough to hear him from that distance.

“You just had to say it,” Imp snorted.

The scavenger bolted out the backdoor- the woman in the hoodie, presumably a Thinker, pointed, and another hurled a tennis ball over the fences and into the backyard, then teleported to the ball as it landed. The scavenger skidded to a halt at the sight of her, falling on his ass. “Should have stayed on your turf, bitch,” the teleporter spat, drawing a knife.

“Here she goes,” Needler noted. “So much for being quiet.”

“Okay, we’re switching to interrogating the locals,” I announced, drawing a baton. “Follow the noise.” I teleported into the backyard at once.

The teleporter stumbled back with a shriek, and I slapped the knife from her hand. The rest of the group was charging through the house, just in time for me to unfold the waldos and point guns at them. “Don’t even think about it,” I said, my bugs amplifying the words.

“Who the fuck are you?” said a black man with a faint shimmer around his body and iridescent patterns on his cheekbones. Another bang from the anti-Dragon cannon or whatever that was underlined his question.

“Elpis of the Undersiders,” I said. “I don’t know if you’ve heard of me-”

The Thinker woman shook the man’s shoulder. “She’s the one that killed Jack Slash,” she hissed. The capes started at that, staring at me with new interest.

“How do you know that, anyway?”

“I saw you on TV,” the Thinker explained. “Heard you messed up some kidnappers.”

“Yeah, I don’t like people who hurt kids.” I glanced pointedly at the scavenger, who looked younger than me. He gave me a wide-eyed look as he slowly got to his feet, looking ready to bolt at any moment.

“They have TVs here?” Bearskin wondered.

“They probably have some tinkers keeping stuff running,” Nemean pointed out. “Like in the Birdcage.”

“Look, let me talk to whoever’s in charge here,” I said, slowly pointing the guns away from them. “I’ll handle my business here and get out of your way.”

The Thinker woman suddenly whipped her head around as the Undersiders rounded the corner on the dogs.

“Or you could try to handle me and my team,” I added. “Your choice.”

The leader looked at the Thinker, who frantically shook her head.

 

 

After letting the scavenger go, a few minutes walking through town brought us to a neighbourhood that was covered in bluish translucent crystal. Walls of the stuff surrounded the area, topped with spikes, and the crystal grew over the houses inside like a shell. It was smooth to the touch, glinting oddly in the summer sun.

“Somebody’s really into the bling,” Anchorage noted.

“Let me go first,” said the squad leader, whose name turned out to be Shimmer. “They see all of you walking up, they’ll think this is an attack.”

“Hang back guys,” I said, arranging my insects in the ‘be ready’ signal.

There was a gate made of a couple of shed doors coated in more crystal. As I approached with Shimmer and his squad, a puddle of amber liquid seeped under the gate, and rose up into a vaguely human shape. A mouth appeared, and a voice like a gurgling drain said, “Who the fuck are you?”

“It’s like a sewage monster,” Quarrel said in disgust.

Tock Tick gave it a considering look. “Nah, I’d say it looks more like maple syrup.”

“We’re the Undersiders,” I said. “I’m Elpis.”

The blob’s head tilted to the side- the liquid sagged downwards, so its entire head drooped at the gesture. “Huh. Heard of you,” it gurgled, strings of liquid stretching and snapping across its mouth as it spoke. “You’re the one that killed Jack Slash, right? What’re you doing here?”

“I’m here for the pieces of flesh.”

“The flesh?” the blob asked, turning its head back upright.

“The bits of the person that grants powers.”

 The blob’s shrug was more like a ripple in the liquid. “Not happening.”

“This is important. Thinkers say something’s going to happen that causes the end of the world. And you guys might be pretty cut off in here, but you’re still part of the world.”

Shimmer’s head snapped around to stare at me. The blob rippled all over for a second, like a full body shudder. “Wait here.” It collapsed back into a puddle and oozed under the gate again.

“We don’t have time to talk to them,” Needler said at once.

“Which is why we’re not waiting,” I replied, turning around to the others. “I’ll stay to talk with these guys, I want the rest of you to keep moving. Look for other territories, introduce yourselves, ask around for anything causing trouble, anything that might be the catalyst.” I made another signal with my bugs, ‘I’m watching’. With Amy’s relay bugs, I was gradually spreading my range over the entire zone. It was incredible- I’d never had so much to control before.

It was how I picked up on something approaching- a large group of parahumans, with weapons and armour. At their head was a massive reptilian thing, like an alligator’s skin stretched over an elephant, and on its back was a black woman’s jumpsuit, holding a scythe. There was a cloud of black smoke where the head should have been.

“Never mind, we’ve got incoming. Battle up!” I sent insects past the gate to find the blob, and the woman it was talking to. She was black, mid-twenties, with little bits of blue crystal in her hair and all over her clothes like beads. “You’ve got incoming- stop screaming- there’s a huge group headed this way. Big lizard and a woman with a black scythe.”

“I was right about the bling,” Anchorage noted.

“Dullahan and Grim Gator,” the crystal woman blurted, staring at the ball of insects I was speaking to her with. “They must have got riled up by the dragons.”

“This conflict might be what causes the end. Destroying the flesh is our best bet. Where’s your piece?”

The crystal woman swallowed. “We don’t have any more. It rotted years ago. Triggerman died last spring too- somebody got explosive powers from him and blew up the building.”

“His name was Triggerman? That’s fucking stupid.”

“Where’s the rest of it?”

“Most of the other gangs lost theirs too- when Triggerman died, the effect keeping the pieces going dropped. Most of ‘em rotted. I think Dullahan has a chunk though- she’s got a Tinker that makes water stuff, and ice. She trades us fridges for stuff- maybe she’s got her piece in a deep freeze.”

“Got it.” I tapped my earpiece. “Dinah, the advancing force- what colour?”

“Red.”

“Thanks. Alright kids,” I said out loud, drawing weapons and flexing my waldos, “We’re going to have to go through them! Get your bodycams ready, give Tattletale all the data she needs- if they’ve got the piece we’re looking for, that’s where we need to go!”

The Undersiders roared, forming battle lines. I was so damn proud of them. Ironclad took point, with Clean-Cut and Boilerplate on his flanks; Smokescreen, Vortex and Damsel in the second rank ready to jump in. Grue, Whirlygig and Cerberus stayed on the dogs, as the most experienced riders.

“Boss,” Tattletale said through my earpiece, “Don’t forget your camera.”

I clicked the camera in my helmet on. “I’ll try to get Dullahan and squeeze some answers out of her. Keep me updated.”

I pulled insects together into a row of figures in front of the advancing column, which stopped them dead. “Dullahan,” I said, “I want to talk. I’m Elpis.”

Dullahan made a scoffing sound that sounded like it was coming from the bottom of a well. “Oh, the hero bitch wants to talk,” she sneered. “Well, fuck you! We don’t need you coming in here and messing with our stuff! Right, people?!”

The crowd roared and brandished weapons- most of them had the markings of induced powers.

“Listen to me. The Thinkers say that there’s a disaster coming- something that’ll destroy the world. And whatever starts it off is here.” The crowd went quiet at that, looking uncertain, and I pushed ahead. “Listen, the most likely thing would be Triggerman’s flesh, and the word is you’ve got the last bit of it. Just tell me where it is, and we’ll go.”

“Really hard to read someone who doesn’t have a face, but her legs just twitched,” Tattletale reported. “She’s thinking of the direction where the flesh is stored.”

“Appeal to her ego,”

“It’s not like you need it anymore- look at the force you’ve got just here.” I sent relay bugs in a chain away and around the group, headed for the direction they’d come from. I moved insects into the area, carefully- I could have just flooded the place, but Dullahan might have a warning system or booby traps. “Cassandra, I’m moving insects south-east of my position. Colour?”

“Red. Keep going.”

Dullahan scoffed. “What, so I’m just supposed to give up my best asset because you say so? How do I know you’re even really Elpis? How do I know Lapis didn’t just dig up someone else who can control bugs for some trick?”

“Do you think Lapis could find a way to fake Dragon bringing multiple aircraft here?” I asked, turning one of the figures into an arrow that pointed up to where the Dragoncrafts were holding steady a few hundred feet up. “Just give us the flesh and we’ll go. We can make it worth your while- maybe extra supply drops for your territory.”

Dullahan swung her scythe from side to side in a thoughtful manner, then tapped the end against the hide of Grim Gator, who tilted his head so one yellow eye was looking at her. Something passed between them.

“That’s a no,” Tattletale said just as Dullahan raised her scythe.

“Your powers go to whoever kills you, right?”

“Don’t-”

“So how about I just take your powers and do whatever the hell I want?”

“Okay, I tried.” The figures dissolved as I threw insects at the crowd.

People screamed and yelled, but a woman with a water cooler tank on her back stepped forward, spraying water from a hose in her hands. It came out as a fine mist, and every droplet froze an insect on contact, carving a hole in the swarm. I drew in more insect from the surrounding area.

“Charge!”  I shouted, breaking into a run. The Undersiders followed, on dogs and on foot. Vortex leapt up on Ironclad’s back as he thundered along, cracking the asphalt with each step.

Grim Gator bellowed and surged forward, Dullahan letting out a war cry. The rest of her gang followed, one taking to the air and aiming straight for me. I opened fire on her with two guns, the other shooting at Grim Gator. Gator took some damage, the scales on his head cracking and breaking, but the flying woman just grunted as she dived at me feet first. I hit her with pain and leapt back, swinging my flail into her face. She was sent tumbling back, but flipped in midair and came at me again.

“Tough bitch,” Nemean snarled.

I fired on Dullahan instead- bullets punched through her costume, and she fell off Grim Gator as the dogs tackled him, but she rolled as she landed and came up swinging at Clean-Cut, who had to use both katanas to block her scythe. She twisted her scythe to yank one from his hand and grabbed it for herself. The scythe disappeared, and the katana turned black as she stabbed forward.

The Alexandria package came at me again- I flicked the flail down at the ground, bouncing it up into her gut. She grunted and slowed, and I punched her in the ear. Even Brutes tended to be weak in the eardrums. Sure enough, she collapsed screaming and clutching her ear. I kicked her in the face to make sure and charged forward, firing a burst into the ice tinker’s tank. Water gushed out, freezing their boots in place and turning the street into an ice rink. A couple of villains were caught, but a man with glowing yellow lines from hairline to chin fired lasers into the ice, melting it around him and others.

“Elpis, there’s two incoming objects descending from the east,” Dragon reported. “One is confirmed to be Scion, about ten minutes out. The other is approaching visual range. It looks like… Oh no.”

“What the hell is so bad that Scion coming isn’t good enough?” Vladimir wondered.

I gathered bugs into an eye to look even as I decked the laser guy and sliced through a cat that had its legs and half its head replaced with metal. A second later I teleported back to get some room and look with my own eyes.

“Cassandra,” I said, lenses in my helmet adjusting to zoom in on the armoured suit hovering over the quarantine zone. A Dragoncraft was holding position close by, ready to fight. “Colour.”

“Red.”

I teleported high, on top of the Dragoncraft’s hull, pointed my arms and unfolded the waldos. Six guns opened fire at the Dragonslayer suit.

The fucker raised a hand, and a circle of golden light spread out from his palm like a shield. The bullets hit and stopped dead, falling out of the sky. I curved the bullets from my right wrist around the shield, hammering into his armour, and he flinched.

Sigurd was a mystery- he’d taken over the Dragonslayers, moved them away from attacking Dragon and towards heroic work. PRT suspected he was a Tinker with a speciality in light, based on how all the equipment he used harnessed it in some fashion.

“I want to help!” Sigurd shouted, voice amplified by his suit. There was distortion in there too- certainly deliberate, to disguise his voice.

“You expect us to trust that?” Dragon demanded, projecting her voice through the craft.

“Not really,” Sigurd admitted. “But I know about the prediction. I heard from someone that the odds are better if I’m here.”

“Cassandra,” I whispered.

“The immediate futures are better,” she answered. “There’s a limit- maybe ten minutes. If he stays too long then things get worse. I think. The future’s getting fuzzy- you have to move quickly.”

Scion’s presence interfered with precogs, I remembered. Not good.

So Sigurd could help if we moved fast, or make things worse if we took too long. Shit. What was so important about him?

“Dragon. It’s your call.”

Dragon was silent for a long moment. “Fine,” she bit out.

“For what it’s worth, I never agreed with what Saint was doing to you,” Sigurd said. The thrusters on his armour dimmed, and he dropped towards the fight.

I stepped off the Dragoncraft after him, falling towards the ground. When I was about to hit, I teleported- the extra kinetic energy was converted into more flames at the arrival site, knocking Grim Gator off his feet.

“I’m going after the flesh. Tats, Cassandra, guide me.”

 

 

The entity observed the human interactions from above. Various senses allowed it to gather information within a wide radius, and there was interesting data to be found.

The majority of the humans present had powers derived from one of the inducer shards, designed to maximise the spread of powers in a small area and create intense localised conflict. Their connections were strong, well-fed through years of conflict within a confined area.

However, they were outmatched by other figures- full shards, some crippled, like the perception shard meant to prevent the host species becoming aware of the entities when the shards connected. Even crippled, it allowed the female host to move unnoticed and strike without resistance. Another female commanded enhanced animals, and a third used a telekinetic hurricane to fling random debris.

The entity recognised one host it had seen before- the female host connected to the Administrator shard, and to fourteen others. A quirk of one shard focused on induced nervous stimuli- it had transferred its connection to another host, and caused the shards to accumulate around a single host. The shards were also retaining the memories of the hosts with far greater detail than was typical. A residual expression of the accretion process by which the entities recombined themselves.

The entity felt an emotion in its human avatar, and dismissed it. Simulation of the host species psychology was only that- a simulation.

The administrator used multiple abilities in combination- enhanced strength, enhanced senses, an ability that accelerated rot, another that shaped matter. Lengths of organic fibre carried by small invertebrates entangled limbs and restricted movements.

Constant activity from the joined shards as well- drawing on the memories of the previous hosts. Fascinating. Similar quirks had occurred in previous cycles, but never to this extent, and not with an administrator shard. Useful information.

Unfortunately, not information the entity could use. Not without its counterpart.

The administrator host battled its way to the centre of a structure, tearing through a wall to uncover a refrigerated storage unit. Inside was a lump of human flesh, emitting the matched signal to most of the hosts present. The humans must have separated the inducing shard’s host into multiple parts for maximum efficiency. The administrator seized the flesh and exerted her decay power, causing the flesh to rot.

The entity checked the surrounding area. There were no remaining instances of the emitter host’s flesh. It had served its purpose well at any rate.

“We got it!” the administrator host communicated, using the smaller invertebrates to replicate human speech. “The flesh is destroyed!”

Most of the hosts stopped fighting when they heard that, but a few of the induced hosts fought with renewed vigour. The entity noticed one that was using weapons reinforced with her power to attack a host in armour.

The armoured host was unusual- the Stilling shard. A dead shard, from the counterpart, not meant to be given to the host species- the stilling was always kept as a weapon and defense. Rather than being directly expressed through the host’s body, this was expressed through technological constructs.

The entity had witnessed it before, when engaging the conflict engines. The host was different though- physically younger, and the host’s connection to the shard was immature, not as strong. Possibly a deliberately created host. It was rare for a host species to experiment with shard connections in such a manner- effectively restoring the original host.

Another emotion came from the avatar. The entity dismissed it as well, mildly puzzled. Two emotions in a short period was unusual.

“It’s over!” The stilling host shouted, firing beams of energy at the host, who spun away and created a long-handled blade with her power, swinging at the stilling host. “Why the fuck are you still fighting?”

“Because fuck you!” The blade wielder swung uselessly at the stilling host. “I built something great here! You fuckers took everything from me! If I’m going down, I’m taking you all with me!”

The entity considered the sentiments behind the statement.

Creation. The hosts had created a micro-society within this restricted area, using the powers of their shards to accelerate the process. The entities did not work in large groups, but the search for new data was similar.

Destruction. An outside force had destroyed what was built here, for their own purposes. The entities destroyed as a matter of course, to advance their goals. There was also loss- the entity did not know how to advance its goals without its counterpart.

Spite. A petty or malicious desire to deliberately irritate or harm another. Rooted in instinctive actions. The entities did not harm one another due to emotion, but only to perpetuate the cycle- travel, experiment, reproduce, continue.

The stilling host’s question as well- motivation. The entity’s motivation was the cycle. Now that the cycle was broken, it had no motivation.

The stilling host defeated his opponent with a blast to the chest and turned to look at the entity.

The entity looked to the future, looked to possible worlds, and saw how this could have unfolded. It burned a year off the entity’s remaining lifespan, but it had thousands to spare anyway. There had been possibilities of the host of the broadcast shard speaking to the entity- those possibilities curtailed with his death. There were possibilities where the entity had watched the species for many years further and gradually come to the same conclusions.

It had done good deeds for years, at the suggestion of a single human who spoke to it, and had received neither reward nor realisation. It had continued despite a lack of conclusion because it did not have the imagination to seek out alternatives- that was the role of the counterpart, the Thinker to the Warrior. It only had power.

Still, it could experiment.

The entity moved, leaving the hosts below far behind, not returning to the task of saving lives. It continued to fly until it returned to the spot where it had first appeared.

Creation. Destruction. Loss. Spite.

The entity gathered its power, then aimed at a population centre. The birthplace of the human who had given the entity the instruction.

The golden light struck the landmass, crumpling it like paper in a fist. Parts of the island rose out of the ocean as others sank and crumbled. The entity did not eliminate the smoke or the waves that followed, letting them play out.

The simulated mind within the entity felt an emotion, and it did not dismiss it this time. Pleasure? Satisfaction? Relief? Perhaps this was spite?

Perhaps an instinctual response, tied back to the very beginning, before the beginning, when the entities first fought each other. Something deep within responded to the emotions in similar fashion.

The entity extended its perceptions outward, feeling the reaction of the host species. An interesting experience. After so much focus on the species as a whole, the development of shards, the shared path with its counterpart, the cycle… Now that it was alone, it felt that it was evolving as an individual.

The entity opened fire once more, and this time it struck out at the coastline on the opposite side of the ocean.

Chapter 159: 15.13

Chapter Notes

Woo! AO3 back up baby! Here's a catch-up update, the next chapter will be on the regular schedule ie a week from now.

Friday 20th June 2014

News of the attacks kept flooding in as we made it back to Brockton Bay- Libya, Russia, France, Sweden, Iran, Russia again, China. As the Dragoncraft flew over the city we could see people fleeing, heading out of the big cities, running for safety. But there wasn’t really anywhere safe to go.

Well, that wasn’t true. There was.

“Oh god,” Flinch murmured as we approached the East Coast. Cracks and fissures split the landscape, with fallen bridges and broken highways. More and more people were abandoning their cars to try and make it on foot.

I felt my heart sink as we reached the coast. Mountains I’d grow up with weren’t there anymore. Dragon had to slow down and steer us carefully through airspace choked with rescue aircraft.

The city had collapsed. The blast had only struck the northern edge, then changed direction to carve through the bay itself, slicing the very foundation the city rested on. Buildings had been dropped thirty or forty feet, and plenty had collapsed, mostly the taller ones. No section of ground more than twenty-five feet across was intact.

The portal building was still intact, like an island amidst the chaos, and I could see work crews desperately trying to rig something up so people could actually reach the damn thing and get onto Earth Gimel.

At the coast, there was a shimmering forcefield, the one that used to shield the Protectorate headquarters on the rig before Leviathan had smashed it inland. They’d repurposed it to hold back the water, but every few minutes it would flicker for a fraction of a second, letting water in. Still, it was holding enough to keep the city from being flooded.

“We should have told more people,” Anchorage muttered. We’d contacted everybody we trusted well before today- the Butcher’s families, close allies, even some of the lesser villains, warning them that something was going to happen today, to take a day trip to Earth Gimel just in case. Dad was there, Amy was there, Tattletale was ensconced in a command centre there, Flinch’s, Tactical’s and Anchorage’s folks had made it in time. Quarrel had sent her parents a letter, but we didn’t know if they’d taken it seriously- there hadn’t been time to check.

“I’m going to the portal,” I said, standing up. “Meet me there- we need to rig up an evacuation route. Somebody contact Vista, she’s our best shot.”

“And then what?” Aisha asked, clutching her bullet necklace. “What the fuck do we do then?”

It was a fair question, and one that I didn’t have an answer for. How the hell could we fight Scion? Someone more powerful than Behemoth, faster than Leviathan, more devastating than the Simurgh?

“I don’t know,” I admitted. I teleported outside with another word, falling towards the ground. I used another teleport before I landed, converting my momentum into fire and noise.

From the second my feet touched the ground, I was working. Brute strength and Stoneknapper’s shaping let me move debris and pile it into crude roads and staircases for people to reach the portal. Vista turned up, twisting another patch of space into a gentle ramp while I built something more solid, and people started rushing across. When the others reached the ground, they helped out- Ironclad and Whirlygig lifting the rubble and setting it down for me to sculpt into a road that switched back and forth to allow people to drive a car thirty feet up, while Grue and Cerberus used sheer muscle.

When the road was finished, and people started piling onto it to flee Earth Bet entirely, we headed out into the city. New Wave and the Protectorate were already rescuing people- Parian’s puppets hauling wreckage, Brandish cutting through to survivors, the Pelhams using forcefields to prop up unstable bits. Dauntless was ferrying groups of people along with his forcefield bubble like a blimp, and Gargoyle was leaping from place to place to give support.

Once, a streak of golden light cut through the sky in the wake of Scion’s flight, just on the horizon. A thinner beam being aimed at the ground as he passed. It took time for the aftershock to reach us, shaking the ground. I had to teleport out of the broken building I was clearing.

Minutes bled into hours. The sun had set when Tattletale called me through my earpiece. “Boss. It’s Cauldron. They’re calling a meeting, all the big names. We’re invited.”

I tossed aside the chunk of broken brick wall I was moving. “Fucking took them long enough. Where is it?”

“Just say ‘door’.”

“Ah crap, not this again,” Bearskin groaned.

“I hope we get to hurt them,” Nemean growled.

“Door,” I said out loud.  Right in front of me, a hole opened in the air, leading to a wide corridor of dark stone. I glanced down at myself, at my hands coated in dirt, my armour still spattered with dust and blood, and directed insects to crawl all over me, cleaning my armour from top to bottom. When that was done, I tucked the bugs into various compartments, folded in the waldo arms on my back, unfurled my cape, and stepped through with gritted teeth.

If it was the same meeting room Cauldron had brought me to after the death of the Nine, they’d changed the layout significantly. Large light panels, floor to ceiling, eighteen by five feet, arranged in a circle. Smaller panels flanked the big ones, two or three feet wide, to cast light at a different angle. A semicircle bar sat below waist height, with a crescent-shaped desk on the inner curve, documents laid out to read.

Other portals opened behind me, and the Undersiders stepped through- I glimpsed Tattletale’s command centre, and the ruins of Brockton Bay, before the portals closed behind them.

One more portal opened last, and Amy stepped through from what must have been the hospital in New Brockton. “This is where they took you last time?” she asked, looking around.

“I think so.”

Amy stepped closer to me. “Here’s hoping they’re more helpful this time.”

I snorted. “Yeah.”

We entered the booth as a group, Tattletale pulling out several devices as she began shuffling through the documents. I noticed a logo on our panel- our team name, drawn in thick letters with a Greek-looking font.

The rest of the groups were cast in shadow from the light of their panels, faces obscured. “Fucking stupid,” Butcher snarled. “World’s ending and they’re worried about their faces?” I wordlessly agreed.

Cauldron was present- the woman known as Doctor Mother, her bodyguard Contessa, and a blonde man in button-down and slacks who looked like an office worker. The real shock was seeing a young girl with curly blonde hair in a little lab coat. I almost drew a weapon at the sight of Bonesaw.

“How the fuck is she still alive?” Needler demanded.

“Fuckers must have snatched her up right before the bomb,” Bearskin grunted. “Or maybe they cloned her.”

Legend was here, alongside Chevalier, Myrrdin, and various team leaders. I saw the dust and bloodstains- they looked as rough as I felt. Chevalier had laid his cannonblade along the railing, and the elaborate, heavily embellished weapon served to frame the group.

The Guild, with Narwhal and Dragon at the centre. Armsmaster was stood a little behind Dragon, along with Masamune, the mass production Tinker they’d found in the ruins of Kyushu.

The Dragonslayers were in a booth opposite them, Sigurd radiating weariness even through his armour. “Man, he looks like someone gutted him,” Dirty Rotter noted.

One station held a woman in black, accompanied by a massive shadowy thing with an auroch’s skull for a head. I recognised her from PRT files- an African warlord called Moord Nag.  When I slipped some insects over to check, the shadow moved to block them, killing them instantly.

Further down, I recognised the cell block leaders of the Birdcage, Glaistig Uaine at their head.  Marquis spotted us and briefly raised a hand. Amy reflexively raised a hand back, then dropped it with a conflicted look.

The Thanda, from India- I’d talked to them after the death of Behemoth. Tough people, one and all. They had a five by five grid of letters for a symbol.

Faultline’s crew, their symbol a wavelength, like a reading on a seismic monitor.

A group of the Yangban, with their flowing uniforms and jewel-like masks. The Elite- I recognised Nonpareil and Patrician, Agnes Court and Blueblood.

Adalid from South America, alongside Califo de Perro, the King of Dogs, and someone who I guessed was an interpreter.

The Suits from the United Kingdom, with their playing cards theme- hearts, diamonds, spades and clubs, plus the older suits of wands, swords, coins and cups. No sign of the King’s Men, who were supposed to be the better group overall.

The Three Blasphemies were standing at one booth, three woman with white hair, skin and dresses, each wearing a ruby-lipped mask of a smiling, frowning, or snarling face. They were unsettlingly silent and still. I flickered through bloodsight for a second and saw no signs of blood in them. That just raised further questions.

The last group was led by Weld- not an official faction, but the Case 53s had pulled together over the last few years with the hints about Cauldron and artificial powers. People called them the Irregulars. I saw Gully with her shovel, Sanguine blood-red in skin and hair, Gentle Giant towering over all of them, Tether keeping close to Weld, even more pale-faced than normal, making the Omega mark on her cheek stand out more.

“Thank you for coming,” Doctor Mother said, looking around the room. “My name is Doctor Mother, and I am the founder of Cauldron.”

I heard growls from Faultline’s group and the Irregulars. “Give us one good reason why I shouldn’t let my people tear you limb from limb,” Weld demanded. “We know what you do, what you’ve done. Everything seems to tie back to you.”

“You’re blaming us for this.”

“You’re the most likely culprit,” Weld said.

“No,” the Doctor replied. “We have sources who can corroborate the story. Our organisation was founded with the purpose of preparing a response for this day.”

“They knew,” Vladimir hissed. I clenched my fists around the metal bar, and the squeal of metal turned people’s heads.

“You knew about this,” I snapped. “You knew Scion would do this, and you just stood back and let this happen?”

“It’s better that this happens now,” Doctor Mother said calmly. “From what we know, and I do want to express that we are happy to compare notes with other parties, it was inevitable. Scion was always going to go rogue. A few years earlier or later, and we might not have had the numbers of powers that we do now.”

“We could have used more time to figure something out,” I growled.

“We did try to help,” the Doctor said. “We offered as much assistance as we could without hamstringing ourselves for what comes next.”

“You made this happen,” Sigurd said from his station, straightening up, anger building in his voice. “You told me going to Flint would give better odds, but this still happened.”

“It could have improved the odds,” Doctor Mother said simply. “It was conditional- there were many factors at play. Regardless, it has begun, and we must respond. A very large number of powerful capes remain alive and active, ready to combat this threat. We’re already managing a large-scale evacuation. We consider it a priority to keep Scion unaware, so we are evacuating the landmasses on the opposite ends of the globe in hopes he won’t be able to respond or act.”

“So it all comes down to this,” Faultline spat. “Millions or billions die and you get to step in now and be the big heroes.”

“We have no intention of doing so. Truthfully, as much as we’ve stockpiled countermeasures, gathered information and planned ahead, we still expect to fail.”

“Fuck,” Tattletale muttered beside me. Amy’s hand slipped into my own, squeezing hard. I squeezed back.

“Everything you’ve done- kidnapping people, experimenting on them, creating monsters, working with fucking Bonesaw,” Faultline stabbed a finger in her direction, getting a few shocked noises from people who hadn’t recognised her, “And you’re saying it’s for nothing?”

“It’s very likely,” the Doctor said, totally unruffled.

“So your entire organisation is a crazy Hail Mary just in case there’s a chance we can survive?” I asked.

“Essentially, yes.”

“She fucking sucks at motivational speeches,” Tactical snorted.

“Agreed.” Out loud I said, “We’ll punish them for their crimes when and if we survive this. Let’s talk about now. Scion- what the fuck is he, and how do we kill him?”

“Scion is an alien,” Doctor Mother said. “He and his counterpart are the source of all parahuman powers, fragments spread out across multiple Earths with a small fraction of his power, linked into human beings as a way to essentially stress test them, using human imagination and motivation to figure out new ways to use these abilities or create new ones.”

“Fuck me,” Sanguine said.

“Furthermore, after distributing all the powers he could, he retained a small core of the most potent abilities, the centre of his being, to watch over the process and intervene if necessary.”

“Wait a second,” Firecracker said urgently. “She said a counterpart? There’s two Scions?”

“Oh crap,” I blurted, drawing people’s gazes. “Scion’s counterpart- where’s he?”

“She,” Doctor Mother said. “Insofar as their species seems to have gender. The counterpart, which we termed Eden, crashlanded on an alternate Earth a few years before Scion first appeared. We were able to critically wound Eden while it was recovering, and use its body to start Cauldron.”

“Use its body-”

“Oh Jesus,” Quarrel said. “If powers come from bits of alien connected to humans, then their vials must be too.”

“Your vials are made of alien flesh?” I exclaimed.

“That’s what we drank?” Sigurd yelled.

“Yes.” Doctor Mother raised a hand as people started shouting. “Please let me continue.” When the noise subsided, she went on, “Scion cannot complete their usual life cycle alone. We believe that’s why he drifted aimlessly at first- he lacked purpose. At some point someone or something pointed him towards acting like a hero, and now he has pivoted towards destruction instead. This would be a manageable problem if it were simply mindless destruction. We could evacuate this world and let him burn himself out, or convince him to abandon this. However, there’s another issue.”

She touched something on her desk, and the panels changed to screens, showing the same footage of Scion’s rampage. He hovered over a city, then unleashed a glow of golden light. When the glow faded, the camera dropped and hit something solid.

“Scion is performing calculated strikes, reversing what he did at the outset. In Mali he targeted only people who had hit puberty, leaving only orphans. In Russia he started fires from the outside in and waited for the flames to spread and kill everyone. He appears to be experimenting, and we don’t know what patterns might emerge as he continues.”

“That is so much worse than I thought it would be,” Muramasa whispered.

“So what do we do?” Legend asked.

“We run. Save as many people as you can, muster your forces. Strategize, think outside the box. If you have ideas, share them. If you have resources, offer them.”

“Can we find out why he started acting like a hero in the first place?” Faultline asked. “Maybe we can do it again.”

“I found something a while back,” Sigurd said. “An email from a woman who claimed she could talk to Scion. She said she’d been given the, ah, position from a man called Kevin Norton in England.”

Dragon’s head snapped around to look at Sigurd. “That message was sent to me.”

“Saint had a backdoor into your systems,” Sigurd admitted. “I’ll hand it over to you, help you close it up. Maybe we can find Norton, or the woman, Lisette, and find out what they specifically said.”

“Can we have access to Cauldron’s resources?” I asked. “Your portal network?

“Of course,” Doctor Mother said. “We’ll be observing you at all times. Simply say ‘door’ and your required destination, provided you aren’t on the same continent as Scion.”

“Good. Follow up question.” I pointed at Bonesaw like Faultline had, only I popped a claw for emphasis. “Why the fuck did you recruit Bonesaw?”

“Bonesaw has been a great help in refining the formulas we use to grant powers,” Doctor Mother said. “She’s also helped on some other projects that may help- recreating some of the powers that were lost to attrition.”

“Oh my god, it’s fucking clones again,” Tock Tick said. “I am so fucking sick of clones!”

“We’re all sick of fucking clones!” Bearskin shouted.

“If she so much as twitches in a way I don’t like, I’ll blow her head off myself,” I said.

Bonesaw shrugged. “Fair enough,” she said in an older, more mature voice than the childish giggle that haunted my nightmares. She looked taller too, sharper features and serious clothing. I didn’t trust it.

“Glaistig Uaine,” Needler said, who’d been watching the Birdcage faction through my bugs. “She doesn’t look surprised by any of this. She talked about powers before.”

“Glaistig Uaine,” I called across the room, “Does this fit with your understanding of things?”

“Indeed, Queen Administrator,” the Fairy Queen replied. “Scion is one half of the whole play, king of one of the courts of the fae. The other, Eden as Doctor Mother named, is absent, else events would be quite different. The end is not meant to come for 300 years more.”

“What would the end look like if things had played out the way they’re supposed to?” Legend asked. “They leave the planet and go somewhere else?”

“Indeed. Myriads of children would spread out among the stars to continue their work.”

“By absorbing energy and matter from countless alternate Earths and then detonating them all at once to propel themselves,” Doctor Mother added.

That got another round of disturbed murmurs. “I was gonna say something about tricking Scion into thinking he can still do his thing,” Anchorage admitted, “But let’s not fucking do that?”

“Agreed,” I said.

“So we are in agreement?” Doctor Mother asked. “We evacuate who we can, and fight Scion.”

“Agreed,” Legend said, although he was glaring as he said it. “We’ll get as much firepower as we can.”

“We’re ready to help,” Marquis said. “We fought to help save the world before, we’ll do it again.”

“When the hell was that?” Nonpareil asked.

“Long story,” I said. “Not everybody in the Birdcage is going to be cooperative though.”

“We could manage a controlled release,” Legend said. “Amnesty for people who can be checked and trusted to fight.”

“What about Cauldron’s vials?” Butcher asked cautiously, glancing at Nemean across the mindscape. She growled but didn’t lash out.

I understood his meaning. “How large a stockpile of power vials does Cauldron have? If we’re talking desperate measures, finding volunteers to become new capes might be an idea.”

“Are you kidding me?” Weld demanded, features distorting with anger.

“Volunteers,” I stressed. “Come on Weld, you know me. I’m not saying we copy their sins, I’m saying we find people who can give informed consent. When this is all over, if you guys want to chop Cauldron into itty pieces, I’ll hand you the knife. But first we need to survive.”

“We have some several thousand vials in reserve,” Doctor Mother said, calm as ever. The prospect of being hunted down and ripped apart by the Case 53s didn’t even seem to have registered to hurt. “Including some particularly powerful samples that we believe may produce particularly useful powers.”

“We’re not trusting you with handing those out,” Faultline said. “Somebody else should make the offer.”

“If you wish to find candidates, that’s fine,” Doctor Mother replied. Faultline flinched back like she’d been struck.

Legend slapped a hand on his desk. “Let’s get moving. Scion’s still attacking. We can sort out the details as we go.”

 

 

New Brockton, Earth Gimel

Dad didn’t want to let go of me for a while. I eventually had to pull his arms off me and take a step back.

“You don’t have to go,” Dad said quietly. “There’s plenty of other people. I mean, what are you going to do against Scion?”

“I don’t know,” I admitted. “Search and rescue, maybe. Or maybe launch bombs- I can make sure they’ll hit. But this is going to take everyone.”

Dad looked like he might start crying, but he didn’t object or shout or beg me to stay. He just said “Come back to me.”

“I will, Dad. I promise.” I pulled my cowl back up over my head, then stuck my helmet back on, rolling my neck to pop all the connectors in. “Door to staging area.”

A portal appeared to the side of me. Dad stared at it. “That’s new.”

“Yeah. Easy way to get around. I’ll be back, Dad. Just stay safe.”

“Okay,” Dad managed as I stepped through. I turned to look at him as the portal shut behind me.

“He’ll be alright,” Flinch said comfortingly.

“Hell, when all this is over, he’ll probably be running shit,” Bearskin said. “Hard-working man, lots of connections with the local workers and capes- I’d vote for him.”

“Hebert for Mayor,” Vladimir snickered.

The staging area was a drilling platform, out in the ocean. From horizon to horizon, nothing but water, dark as the sky above.

Scion was beginning to show a pattern when the data was fed through Dragon and Armsmaster’s analysis engines. He veered between extremes, first hitting a major population centre, then scaling down to strike specific targets- individuals, categories of people like adults or capes, or buildings. The attack was planned to hit him just as he came out of his current lull, and hopefully buy us time to finish evacuating. Hopefully we could find some limit, some weakness, weapons that worked.

So we had the heavy hitters. The Triumvirate, Legend standing a noticeable distance from the other two. Sigurd, huge guns added to his armour. Some of the Birdcage leaders. Chevalier, Myrrdin, Rime, Revel, Dauntless, Kudzu, Strider. Clockblocker and Vista, to my surprise. About eighty people in total.

Some of them were supposed to be dead. Cauldron had shamelessly admitted that- with Blasto in PRT custody and Bonesaw working for them, they’d used DNA samples to clone back capes who’d died.

Some of the first Wards team were here- Yami, Searchlight, Phalanx. I recognised Mama Mathers, who glared at me but did nothing- she was only being used as a backup communication system. Even some of the Slaughterhouse Nine- Shatterbird, a middle-aged man standing next to the Siberian, and older members like Chuckles, a crazy clown with superspeed in his head and legs, and super strength in his arms and torso.

I was the only Undersider. I’d pulled rank- none of them had the offensive or mobility powers to keep up with this fight. Tattletale was on the comms to provide information, Amy was standing by to receive wounded, but the rest weren’t getting anywhere near this.

“Yo, Butcher!”

Bakuda swaggered across the platform, hauling a wheeled platform like they used in warehouses to move boxes. Several crates were stacked full of bombs, labelled with various numbers. Bakuda was wearing a long coat with a braid of wires slung over one shoulder, plus a tricked-out grenade launcher. Her mask hung from her belt; she had blue eyes with a manic gleam to them.

“I was hoping you’d show. You did good with my bombs last times we worked together. Here.” She picked a bandolier of bombs from a crate and held them out. “Disintegration, transmutation, time bubbles. All my greatest hits.”

I took the bandolier and strapped it around my waist, checking the bow on my back at the same time. “Thanks. And thanks for showing up.”

Bakuda shrugged. “Hey, it got me out of prison.” She moved on, passing out bombs to more people.

“Mental,” Dirty Rotter said.

Galvanate was circulating, touching hands with everyone, passing out his invulnerability power, even to people who were already invulnerable. It might not stop more than a glancing hit from Scion, but it was better than nothing. Lab Rat was doing the rounds as well, handing out devices- earpieces and armbands for communication, plus little plastic cases the size of matchboxes, to be worn on the arm. He already had the full set over his white labcoat.

“I’m guessing these are some kind of emergency transformation thing,” I said, taking one and peeling a section of armour aside to stick it on my bicep.

“Yeah. The forms are all capable of swimming or flying, so they’ll help you hold out long enough if you get wounded.”

“Good to know.”

The armband showed fourteen points around a square- alternated attacks, to find out what worked. Fourteen groups with different approaches.

“Everyone get ready!” Legend bellowed, rising up in the air so everyone could see him. Eidolon, Alexandria, Sigurd and Glaistig Uaine rose with him. “Doors!”

Fourteen doors opened, spaced around the rig. Legend’s group went through the first. I had some sense of what was going on through my bugs, five ultra-powerful capes against Scion.

Lasers and waves of energy lashed out, Alexandria shot forward to punch Scion, Glaistig Uaine summoned ghosts to attack. I recognised Jack Slash’s Abattoir ghost, flicking a knife while commanding a miniature sun to chase Scion.

“Jack Slash saving the world,” Needler sneered. “I hope he’s aware enough to hate it.”

“Second group!” came the command. Clockblocker, Gentle Giant, a few others I didn’t know, advanced through the portal. A spread of powers, with mobility and timelocking. If we could freeze the fucker, that could buy us precious time.

The world on the other side of the portals rumbled. Even with portals miles apart, the rumble was felt equally by all of them.

The third group was Chevalier with Citrine, who was projecting her golden sphere around him. She could use that sphere to adjust almost any aspect of reality- temperature, gravity, friction. With a little tuning, she could mess with powers too- cancelling them out or amplifying them.

Chevalier stepped through and raised his sword. It grew to its maximum size, and kept going, twice as large as I’d seen it at Endbringer battles. It was too heavy for him to lift, so he let it crash down, the serrated edge biting into the ground on the other side of the portal. He fired, and the combination of the detonation and recoil wiped out my bugs.

The only person I recognised in the fourth group was Shuffle, from Chicago. He could teleport entire chunks of landscape, buildings and all their contents.

The battle was intense- lasers split the sky, impacts shook the earth. Fire flickered through dust and smoke, while crashes and explosions echoed. I briefly glimpsed Scion himself, entire buildings being dropped on him by Shuffle as Legend and Sigurd unleashed white-hot lasers that Eidolon took and amplified into something that my eyes couldn’t fully grasp. It struck the buildings piled on Scion, and they simply evaporated.

“Fifth group in! Everybody else out!” Tattletale called over the earpieces.

The fifth group was just one person. String Theory. The Tinker who’d once built a weapon that could have knocked the moon out of orbit.

“Open a portal,” she called out, typing on a laptop. “One end pointed at Scion, the other in my lab, at the end of my G-Driver.”

Capes were returning from the periphery. Citrine and Chevalier, his cannonblade missing in action. Chuckles carrying two wounded capes, Clockblocker covered in ash.

“He wasn’t even aiming in our direction and he took out most of us,” Clockblocker muttered. “Fuck!”

“Give me coordinates!” String Theory yelled.

“Patching you into the Number Man,” Tattletale reported.

“And let me watch,” String Theory added. “I want to see- don’t argue or I’ll make it miss.” A portal opened at the platform’s edge, showing grassy fields with steep hills, a fence in the distance, trees burning on the highest peak. Huge gouges had been carved through the landscape, and plenty of it was on fire.

Scion turned in the distance and began advancing towards the portal.

It wasn’t like the shot from a gun. More like the zap from a bug zapper. One second Scion was there, then there was a distortion in the air, and he was punched out of the sky, trailing a golden streak of light. The path suggested he’d disappeared right out of the atmosphere.

“Holy fuck!” Tock Tick whooped.

“Now that’s what I call a gun,” Quarrel said as String Theory pumped her fists in the air like a conquering champion.

“The fucking G-Driver,” String Theory announced, sounding very pleased with herself.

“He’s coming back,” Tattletale reported. I wasn’t surprised, but I felt a bit of hope. We’d found something that could knock him around at least. We could land a blow.

“Sixth group, get ready.” The sixth group was mostly Thanda capes, plus some Birdcage capes I didn’t know. Heavy Hitters.

“He’s gone,” a voice I didn’t recognise said over the earbuds. Everyone went still. “Checking now- bastard’s hard to keep track of.”

“We need to get ready to run,” Tactical said. “With how fast he moves, he could be coming for us.” I agreed, pulling bugs together near Strider.

Through other bugs, I felt movement up above. I looked up.

Scion was here. Directly above us, so far up he was barely a speck.

“Strider,” I said through my bugs, “Grab everybody you can and get the fuck out of here.”  Cauldron had made it clear they wouldn’t open portals on the same continent as Scion. We hadn’t thought he could move that fast, let alone through dimensions- but here he was.

Other people looked up, maybe wondering what I was talking about. Someone gasped. Someone else screamed.

There was a mad rush to grab hold of him- Lab Rat and String Theory were shoulder to shoulder as they grabbed at his left hand, Clockblocker grabbed Vista and pushed through the crowd with her. Bakuda punched someone in the face to get through the scrum.

Strider teleported with a thunderclap, emptying about half the platform. I didn’t know where he’d go- this was an empty alternate world, no settlements whatsoever. Maybe a clear field on the other side of the planet for Cauldron to portal them away.

Scion just hung there. When I’d seen him close up fighting Leviathan, I’d felt curiosity from him. Now I sensed bloodlust- not anger, nothing so personal as that. The feeling of wanting to crush something, to tear it apart, to hurt it.

But he was watching, waiting. Toying with us.

“Everybody get ready,” I said, unslinging my bow and fitting Bakuda bombs to arrows. I rolled my cape up too.

“Boss, what are you going to do?” Tattletale asked.

“I’m going to run like hell,” I said, nocking an arrow. “And I’m going to see if I can land a few shots as I go.”

The golden glow above intensified, like a sun at night. Solidifying into a sphere.

“Run!” I shouted through my bugs, grabbing the nearest person- Sanguine, here as a healer- and diving off the platform. I grabbed the leg of the rig on the way down, sparks flying from my armoured palm as I slowed my descent. I used Anchorage’s power as I hit the water, increasing the surface tension enough to walk on it, and broke into a sprint, Sanguine yelping as he bounced along on my shoulder.

Other people were trying to run as well, but there was nowhere to run to. Strider’s teleport had cleared the people in the centre, but there were people who weren’t going to make it in time. I saw someone raise their hands and glow, the glow swelling around them into the form of a giant. Lustrum- her power absorbed ambient energy to create her powered form. I saw the sphere shrink a little, but not stop.

I drew the arrow back and loosed, curving its path upwards against gravity. The arrow detonated before it hit Scion, maybe some side effect of his power. The air froze solid around him, a milky white bubble that began to sink.

Scion broke the effect, disintegrating it with golden light, and remained hovering as the sphere hit the platform. I expected it to make some noise as it sheared through metal, through people, and ploughed into the ocean.

The platform was collapsing, only two legs staying put, and even they were slumping into the water. Lustrum’s form stood on the water’s surface like me, a great smoky shimmering figure holding a dozen people against her arm, as tall as the oil rig was.

“Goddamn,” Needler murmured.

“Hit him again!” Tactical bellowed. I grabbed an arrow, nocked, drew and loosed. As it flew I unfolded the waldo arms and helped Sanguine shift himself around to cling to my back like a koala.

The arrow hit Scion, and a grey sphere formed around him. A time bubble.

For a few heartbeats he stood still. Then he broke the effect and turned towards me.

“Oh fuck,” Sanguine blurted from my back, tightening his grip.

“Can you swim?” I asked, nocking another arrow.

“Yeah?”

“Good. I might have to drop you.”

“Aw crap,” Sanguine whimpered.

I drew and loosed again. Scion raised a hand, and a pencil-thin beam disintegrated the arrow.

“Okay, that’s good, right?” Firecracker asked. “If he’s actually blocking the arrows, that means it costs him more to get hit. Right?”
