“Yes, except now he’s going to come for us,” Nemean pointed out.

Lustrum was backing away, scooping some more people out of the water and depositing them on the remains of the platform. Scion didn’t turn to look at her, but he did tilt his head up.

The Triumvirate unleashed their attacks, lasers from Legend twisting around to strike from all angles. Eidolon let out a hail of multicoloured bubbles that imploded, giving off bursts of darkness and pulling in matter. Sigurd fired a beam right down the middle, and Alexandria flew through it all to engage Scion directly.

Scion flew up, taking the fight to them, and I started towards the platform, passing my bow to one of the waldos. Sanguine adjusted his grip as I ran, grunting as the movements bounced him up and down.

“So-o wha-at the fu-uh-uck do we-ee do no-ah-ow?” He managed as I reached a platform leg.

“Retreat, regroup, try again,” I said, swarming up the leg with super strength, making handholds out of the concrete base, then the steel pillars. A few people were on top of the platform still, mostly the Irregulars. Sanguine let go of me and hurried over to the wounded.

“Try the Lab Rat boxes,” I said, following. “They transform people temporarily. Not sure if they’ll heal completely, but it could buy some time.” I knelt and drew a knife, slitting my palm open. Blood welled up, and Sanguine pulled at it, forming scab bandages over people’s wounds.

Weld grabbed a box and pressed it against another wounded. It beeped, a light flashed, and the cape convulsed, veins standing out along his arms and legs, scales beginning to sprout from his skin.

I scanned around, with bloodsight, with bugs, with tiny plankton in the water. Plenty of people were dead, but I found a live one- one of the Thanda maybe. I teleported down onto the water and scooped them out, then fired my grappler to haul us back up. I wasn’t optimistic of his chances- his body was simply gone at the waist.

Weld swore at the sight of him, grabbing another box and pressing it to the man’s wrist. It beeped, and the flesh began to seal up, twisting into something hard and ridged, like a lobster shell.

Above us, Glaistig Uaine had created a spirit that was spreading across the sky in geometric patterns, faster than Scion could destroy it. The other two spirits were working together, one duplicating the other to throw projectiles that created patches of a strange, nebulous darkness.

“Scion’s attacks are all about light, no sound, just disintegration,” Muramasa mused. “Perhaps there is a vulnerability to darkness and noise?”

“That sounds a little too neat,” Bearskin said.

“Maybe we can find some disintegration power against him though?” Stoneknapper suggested. “Something that clings and eats away at him, like napalm?”

I had a brief thought of some super-charged form of Dirty Rotter’s power, decaying Scion into golden mush. “It’s a good thought.”

“They’re not going to open portals until Scion’s gone,” Weld was saying. “And I don’t think Strider’s coming back.”

“Driving Scion off or leading him away might be possible,” I said. “Or we get out of here. I can make a boat out of the platform.”

“We’ll be sitting ducks,” said a girl with a head that was many sizes too large and a frail body.

“We’re sitting ducks now,” I said. “I’d rather try and move.”

“She’s right,” Sanguine said.

I slapped my hands to the platform, peeling large swathes of metal up and fashioning them into simple canoes with Stoneknapper’s fizz. I tossed them over the side, then hooked my grappler to the railing and detached it from my wrist so people could rappel down. I turned some more metal into a thick chain as well, feeding it down to the water.

“I’ll carry the wounded,” Tether said, unfurling her arms into long thin ribbons. She gently picked two people up and slid them under the railing, then unfurled her legs and wrapped them around the chain, quickly sliding down.

“Let’s move,” Weld said. “There’s nothing more we can do here.”

“I’ve still got some bombs,” I said.

“Hey, woah,” Butcher protested. “Those bombs didn’t do shit.”

“They slowed him down,” I said to both of them. “Maybe I can lock him in place for an attack that’ll do some real damage.”

Weld shook his head. “I hope you’re right. Good luck Elpis.”

Scion erupted with golden light in every direction. It wasn’t the sort of attack you dodged. I grabbed Sanguine again, and swung both of us under the railing to the underside of the platform. Sanguine squealed and clutched my arm desperately as I waited for the light to die down.

Weld had taken cover, but he looked polished, his clothes burned. I grabbed my grappler and checked- the mechanism was worn down. I quickly reshaped some metal to keep it held in place.

“Getting real sick of you dragging me around,” Sanguine managed.

“Sorry.”

The attack had worn away the cloud cover, letting more light in. More to the point, it had destroyed Glaistig Uaine’s ghost, the one that had spread across the sky. He turned his attention to her. Eidolon appeared next to her, grabbed her and teleported while the others launched more attacks.

“Okay,” Weld said. “We definitely need to go.”

I helped lower them to the boats below, carefully- the water was frothing and boiling from Scion’s attack. Tether was manning the oars of one canoe, and Weld took another. The oars bonded to his arms at once, but he didn’t say a word.

“Get going,” I said, gesturing to them.

Golden light speared into the water- Scion targeting some remaining capes.

Glaistig Uaine appeared behind him, with three ghosts. One duplicating the other two, the second of which was terrifying.

Gray Boy- the most terrifying of the Slaughterhouse Nine, one of the original lineup. Supposedly unkillable until she’d claimed him.

The Gray Boys raised their hands, and Scion was trapped in a bubble of looped time, turning monochrome. It made Bakuda’s time bombs look weak by comparison.

Scion broke the effect, only to be trapped again.

Legend and Alexandria used the moment to grab more capes from the water and disappear off towards the horizon. Sigurd swooped down to us. “I can tow you,” he said, pulling cables from his suit.

I moulded loops onto the prow of each boat and Sigurd tied himself to them, then hit the thrust. They took off at motorboat speeds and accelerated, leaving sprays of white froth in their wake.

I teleported back up and grabbed the grappler rope, along with every other strand of silk I had, picking them apart and joining them together with more silk, until I had a single strand maybe a quarter of a mile long.

I had an idea, about locking Scion in place. The time bombs had held him, the air bubble had held him, the Gray Boys had held him. And I’d noticed one of the Thanda helping some Birdcage capes, using his power to fix them in space so they stood above the water.

One end of the silk zipped upwards, carried by dragonflies to wind around Scion’s eyes. He didn’t seem to even notice, too busy burning through Glaistig Uaine’s ghosts. She swapped her ghosts in and out rapid-fire, but I could see less variety. The ones that Scion destroyed didn’t come back.

The other end of the strand, I extended down to the Thanda. “Hit it,” I said through my bugs.

The Thanda gave it a curious glance, but froze it in space. The entire strand froze, immobile, and Scion was pinned in midair. Massive attacks crashed into him, the sort too slow to use normally.

“He keeps attacking the ghosts instead of Glaistig Uaine,” Anchorage said. “He’s not human- maybe he doesn’t think human. He’s done dumb stuff before.”

“Like in Endbringer fights,” Vladimir said. “The Simurgh fooled him a few times, I think.”

I drew my bow and pulled out every bug I had, pulling them into the air, forming a decoy. No reaction from Scion, so I split it into two as I nocked an arrow, then split those two into four as I drew.

Scion turned and blasted the swarm out of the air, and I shot. Scion shot the arrow out of the air as well, but that left him open for Glaistig Uaine to hit him- blotches of darkness drew together out of the air and concentrated into a single point, pulling Scion in. He resisted, and I sensed something from him.

We’d got a reaction from him.

Eidolon used a power, reversing the effect. Scion was slammed down into the water, too deep to see. I grabbed more arrows, fired them straight down into the water, every last one. I couldn’t see the effects, but the water erupted, froze, boiled again, turned green and foul-smelling.

A few seconds past.

Scion rocketed up into the air, spraying the bitter liquid everywhere. Some of it landed on my armour and started to smoke.

“So we managed to hold him down and piss him off,” Dorty Rotter said. “Yippee.”

“We’re not done yet,” Flinch said boldly.

I felt the air pressure change- portals opening as Scion chased Eidolon and Glaistig Uaine across the sky. One for me, one for the Thanda and Birdcage capes.

“Would have been really nice to have these before,” Tock Tick snarled.

“Flinch is right,” I said. “This isn’t over.” I stepped through the portal to safety.

“Not by a long shot.”

Chapter 160: 15.14

Chapter Notes

With this chapter, I've now posted over one million words of fic to AO3! The vast majority of it is obviously from this one story, but that's still one hell of an accomplishment! Woo! Go me!

Tuesday 24th June, New Brockton Refugee Camp, Earth Gimel

The lights above me shut off, and the containment chamber beeped. “You’re clear,” Sigurd said, opening the door.

I hopped off the bench, paper robe crinkling, wiggling my freshly-grown toes and my right hand. I was luckier than most- I’d only been hit by a glancing shot, and I’d managed to carve off the parts of me being worn away by Scion’s power before they could make much progress. After that, it was just a matter of time- and decontamination.

In the days since that first assault from the oil rig, when Scion had crossed between worlds to attack, when Eidolon had fallen battling him, dozens of plans had been tried. String Theory and Bakuda had flatly refused to take the field again, but we’d managed to convince them to keep making their tech- in Bakuda’s case, Masamune had helped to figure out how to mass-produce her bombs, to her glee. Meanwhile, with the help of Dragon, Armsmaster, Leet, Sigurd and several other Tinkers, we’d managed to get the G-Driver working again, without the set countdown that String Theory’s work usually suffered from.

Somebody had said it was only pushing Scion around, not hurting him- but Stoneknapper had pointed out that pushing someone into something dangerous might work. He’d know, after all those spike traps he’d made back in the day.

“Shame there isn’t a parahuman wood chipper we can throw him into,” Bearskin muttered, forming a mental image of a pile of shredded golden flesh. I wordlessly agreed with him.

The first time, we’d managed to knock Scion into the Sleeper’s multicoloured stasis miasma in Mordovia, Russia, it had bought us 75 minutes while Scion meandered through the haze. He’d eventually done something that dispelled the effect and killed a quarter of the city, but those people had been written off as dead for years.

If I kept telling myself that, I might stop feeling sick about it.

After that, we went down the list- the next shot knocked him into the Machine Army in Eagleton, Tennessee. That only lasted 36 minutes before Scion burned the place into a glass crater- but Thinker scans confirmed the Machine Army wouldn’t be coming back, so at least we didn’t have a swarm of self-replicating machines to worry about anymore. Small blessings.

“I mean, getting fucked from behind by robots while we’re trying to deal with the golden fool would be a dumb way to go,” Quarrel pointed out.

Next was Nilbog and his creatures in Ellisburg, New York. It took Scion just over two hours to finish killing everything in that city down to the microscopic level. Nobody was sure why- maybe he preferred live prey to hurt.

“We saw him get distracted by Glaistig Uaine’s ghosts, and the swarm clones,” Tactical pointed out. “Maybe he gets more distracted by multiple targets.”

“We could use that,” Muramasa said. “If Blasto can create large groups of clones, that could at least occupy him for a time.”

“I’ll keep that in mind,” I said.

Ash Beast wasn’t S-Class, but we’d hoped for another long stretch. Unfortunately, when the next shot had thrown Scion at him or her or it or whatever was at the centre of the perpetual explosion that wandered across Africa, Scion killed it within five minutes.

In between, the remaining members of the Triumvirate, rotating squads of heavy hitters, and Dragoncraft loaded with exotic weaponry tried engaging Scion. Bakuda bombs, lasers, masers, phasers, and something Leet had got out of an old sci-fi novel which could cancel out the charge on protons. That one had carved deep lines into a mountain range before Scion destroyed the ship carrying it. Nothing could hold him for long.

It all bought us time though- time to evacuate people to empty Earths, time to heal the people who’d been wounded in other attempts to hurt Scion, time to come up with new plans and gather the insane resources needed for insane plans.

Like nuclear warheads stolen from across multiple worlds. We’d drawn Scion in, then fired one bomb after another, blasting him with enough radiation and heat to kill a continent. Scion hadn’t shown visible damage, while I’d taken enough radiation that if Sigurd hadn’t had his radiation negation chamber ready when I escaped, I’d have glowed in the dark.

“You’d be like a little firefly,” Dirty Rotter giggled, a touch maudlin.

“Where’s the fucker now?” I asked, grabbing the undersuit Sigurd offered me and slipping them on under the paper robe, before tearing it off and flicking it into the garbage.

“Still travelling between parallel worlds,” Sigurd said while I attached the bits of armour that had survived. “Bet is mostly evacuated now. We’re spreading the refugees out among multiple worlds- there’s greater chance he might stumble onto a settlement, but frankly it seems like he knows where to find everywhere, so we’re just trying not to put all the eggs in one basket. We’re assembling people for another assault when he comes back this way.”

“How many of us are left?”

Sigurd’s helmet hung low. “About two-thirds of Bet’s onetime population is gone. Plus there’s a lot of important infrastructure gone, and with major population centres targeted, it means there’s a lot of damage around the permanent portals, so evacuation’s slower even with the Doormaker portals.”

“Fuck,” Butcher said.

“Fuck is right,” Vladimir agreed.

“And the Trucebreakers?” It seemed like too small a word, too weak a term, for the people we’d heard about. People who’d started taking over settlements, or attacking other settlements. The Yangban, some Elite cells, a few Thanda members, and so on, who’d decided to focus on themselves instead of saving the world. Running away was one thing, but actively fucking over the rest of us was insane.

“Cauldron’s got some of their people handling the worst,” Sigurd said. “Contessa and the Number Man handled a Yangban attack a while ago. Protectorate capes and other heroes are dealing with the rest.”

“The Number Man?” Nemean asked through my bugs as I gathered some up. “What is his power anyway? How is he tough enough to do that?”

“He understands all forms of math instinctively- acceleration, force, vectors. So he could know exactly how much force to hit someone to kill them with one blow, or exactly when to dodge to avoid a bullet.”

“Combat Thinker. That’ll do it.”

And that guy was just their accountant. That struck a thought- Cauldron had thousands of vials, they’d operated for years, and we’d only seen a handful of their members, the leadership. How many more powerful capes were in their ranks, and why weren’t they fighting yet?

“I think we need to have a talk with Doctor Mother.”

 

 

I took a few people with me. The Undersiders and several of Cerberus’s dogs, minus Tattletale back on the comms, but also Weld and Tether to represent the Case 53s. I would have invited more, but apparently most of them were raring to tear Cauldron apart limb from limb, get some final payback before the end of the world robbed them of their chance.

I understood that urge very well- I’d promised that once we survived, I’d hand them the knife if that was still what they wanted. But first we had to survive.

The door opened in midair, to a spotless white corridor. “Man, this is bright,” Imp commented, sashaying through the portal.  “I feel like I’m gonna track in dirt with every step. The hell kind of bleach do they use?”

“Probably some kind of power,” I said. “There was a person at the meetings, made of air. Multiple bodies. Maybe she sweeps up.”

“What, like a janitor?” Ironclad asked, hammer resting over his shoulder.

“She is called the Custodian.”

“Jesus!” Flinch hissed.

We all wheeled around. Contessa was standing there, Cauldron’s boogeyman in hat and suit. She looked surprisingly normal, dark hair and pale skin. Yet I hadn’t sensed her with my bugs or any of my enhanced senses.

“This way,” Contessa said, gesturing down the hallway. “Door- staggered pattern to Doctor Mother.”

Another portal opened- this one to a grassy field. Contessa stepped through.

I tapped my earpiece. “Tattletale?”

Nothing. The closing of the portal had blocked our connection. All we could do now was follow, so we followed cautiously. The portal shut behind us as we stepped onto the grass, and then another portal opened, this time to a desert.

After the desert, a rocky beach, then a snowy forest, then the white tiled facility again- a confusing path across dimensions. I would have called it needless paranoia, wasting time, if we were up against anything else.

Doctor Mother was at the head of the group, with a blonde man in glasses and shirtsleeves- presumably the Number Man. A group of young boys that looked just like him were spread out behind him- no glasses, but all with composed, faintly smug expressions. Most concerningly, a portly middle-aged man, who I wouldn’t have noticed in a crowd, standing next to the Siberian. I kept an eye on him- if I curved a bullet I could kill him before Siberian could do too much damage.

“I guess Cauldron wanted to copy capes that they could rely on,” Tock Tick said.

“Did they clone any of the heavy hitters?” Firecracker wondered. “Another Eidolon would have been fucking great- or another Legend, or Alexandria…”

“I don’t see how they could have got DNA from Alexandria,” Needler pointed out. “But yes, that would be useful.”

“Maybe that’s part of their next plan,” Anchorage suggested.

“I’m guessing all this is part of it too,” Stoneknapper said, gesturing around.

 The portal shut behind us, leaving us in a corridor, every wall covered in little glass vials, set in an arrangement of wires that kept them lined up, multiple vials of the same colour lined up beside another arrangement of vials. But almost every vial was empty. The ones that were left- maybe two hundred out of tens of thousands.

“Holy crap,” I heard Whirlygig mutter.

“The remainder of our stock,” Doctor Mother explained. “We gave the formulas out for free, in hopes of turning out parahumans that could do damage to Scion. We retained only the volatile ones.”

“What makes them more volatile?” I asked.

“Volatiles kill three quarters of whoever drinks them,” Doctor Mother said. “Or creates Case 53s we can’t use.”

Nemean snarled.

“Use,” Weld said flatly.

Doctor Mother regarded him without emotion. “Yes.”

“You tested these on people,” Tether said, fingers writhing as they almost-but-not-quite split into ribbons. “To make weapons.”

“Yes.”

“I remember, you know,” Tether said, smoothing her dark hair back, fingers brushing against the omega symbol on her cheek. “I was a fisherman’s daughter. There were these beautiful little huts with flat roofs, orange clay bricks against grey mountains, with green grass and blue ocean. It was cramped, and I had to share space with my family, my siblings- but I loved it. I’d draw, and it was peaceful. I couldn’t draw for so long, because my tendrils would break the pens and brushes.”

“We’ve caused you difficulties,” Doctor Mother said, turning and gesturing for us to follow as she headed down the corridor. Her group followed, and so did we, Tether still speaking.

“I can’t remember my mother tongue, or my parents’ faces, or either of my brothers. I’ve just got the faces I see in dreams, when you sent people like me to take me to your lab and unravelled me with that drug of yours, and dumped me in a forest with just enough memory to know I should be human.”

“I understand where you’re coming from,” Doctor Mother said, “But we have more important things to think about.”

“Thiis is important to me,” Tether snapped. Weld put a hand on her thin shoulder, but she shrugged it off impatiently. “Don’t you care about the lives you’ve destroyed? How we’ve suffered? Do you even remember us? My name? The name my parents gave me, or the one you gave me when you moved me to a cell along with the rest?”

I felt my claws grow a little as Nemean growled inside my head. After years of trying, she’d uncovered vague memories of her past, helped by the file they’d given us, but barely anything, and she was furious. Not at Tether, never- but furious at Doctor Mother, who seemed more impatient than anything else.

“What do you want from me? An apology?”

Tether’s face creased in anger as her fingers split fully apart into ribbons. The Number Man and his clones reacted at that, settling into ready stances.

There was a thunderous crash from above. Doctor Mother glanced up, eyes wide. “He’s here. Doormaker, remove yourself and Clairvoyant to a safe location- the facility is compromised.” Which meant that their portal network had two people at least- one to watch for where people were, and one to make the portals themselves.

Number Man turned to the Siberian’s master. “Drop the column.”

The master nodded, giving Siberian a peck on the cheek before she stepped towards a panel and hitting a button. I felt a sudden lightness- I switched on bloodsight and saw levels of silhouettes passing us by as the room sank- mostly humanoid, but there were plenty that didn’t look normal. A body made of floating pieces with nothing but empty space between; something with flippers for limbs and tentacles coming out of the hole that was its face; and a body that was rippling from small to large to male to female every half-second. The extreme Case 53s the Doctor had talked about.

“This place is an elevator?” Grue asked, spreading his feet as we descended further.

“In a sense,” Number Man. “This entire section is our panic room, built into the bottom of a column of metal 2500 feet tall. It should give us some time.”

“They must have used powers to make it,” Tactical began.

“Wait, the people up there,” Bearskin interrupted. “Scion’ll rip them apart!”

“Can you open the cells from here?” I asked Doctor Mother.

“The cells don’t have physical barriers-”

“Can you let them out?! They’re sitting ducks, for fuck’s sake!”

Doctor Mother paused, then nodded. “Custodian,” she said, and I felt that shape in the air again, brushing some of my bugs aside. “Release the cells of whichever floor Scion is on. The prisoners may have greater success in stalling him with room to manoeuvre.”

“That’s not-!” I gritted my teeth. “Whatever the Case53s do to you when this is over, I hope it’s horrific.”

“I’m sure it will be,” Doctor Mother said, totally unfazed.

“So were you a sociopath before you got into the human experimentation business, or did you have to work at it?” Ironclad asked. I heard popping sounds from within his armour as he cracked his knuckles.

“I simply prioritise the sake of all humanity across the multiverse over the lives of a few individuals,” Doctor Mother said with an exasperated tone, heading down the hallway. “I must say, the reason that we allowed you in was because I thought you would understand, Elpis.”

“I understand,” I said, glaring daggers at the back of her head as we followed. “That doesn’t mean I think you’re morally justified in the things you’ve done, and it doesn’t mean I don’t think that being skinned alive and rolled in salt is too good for you.”

“Jesus Christ, which one of the Butchers came up with that?” Grue asked.

“That was all her,” Butcher said through my bugs. “We’re all very proud of how far she’s come.”

“Regardless of your personal feelings,” Doctor Mother cut in with a frustrated voice, “I’m expecting you to help rally people. We didn’t anticipate so much moralising about preventing the end of the world- you’re well regarded by many factions, including the Case 53s. Hopefully you can convince them to cooperate for all our sakes.”

“Best I can do is keep them from killing you immediately,” I snapped. “And frankly, you don’t seem to have any power worth talking about, so you’d better show me a good reason to argue that much.”

“Here,” Doctor Mother said as we entered a lab. “These are the most powerful vials we have left. We were about to look for recipients when you contacted us.”

There was a table with a dozen vials set into a centrifuge. The liquid inside was nearly black.

“So these are what, super volatile?” Weld asked, looked at the vials with a revolted expression.

“There is a foreign agent in them. The entity altered each power he granted to ensure they would not be able to affect him, cross the boundaries he set in dimensions, or in affecting other powers. There are no alterations to the elements in these, only to the abilities granted. They also don’t cause the recipients to forget the visions they see. Eidolon was one such case, and the extreme deviants on the special containment floor make up much of the remainder.”

“Extreme deviants,” Tether said with a scowl.

“I’ll need to dilute this, or I’ll be no use to anyone,” Doctor Mother said. “Number Man, the Balance formula is in the fridge, please. Yes, extreme deviants. Deviants like Weld and his friend-”

“Tether. Or Sveta. You called me Garrotte when I refused to take a name for myself. I was recipient one-six-one-six.”

“Tether,” Doctor Mother said. “Deviants like them are a rare thing, particularly with the Balance formula in the mix. Extreme deviants form a subset within a subset, with physical mutations that go well out of bounds of solid reference point we have on Earth.”

“And you think outlier results might produce a power that’ll let you do serious damage to Scion.”

“Exactly,” Doctor Mother approvingly as Number Man handed her a vial of clear liquid. She used tongs and a funnel to pour clear into dark. It didn’t overflow or visibly change volume- the colours inside turned to a deep red. She clamped the vial into the centrifuge and started the machine. “Best freshly shaken, so the layers don’t separate. William, can you send the Siberian out? Keep a watch, buy us some time.”

“Alright,” said the Siberian’s master. The projection walked back down the corridor we’d come. I sent some bugs after it, along with a few relays, to monitor things myself.

“Why didn’t you ever drink a vial before?” Weld asked.

“I have a corona pollentia. It increases the odds of deviation if a vial is taken. I wanted to leave the door open for natural powers if needed, or to take a vial at a critical juncture.”

“Doesn’t get much more fucking critical than this,” Quarrel pointed out.

“We should put some distance between ourselves and him before I take this,” Doctor Mother continued. “A trigger event may draw his attention- and we’ll be comatose for a moment as the power takes hold.”

“My dogs can carry us,” Cerberus said.

“Let me drop my armour before you drink that thing,” Ironclad said. “The dogs won’t be able to carry all the metal.”

“Good thinking,” I said as the centrifuge whirred away. “What about the rest of the vials? Should we take them?”

“Yes, but they won’t be useful immediately. The powers are poor. When we tested them, we got a defensive power utilizing warped space, and a power that allows one to take over a nearby parahuman’s mind, body and powers automatically on death.” She glanced at me as I went still. “No connection to the first Butcher, I assure you.”

“What happened to that person?” I asked urgently.

“We placed her on an alternate world to steer political events,” Doctor Mother said. “However, her last death occurred when an enemy performed a suicide attack with high explosives. Apparently there wasn’t any living parahuman close enough for her to transfer to. So she died permanently. In any case,” she continued, “This vial should grant attack or mover capabilities. And even with the Balance formula, I’ll most likely be heavily mutated. This will probably be the closest you’ll ever get to revenge, Tether.”

Tether just glared as the machine stopped and Doctor Mother plucked the vial out, fitting the rest into a small briefcase, along with a large container of Balance formula. “Let’s go.” She crossed to a heavy door and input a code, then opened it and led the way down a staircase to another level.

“Number Man-”

“The EM readers, yes.”

“And the fixators.”

“Good idea.” He darted off into a side corridor.

“This is it,” Doctor Mother said, pointing to a vaultlike door at the bottom of the stairs. “The last room. Lowest level in the complex.”

“Please tell me there’s an escape tunnel,” Whirlygig begged.

Doctor Mother turned the wheel on the centre of the door about halfway. “It’s stuck.”

“Possibly Scion’s entrance damaged something,” Number Man said from behind us, holding a pair of paddle-like wands.

“I got it,” I said, pushing past Doctor Mother none too gently and setting a hand on the door. It was thick, with a tang of titanium alloy to it, but Stoneknapper’s fizz let me peel it aside like putty. That gave me a clear view of what lay beyond.

Imp swore, Whirlygig gasped, Tether gagged. Weld’s jaw dropped, and Grue’s darkness billowed in a way I knew meant shock. None of Cauldron reacted much- this was old news to them.

“What the fuck is that?” Rachel asked.

The room looked like an aircraft hangar. I reached out, and my bugs could only sense the three walls closest to me.

And filling it was a mass of soft grey matter, disturbingly beautiful in how it was shaped. Like an artist’s sketchpad, half-formed shapes in all manner of positions curled around one another. Here a long-fingered hand beckoned, there a child-like hand was exposed, and over there yet another with water running down it, trickling between the fingers, more art piece than a limb intended for use. It might have been menacing, but every line was soft, and every part had a gentleness to it.

“Fuck me,” Dirty Rotter breathed. “It’s female. It’s the female. Scion’s other half.”

Nearly three stories high, like ocean waves of flesh. Here and there pieces connected strangely, exposing muscle and bone, or tapered off into fractal patterns that tapered off where I couldn’t see, like it had turned a corner that didn’t exist.

“A giant alien,” Stoneknapper said in awe. “And Scion’s this big?”

“Maybe even bigger,” Vladimir said. “If all we can hit is that human body, it’s like trying to carve out a mountain with a spoon.”

Some of the bugs I’d left behind died as golden light burned down through the ceiling. Scion descended into the corridor, slowly looking about as he walked forward on foot. He reached out to touch a vial, gently, almost inquisitive.

“Scion’s made it into the lab,” William reported as Doctor Mother uncorked the vial. “He’s looking at the vials.”

Scion reached out and cupped his hands around the vial. I could see traces of his power burning through the wire that had held it as he cupped it in his hands, staring down at it.

“Alright,” Doctor Mother, raising the vial to her lips, “I’m drinking now. Have your dogs ready to run.”

Number Man handed one of the paddles to William and dug a number of black plastic hemispheres out of his pockets. “Place these against your heads, they’ll help with the Trigger vision.”

“Does it need skin contact?” I asked.

“No, they’re calibrated to work through helmets.”

There was a clatter of metal as Ironclad shed his armour. I quickly set the door back in place, blending it with the stone around it, as Rachel grew the dogs massive.

“Wait, why can’t we just take a portal out?” Imp asked.

“We will, but Scion may follow us,” Number Man said as Doctor Mother tilted her head back and swallowed the deep red fluid. “We can’t afford to have him follow us to a population centre that’s not prepared so we’ll need to be able to-”

Stillness. No ringing in my ears from the lack of noise, no heartbeat in my chest. Different senses altogether.

Two massive beings made their way through the void. One was familiar in a way I couldn’t articulate, the other stranger, more distant. They both shed pieces of themselves, both flesh and not flesh, as they searched for a world, but kept specific parts for attack and defence, for foresight and mobility.

I knew what the familiar one was doing- I felt like I was connected to every part of itself, and I was aware of everything it was aware of.

It looked for a world, a particular variation of that world, possible forms they could take on that world and the possible results, possible futures. In the midst of that, of a trillion images that passed through my awareness in a single instant, one image was hauntingly familiar.

The golden man, surrounded by the broken bodies of humanity. He was utterly untouched, coated only in their remains, blood and pulpier substances dripping from his fingers as people lay bleeding, crushed or burned around him.

And I could see how he saw through the passengers that had arrived before him, and through their hosts, and how he saw through time to navigate his way to a particular ending. Unless he chose to deviate, there was no way for him to lose, not with the criteria he had set. He had enough power, he had enough understanding, that there was no way for the hosts to beat him.

No way for us to beat him.

The thought stuttered, distorted, repeated itself, then repeated itself again and again and again.

I was back in the massive room full of massive flesh. The plastic thing was warm in my hand, pressed against my helmet.

Number Man was picking himself up. “I take it you remember what you saw? We devised these to help fix Trigger event visions in people’s minds- we hoped they might provide some information the entities tried to hide from us.”

“Oh god,” Flinch said. “Oh god oh god oh god-”

I had to shove him into the dark before the rising panic and despair could mess with my head, but the other Butchers weren’t doing much better.

“Why the fuck did we have to remember that?” Firecracker demanded. “We’d have been better off not knowing!”

“What do we do?” Muramasa groaned.

“We get the fuck out of here,” Nemean managed as I got to my feet. “And then… I don’t know.”

“Undersiders, get up,” I called. “Let’s get the fuck out of here! William, what’s Scion doing?”

“Still looking at the vials,” William reported, awkwardly staggering upright. “He’s just dropped one on the floor.”

The vial shattered, and Scion reached for another, held it for a moment, then dropped it as well and reached for yet another.

“If he’s looking at bits of his girlfriend’s corpse, no wonder he’s distracted,” Tock Tick muttered.

“Ironclad, get your armour on, you’ll be faster with it on,” I said, hauling him up by the elbow. “Doctor Mother-”

A squawk was my answer. The clothes were the same, white coat and shirt, dark pants, but torn and bulging around the new physique. Every joint bulged enormously, turning her body into a parody of the human form done in cantaloupes. The skin was grey and wrinkled, so baggy in places that I could see folds dangling out of the cuffs of her clothes. The head was bald and swollen with a bony ridge, and deep-set eyes looked out over a flat nose and a horny beak of a mouth. Doctor Mother raised a knobbly hand and turned it back and forth- the fingertips were so blunt I doubted she could have picked up a pencil. She looked at me and squawked again, then a third time, slightly different.

“Looks like a xenomorph fucked one of those hairless cats,” Anchorage quipped.

“So that’s what you turned into?” Tether said, stepping close to look at Doctor Mother. “It’s still not a fraction of what we suffered through.”

Doctor Mother squawked again, then rolled her eyes and pointed at William, then upward, and made a clawing gesture.

“You want me to attack Scion?” William asked.

A nod.

“Alright.” Back in the lab, the Siberian lunged at Scion, lashing a hand through his chest, then his head, then from scalp to groin. The way their bodies intersected, it was like ghosts fighting. Scion paid no attention to it.

“If he’s got that much flesh to spare, no wonder he doesn’t take us seriously,” Needler said with a morbid laugh. “Little punches won’t do squat.”

The Siberian stepped through him entirely, and I saw golden motes following her as she emerged on the other side, landing and wheeling around. That was a lot more than a little punch “Intersect him,” I said to William. “It’ll burn through his reserves.”

William nodded as Grue gave him a leg up onto one of the dogs, and the Siberian stepped forward to stand in the middle of Scion, their bodies overlapping. She must have been carving through a good hundred pounds of flesh every fraction of a second. Depending on how he regenerated, it could be much more. Turning a strength into a weakness.

He still didn’t seem to care.

Everyone was on the dogs now, except Ironclad and me. “Let’s get the fuck out of here,” I said.

Contessa pointed across the mass of flesh, and Cerberus followed, urging the dogs into motion with whistled commands. I broke into a sprint alongside them, and Ironclad followed along with loping strides- bloodsight let me see him grimace as every step trampled outstretched grey hands.

Back in the lab, Scion reached a hand out, not to grasp another vial, but to flare light from his hand. Every vial shattered at once, fluid pouring to the floor. The Siberian appeared alongside us in the next instant, bounding alongside us with her casual dismissal of physics. “He took action and struck my Siberian,” William explained.

“He’s heading down the corridor,” I reported as Scion killed every bug that came into contact with him. I tapped the holster of Bakuda bombs as I ran along- maybe a few seconds of borrowed time each, if I managed to hit him. “Send the Siberian again.”

The Siberian simply stopped in midair and went back they way we’d came. I sent more bugs with her- I wanted to see. Other bugs raced on ahead of us as we put distance between us and Scion- the landscape of flesh seemed never-ending- skin and muscle and bone and cartilage.

Something caught my attention- a whole body, or close enough. A sexless human shape, with hair that was disproportionately long for its form, dangling upside down where one foot was stuck in the air. The figure was incomplete, fractals extending from portions of its back, its arms and one leg.

“Shit, those bits must be where it passes into another dimension,” Bearskin realised. “Same way Scion passes between worlds.”

“It must have been putting together a human body when they killed it,” Quarrel said. “Maybe that’s when they’re most vulnerable- when they’re changing.”

“I just saw the counterpart’s avatar,” I called as we kept running. “How’d you kill it?”

Doctor Mother gave me a look from where she was hanging on behind Grue, but it was William that answered. “Apparently they managed to stab it in a specific place. Like a tiny aneurysm for a human, that was enough to kill it.”

“No chance we can reach Scion’s vital points to kill him quickly?” Ironclad asked, swatting a couple of giant fingers out of the way.

“Whatever dimension Scion’s main body is located in, it’s unreachable with any power we’ve found,” William explained. “Even Doormaker can’t get to it. The only access point to his main mass is his human avatar, and you’ve seen how that works.” A loud crash and screech of tortured metal filled the air.  “Speaking of, he just broke through the door.  I’ll engage him again.”

“We’re almost far enough to open a portal,” Number Man said, “But we’ll have to be extremely fast, and expect pursuit.”

“We’ll lead him to the next coordinated assault,” I said. “They’ll be ready by now.”

Number Man nodded- and it was a clear nod, none of the jerkiness that most people had from riding the dogs. Did he figure out some formula for staying steady on the back of a giant mutant animal?

The Siberian appeared beside us once more. “Should I attack him again?”

“No, we’re leaving now,” I said. “Just be ready to block any attacks from behind.”

“Door to staging area,” Number Man said. A huge portal opened up ahead of us, tall and wide. I slowed to let the others pass through first, drawing some bugs together near the counterpart’s avatar.

Scion had reached it, and was cupping its chin with both hands. The grey figure was slack-jawed.

He’d looked through possible futures to find his counterpart again- and he had, in a very monkey’s paw sort of way.

“Sucks to be him,” Butcher snorted.

“But this means that he’s not infallible,” Tactical began as Scion’s hands glowed gold. He reached down to the counterpart’s neck and carved through the flesh, severing the head. He gripped the corpse, then rose into the air. The entire structure shuddered as the mass of flesh was pulled with him, shifting through this space and multiple dimensions.

Scion poured golden light through the grey flesh, burning it to ash.  I could almost sense an emotion in his actions- anger, frustration, grief, confusion. Unfiltered, like a child. He was lashing out, trying to find a coping mechanism.

“Would have been pretty fucking nice if he’d just started drinking instead,” Rotter muttered.

“Yeah, but it tells us something. He’s distracted, he’s pointing in a different direction. If we can do something like this again, we can manoeuvre him,” Muramasa countered.

I grabbed a bomb and attached it to an arrow, a waldo arm handing me my bow. “Well, let’s pile on the grief.” I drew and loosed, then darted through the portal before it landed. I caught a glimpse of bright pink flames blossoming all around Scion as the portal shut.

“Okay, I just shot a bomb at Scion while he was lashing out at his dead girlfriend, so let’s get ready for him to be really pissed.”

 

 

Combined Assault Staging Area, Ruins Of Brockton Bay, Earth Bet

We were still using hit and run tactics against Scion, but now that we knew he could travel between dimensions, we had to be prepared for him to come right to us. So this fight had a lot of top-notch Brutes and Masters to engage in melee or distract him with copies. In a horrible way, Scion’s changing patterns of attacks helped. He was scaling down from continent-shattering blasts to city-burning assaults to more individual attacks. Still horrific, but easier to survive if you were on the fringes.

Towers surrounded the shattered city, set on mountaintops and high points of the city itself, crafted to put satellite dishes up high, as well as to mount a few Tinker weapons. Layers of defences were being set up- walls to shelter behind, tunnels to dive into. They wouldn’t do anything against a direct strike, but it made people feel like they had options. Vista had twisted space together too- she’d only been limited by the presence of people, and Bet was now so empty that she could warp vast distances like putty.

We had a lot of international capes- some of the Suits from Britain, the head of the Meisters from Germany, a guy called Vornehm with an army of clay men carrying tinker weapons, some of the Thanda, members of the Elitnaya Armiya from Russia. A lot of them were hanging around Dragoncraft ready to carry them into battle.

Plenty of Birdcage prisoners too, the ones who hadn’t been able to engage the first time. I spotted Gavel, who’d trimmed his shaggy beard into a thin line along his jaw and buzzed his hair flat, and acquired a hammer bigger than he was. Crane the Harmonious was strolling around with a couple of her students, in a martial arts gi with a black belt with red stripes on the end. Glaistig Uaine was present, flanked by her ghost, and people gave her a wide berth.

The Irregulars were gathering around Weld as he made a speech. Their numbers had swelled as Cauldron’s prisoners had escaped and started giving them some kind words and answers. I spotted a couple of more normal looking people- it took me a second to realise they were the Travelers. I hadn’t thought of them in years.

I was also keeping an eye on the incognito Doctor Mother, who‘d switched out her clothes for a sort of loose robe that hung oddly on her distorted frame. She was also keeping a noticeable distance from the Irregulars despite many unaware Case 53s waving her over.

“That’s actually hilarious in a twisted way,” Vladimir noted.

There were also several squads of Blasto creatures, almost but not quite human, enough cape DNA to make them dangerous without the ethical problems of creating sapient life just to throw it into the meat grinder. I noticed some of the Irregulars giving them pitying looks.

“So any ideas?” Vista asked, sipping from a water bottle.

“I think he’s more influenced by having a human body than we thought,” I said. We were gathered on our own in the shadow of a tower, Brockton Bay Wards, Undersiders, and the New Wave kids. It was strange to be costumed but unmasked near the remains of our home. Nothing to go back to, nothing worth hiding. Rachel’s dogs and Parian’s puppets formed a ring around us. “His counterpart’s destroyed, but we might be able to use that somehow.”

“Like what, huck pieces of his wife at him as a distraction?” Chariot asked with a snort. He was eating from a bag of Skittles, chewing thoroughly, occasionally offering them to other people. Imp took a handful and crammed them into her mouth.

“There isn’t anything left to throw.”

“Shit, I was kidding,” Chariot said.

“Do we really think taunting him is going to work?” Aegis asked.

Imp shrugged and spoke through a mouthful of candy. “Fuck knows. But it sounds funny.”

“Swearing helps,” Rachel said, scratching Brutus behind the ears.

“In a fight?” Spitfire asked.

“In general.”

“Emotion powers won’t work on him,” Gallant said, shifting slightly. In his lap, Glory Girl crossed her legs and leaned against him again. “Even if he’d left that vulnerability open, if he’s so massive it’d be like trying to dye the ocean green- there’s just too much to affect.” He scratched his head awkwardly. “To be honest, I’m feeling kind of useless. My power’s no good here.”

“We did find some stuff out from Cauldron if you’re really desperate,” Whirlygig said. “Although a Second Trigger sounds fucking awful.”

“What about Second Triggers?”

“Apparently Cauldron could sometimes induce them on purpose,” I said. “They had these brain scanners to check someone’s corona, see what sort of event they went through, what sort of power they got. Second Triggers means you go through something like your original trigger, but worse, and that pushes the power to break some restrictions.”

“We know that,” Clockblocker said. “Like Narwhal being able to make forcefields through people.”

“Yeah. It turns out I can’t have one,” I said.

“Because of the Butcher thing?” Aegis asked. I shook my head.

“No, because I already had a Second Trigger. I remember blacking out right after I inherited, which isn’t usual. Maybe the Butchers plus all the sensory feedback hit me hard enough.”

“Fuck,” Clockblocker said. “So you got two triggers back-to-back?”

“Yeeeah,” I said, drawing it out. The fact that I’d doubled up on triggers was weird to think of, but in a messed-up way I was a little annoyed that there was no way for me to get more powerful. I was tougher than so many capes, but I was still barely doing more than keeping morale up. I felt like a figurehead when I wanted to be a fighter.

Cassandra had said that I affected our chances of stopping the end of the world. Right now I didn’t feel like I was affecting anything significant.

Gallant went to say something, maybe some comforting words, but I noticed people running around, hustling towards the areas for portals to open, grabbing weapons.

“Scion sighted!” Someone was yelling through a loudspeaker, frantically waving people into action. “Earth Samech! Dragon and the Guild are engaging! Move move move!”

“Alright, they’re playing our song,” I said, grabbing my helmet. “Undersiders, you know the drill, get ready to receive wounded.”

But things were already changing- people were milling around in confusion, falling back into their old groups, looking around for answers. Had the fight already ended?

“Look up,” Flinch said at once. “If this is like the rig-”

I glanced up, and saw Scion hanging over us, same as before, hands loose at his side. The golden light that radiated from him cleaned his hair and clothes, but there was enough blood soaked into his costume that the light wasn’t rendering it as pristine as usual. With his back to the sun his eyes were in shadow, but the edges of his hair and body glowed with light.

“I hate being right,” Flinch blurted.

I drew my bow, ready to attack, but Scion didn’t even raise his hands before he fired. Lights no bigger than basketballs streaked forward, leaving glittering trails behind them. Two Dragoncraft detonated violently, and I heard people scream in pain and terror.

By the time I’d turned my head to see his followup, Scion was in our midst. The capes with faster reflexes were reacting, throwing all kinds of effects at him. He ploughed through them like they weren’t even there, occasionally flying around certain effects.

He stopped in front of one cape, a dark-skinned man in grey. Possibly the man he’d dodged. A swirling grey effect swelled between the two of them. Scion struck it with a glowing hand and it distorted- a second strike and it dissipated entirely. Scion caught the man by the neck- he didn’t squeeze, he just let the golden light eat into the man’s body and costume, before dropping him to the ground.

I sprinted forward, firing arrows as I ran. Too close for Bakuda bombs, friendly fire was a problem here, but if I could at least distract him…

No good. Effects of every stripe rolled off him like water off a duck’s back.

A metal spike shot past me, right for Scion- one of Flechette’s bolts, the kind that could pop the Siberian and maim Endbringers.

Scion spun around and caught it, then let the bolt drop. His eyes were on Flechette as she grabbed a handful of throwing knives rather than waste time reloading.

I pulled a gun and curved every bullet to his face. It didn’t even make him flinch as golden light swelled in his hand.

Parian’s cat doll flared its wings and leapt into the air, clearing fifty feet in a second. The beam struck further back instead, killing people I didn’t know the names of. Flechette hurled the knives one two three down at Scion, but he slapped each one out of the air by the unaffected handles. As the winged lion rapidly retreated, Scion turned his attention to the rest of us, swiping a glowing hand through a man’s abdomen. He fell apart, screaming as the golden light ate at his innards.

Scion very deliberately walked past the wounded cape to attack someone else rather than finish him off.

Maximising pain and suffering over efficient destruction. Sadistic, in a word.

He was definitely getting emotional, but right now that didn’t feel like a good thing.

A pencil-thin beam shot from his fingertips, sweeping across at waist level. It cut through the crowd, through thighs, calves, feet. It swept towards the Brockton Bay group.

Parian’s dolls leapt forward and scooped up who they could, while the fliers grabbed a few more. Vista raised both hands, and the ground beneath rose by five feet. The beam carved through, leaving a line of broken soil through the improvised platform. Alive, all of them.

Other people- I could see the blood. The beam didn’t burn or cauterise, it disintegrated, leaving arteries free to pump blood onto the grass and dirt.

“Undersiders, search and rescue! Grab the wounded and start tourniquets!”

King of Cups, one of the Suits, was already responding in his own way. Pitch black simulacrums of limbs were forming on the stumps of severed legs, stopping the bleeding and letting people climb to their feet. I wasn’t sure if people were pushing through the shock or if the power came with some kind of painkiller effect.

The ground under Scion hardened from dirt to rock, and then hands burst from it, grabbing his ankles. More hands burst from those hands, and more from those, spiked knuckles stabbing at him. I noticed Golem with his hands sunk into the ground, next to Gully and a guy I didn’t recognise, an Asian man with long hair and tattoos ringing his arms. He gestured like he was doing a kata, and the stone hands turned to boiling lave and swept up to cover Scion.

The lava cooled to stone and dissolved to dust as Scion continued forward, not harming him, but it bought people another second to get their bearings. A cape with a tall white helmet was moving groups around like pieces on a chessboard, while another guy next to him was making the ground swallow up obstacles like vehicles and supplies, giving a clear battlefield.

“Stone won’t work, but time stuff does- get a line to Clockblocker!” Stoneknapper shouted. One of my waldos unreeled a line of silk thread, and insects carried it over to Clockblocker.

I formed more swarm decoys around Scion, but he ignored them or walked right through them, targeting specific capes. He threw a ball of light at Glaistig Uaine, high in the air, but the chess cape shifted her out of the way. Another attack- a lucky cape was pulled out of the way by one of King of Cups’ phantom limbs, but the ball swerved for him. A dozen phantom arms of varying sizes blocked the hit and shattered, knocking King of Cups down.

Clockblocker had hold of the thread- I connected the reel to an arrow, then drew and loosed in one movement, curving the path around Scion. More insects pulled the thread along, over and around, forming a loop. An instant before it snapped taut, I told Clockblocker “NOW!”

The thread froze just as Scion moved forward, catching him around the waist. I disconnected the reel from the waldo, covered the thread with insects to mark it and grabbed bombs from my bandolier. “POUR IT ON!” I bellowed, throwing the bombs.

Disintegration carved a crater around Scion and scoured the filth from his suit, the second bomb created a pillar of white fire that engulfed Scion, and the third exploded into a blast of cold so intense I felt it from far away.

Other capes fired and shot and blasted with everything they had, but a bunch of them interfered with each other. A sphere of darkness made contact with a series of ribbons that spiralled around each other, and they were both consumed well before hitting Scion.

“Fuck!” Nemean swore. “There’s no coordination!”

Lines of light crossed the ground as Scion broke the timelock effect on the thread- Queen of Swords was swinging an ornate shortsword, creating lines that connected to others in the crowd.

I turned to help the Undersiders treat the wounded- more bombs would catch people in the blast radius. When there was space around Scion again, I’d fire the rest.

Parian was hastily tying tourniquets around severed limbs. One poor woman in a cloak was clutching one of her severed feet to her chest in a death grip, staring at the sky. Ironclad was carefully carrying people away, while others loaded people onto the dogs. Spitfire was grimly burning some of the worst wounds shut.

“Can we do the thread trick again?” Clockblocker asked, picking a boy in a jean jacket up in a fireman’s carry.

“Not yet, I don’t think. He’s adapting to attacks- we need to keep switching them up.” I grabbed a broad man in a bloodstained white coat- his thighs were gone, and he was gushing blood. I pulled more thread from another reel and tied the wounds tight enough to hear bones creaking, then tore his coat off and ripped it in two, packing the rags around the stumps.

Ghoulish as it was, I absorbed the blood that spilled onto my hands. I might need that speed boost.

Queen of Swords touched the tip of her sword to one of the main lines of the diagram she’d created. A circular blob expanded from the point like a drop of blood welling up, two-dimensional, dark blue and translucent. She drew a gun with her free hand and fired at the blob.

The bullet hit the blob and pushed against it, slowing down as it travelled, stretching the blob into a cone. For a second I thought of old cartoons, that it would bounce the bullet back like a trampoline. Instead, the bullet punched through, and I could see ribbons, darkness, fire and a dozen other effects trailing behind it as it resumed normal speed. It struck Scion as he started aiming another beam at the crowd on the opposite side of me and the Undersiders, and he staggered, the aftermath of a dozen different powers washing over, around and through him in harmony. The beam cut off before it could hurt more than a few people.

“FUCK! YES! THAT’S WHAT WE NEED!” Firecracker whooped. I grinned even as I loaded my wounded guy onto Judas.

Queen of Swords began changing the diagram, breaking old lines and drawing out new ones- changing up the pattern like I’d told Clockblocker, keeping it fresh.

Scion turned towards her, and began drifting forward across the ground.

Walls of earth rose up around Scion as Vista folded the ground around him, raising herself up on a platform. Flechette was perched on the winged lion puppet, arbalest raised. She fired at Scion as he looked her way.

Scion broke through the earth wall to dodge, and maybe it was wishful thinking, but it seemed like it took him some effort. Scion raised a hand and hurled a ball of golden light at the girls.

A massive hammer intercepted the shot midway- the resulting explosion knocked people off their feet. I grabbed Spitfire as she tumbled and pulled her back up, then pulled my bow out again, welding a bomb to an arrow.

The hammer dropped, and Gavel caught it with both hands, stomping forward.

Scion turned his attention to Gavel and hurled another globe, while I fired the arrow. The explosions came so close together they were almost one sound.

Scion was caught in a grey bubble of slowed time, which he broke out of with a pulse of gold light. Gavel was a little scorched, planting the pole of his hammer on the ground to lean on it.

Powers and projectiles hit Scion from every direction, and that seemed to give Gavel the moment he needed to catch his breath and push forward, picking up speed as he found his stride, dragging his hammer beside him.

“Clockblocker, get ready,” I shouted, pulling another reel of thread out.

Scion raised a hand and fired a beam- which was clever, because Gavel’s power reduced the amount of damage he could take at any one time. A continuous beam would be better than multiple discrete attacks. Gavel blocked the worst of it with his hammer, with only a moment’s respite as Queen of Swords hit Scion with another power-infused bullet.

Then another bullet hit Scion- far weaker, but it distracted him a little. A mess of a thing was stood next to Queen of Swords, one of its three torsos looking like her. Another was in black and red armour, and a third looked like Legend of all people. The Legend torso fired a laser that shot over the crowd before turning straight down to hit Scion on the top of his head.

“Wait a fucking minute, that one’s Ballistic! Part of him, I mean! I recognise the costume!” Anchorage said.

Gavel reached Scion, and threw his whole body into a swing like an Olympic hammer-thrower might use the rotation. The hammer struck Scion dead on and smashed him into the dirt, ploughing a furrow fifteen feet long. He half-floated, half-climbed to his feet, and was struck again. It wasn’t hurting him, but it was an inconvenience that let everybody else prepare another shot. Queen of Swords worked on her diagram some more, while the triple-Changer ran through the crowd on all six legs, turning all three heads this way and that like they were looking for someone specific.

Gavel hit Scion a third time, and the damaged hammer broke into pieces. For the fourth hit, Gavel kicked Scion in the ribs. Every hit was less effective than the last- Scion had adapted.

I fired the second thread arrow- not at Scion, but at Gavel, aiming for his shoulder. The arrow struck, not wounding him more than a pin- but it was enough of a connection for Clockblocker to freeze the thread, the arrow, and Gavel just as Scion reached out.

A massive blast erupted from underground, throwing Scion up into the air, so high he was only a twinkle. The ground where he’d been thrown into the air had piled up into a massive hardened spike with ripples along its length, like a drill bit. Projectiles shot up after him, including a miniature sun from the other side of the battlefield that grew larger and larger as it rose, engulfing Scion entirely.

The triple-Changer held out a hand to a guy in a feathered cap, who gingerly took it. The Legend torso shifted to look like the cap guy, and then the Ballistic third raised a hand while the Queen of Swords third tapped her diagram. I noticed this diagram extended to Clockblocker.

Something shot from the Ballistic third’s palm trailing a beam of green light, hit the blob that had risen, broke through, and swerved 90 degrees up into the air just as Scion emerged from Sundancer’s sun. The bullet smacked into him, exploding into ribbons, and then locked into place.

“A Clockblocker bullet!” Quarrel laughed. “Few more of those’ll make him a sitting duck!”

The sun dropped down towards him as people fired up at him- another bullet from Queen of Swords, and a spiralling shockwave that rippled through the air, sending Scion’s hair flying. I traced its path backwards and spotted Doctor Mother standing with arms outstretched. She looked scared.

“Good,” Nemean spat.

The sun swallowed Scion again, then suddenly disappeared. The sharp loss of light left my eyes adjusting for a second as Scion smashed into the ground, the impact throwing people away, then turned towards Queen of Swords.

She shot him again. Scion floated up into the air and towards her. Ribbons sailed through the air, snagging on him and then fixing in the air like they were attached to some invisible tether. It was one of the Swords doing it.

Scion broke the effect, still advancing as more shots hit him. He returned fire, and King of Cups blocked the shots with massive gorilla arms. Scion closed the distance, smashed the hands to pieces with a swipe of his hand, and grabbed King of Cups by the jaw.

But he didn’t hurt him. Instead he extended a finger and swept it over the crowd, like he was pointing something out. The man’s expression seemed to give Scion what he wanted.

I sank into bloodrush, the world going slow and red, and sprinted forward, drawing swords as I went, pouring Dirty Rotter’s ooze over them. My waldos snapped out and picked up fallen weapons- I wanted Tinker weapons with exotic effects, even if I didn’t have time to find out what they did.

“Taylor, for the love of god-”

“We said no melee-”

“Are you fucking-!”

I pushed them down to clear my mind and leapt over the crowd as Scion shot towards Queen of Swords, his empty hand outstretched. I stabbed both blades at his chest, blasted pain into him, then jammed the random weapons I’d picked up against his body and pulled whatever looked like a trigger.

Sparks flew, something unfolded and latched onto Scion’s arm, and one flashlight shaped gizmo did something that had golden motes sprayed from Scion’s foot. Nothing slowed him as he grabbed Queen of Swords and slammed her and King of Cups to the ground.

I tumbled to the ground, rolled and came up with an axe that I slammed into Scion’s face. It broke, and I punched him in the face before I could think.

Nothing. It was like punching a mountain. I grabbed my flail and swung up into his nose. That made his head twitch, but he kept pushing down- only on Queen of Swords, pushing his hand on her face, pushing her head down into the ground. I could hear a pained scream from her, and a scream of horror from King of Cups.

I kicked at Scion, slashed claws at him, fired pain at him. He just kept going.

Capes around me pelted Scion, grabbed at his head and arms and chest, but he was immovable. I could hear people speaking around me too.

“-blocking my teleport-”

“-make him stop!”

“-somebody? Anybody!”

“I saw your girlfriend.”

Scion’s head turned up to look at me. Queen of Swords’ screams eased up for a second.

“Nothing left of her but a slab of meat,” I blurted. “I helped burn her.”

It was thoughtless, it was impulsive, it was meant to be hurtful. It was the kind of thing the Butchers said to their enemies at their worst.

Scion’s expression shifted, ever so slightly. His eyebrows drew together a fraction, lips just a little tighter together. Lines stood out on his throat.

He hadn’t changed his expression once since he’d appeared, not even when he’d started killing people.

I didn’t wait for danger sense- I just teleported to the other side of the battlefield.

Golden light bloomed off Scion- the lines of Queen of Swords’ diagram faded, and King of Cups’ black limbs crumbled into black ash.

Scion rose from the crowd, still being hammered by powers, and spun to look at me.

“You made it personal,” Bearskin gasped.

“You fucking moron,” Butcher spat.

Scion shot towards me.

A hammer struck him in midair- not Gavel’s clean, well-shaped hammer, but a lumpy mess of steel. Almost like a collection of fists.

Gavel caught the hammer and leapt high as Scion turned to face him. The new, improvised hammer, even bigger than the first, slammed into Scion’s face and knocked him almost to the ground.

Gavel landed and swung again. Scion caught it one-handed, then jammed a hand into Gavel’s largest wound. Golden light flared, and Gavel disintegrated from the inside. Flakes of burned flesh traced with bits of gold light flew into the air as both halves of Gavel’s body hit the ground.

Scion let the hammer and corpse fall, and turned to me again.

A bolt flew at him, aimed right at his ear. Scion spun at the last second and caught it, the tip almost brushing his face, and dropped it. Flechette was already frantically reloading.

Scion looked at her, then at me. He seemed indecisive, like he was angry at both of us but didn’t know who to start killing first.

Stone hands rose from the ground again to grab Scion, and then another shockwave threw him up, again leaving a spike of compressed rock in its wake. I saw Golem and Doctor Mother side by side, both with their hands pressed to the ground.

Everyone opened fire on Scion again, and two small suns raced up to hit him, one from Sundancer herself and one from the triple-Changer that was standing next to her, its Queen of Swords third replaced with a Sundancer copy.

Scion extinguished both suns with a beam of golden light, then gathered more light in his hands. As it swelled, I realised this was going to be too big to dodge.

A distortion crossed the sky from horizon to horizon, and Scion disappeared.

“What?!” Tock Tick shouted.

“String Theory,” I gasped, realising I’d been holding my breath. “Her G-Driver- that’ll only buy us a minute or two. We need to fall back. Door to medical centre.”

Doors opened all over the battlefield- Scion must have been far enough away for Doormaker to help us. Everyone started running through them, some grabbing wounded, others taking supplies. I picked up the woman who was still holding onto her severed foot and shouted to the Undersiders, “Let’s get the fuck out of here before he gets back!”

I led the way to a massive room full of bunks filled with people- bleeding people, burned people, screaming people, people who were worryingly silent. I recognised it- one of the buildings on Gimel, created by Agnes Court of the Elite. She planted seeds that would blossom into entire buildings over time- she was making entire cities right now.

“Elpis,” Amy said, hustling over. She was out of costume, and followed by a couple of others. Marquis, Bonesaw, and Marquis’s followers- Spruce, Cinderhands and Whimper. The men had sandwiches in hand, like we’d caught them mid-lunch.

I spotted another couple of healers moving around. Scapegoat, Sanguine, Lizardtail, even Othala- I hadn’t seen her since we’d ended the Empire. She looked smaller.

“I’m fine, but we’ve got wounded. Scion went for the legs.”

“Jesus,” Amy cursed, laying a hand on the woman I was holding. The flesh of her severed legs sealed up with fresh skin, and her whole body relaxed. Amy touched the foot, then shook her head. “That foot’s too far gone for me to reattach it.”

“Is there a bin for biowaste?”

“That way,” Amy said, pointing to a hatch in the wall. “It leads to an enzyme tank that’ll break it down into usable biomass. One of Blasto’s tricks.”

I set the woman down on the nearest free bunk and gently pried the leg from her fingers, then threw it overarm into the hatch. There was a clang as it bounced around the chute within.

“Perfect three-pointer,” Quarrel snorted. I could feel her anger at me getting in close radiating inside my head like a piece of hot metal.

Bonesaw stepped over to the other new arrivals, pulling out needle and thread, bandages and tongs to start sealing the wounds. “Are we really trusting her to treat people?” I asked Amy in a low voice.

“I’m checking her work- and right now we’re swamped. Any chance you can help Scapegoat?”

I looked over at the man himself moving from bed to bed, followed by a man with abnormally thick limbs and leathery skin. “Sure.”

“Marquis, can you start regrowing bones?” Amy asked. “I’ll grab some more mass and follow up on the flesh.”

“Of course,” Marquis said with a polite nod, starting towards the newly occupied bunks. As soon as he was far enough away, Amy popped up on tiptoe and kissed me.

“Fuck, are you okay?”

“I’m fine,” I said. “But I think Scion’s got really angry now.

Amy’s jaw worked for a second. “Fuck.”

“Yep.”

For a second I just studied Amy’s face- her big brown eyes, her freckles all over, the curve of her mouth. Her arms were bare, the sleeves rolled up, and there were splotches of blood and something black here and there.

She looked beautiful, even now, but she looked tired.

“Are we at least wearing him down?”

I thought of the mountain of flesh his counterpart had been, the way he’d started targeting the few capes who could really inconvenience him, the way our own attacks interfered with each other often as not.

“I think so,” I lied. “But it’s going to take a hell of a lot more to kill him.”

Amy sighed. “That’s what I thought. I need to keep going, but find me when you have a chance.”

“Always.”

She kissed me again, and this time I savoured it properly- the softness of her lips, the taste of her spit. She broke contact all too soon and hustled off to save lives.

I headed for Scapegoat, sat down, and made myself some crutches as he swapped a patient’s missing legs for my healthy ones. As my legs started slowly growing back in, I talked with the Butchers.

“That was fucking stupid. Say it,” Tactical ordered.

“That was fucking stupid,” I parroted.

“We agreed, what did we agree? No getting up close with him! We’re not that powerful!” Needler shouted.

“I know,” I admitted. “I thought I could at least buy some time, maybe break his grip. Queen of Swords could do some damage, we needed her.”

“Any chance Cauldron can clone her back fast?” Stoneknapper asked.

“It’ll probably take time,” Vladimir pointed out. “Besides, Glaistig Uaine was there- she’ll have her as a ghost now.”

“That’s still a shitty condolence prize,” Dirty Rotter snapped.

I had insects over by the door, where a guard was checking his phone for updates. I overheard an alert that that last G-Driver shot had knocked Scion over to the Simurgh, who’d descended from orbit for unknown reasons. He was now tearing her apart, possibly following that old drive to fight them. Maybe she was just a big enough target to occupy all his attention.

“Can’t believe even the fucking Endbringers are stalling for us,” Firecracker said.

“It is bizarre,” Muramasa agreed. “Yet even if we had a dozen Endbringers, it might not tip the scales.”

“Real fucking optimist, you are,” Flinch said.

We’d used every other S-class threat at this point- maybe we should have considered the Endbringers before, insane as it sounded. But if there were a way to predict or steer them, nobody had ever found it. Maybe we’d get lucky and Scion would dive down to waste some time tearing Leviathan apart, but I wasn’t holding my breath.

We needed that level of monstrous power- we’d pulled every Hail Mary, crazy, break-glass-in-case-of-emergency plan we could, and it was barely helping. We needed something more, but what was left?

The talk about Second Triggers came to mind- I’d hate myself with the idea of torturing someone into another trigger, but maybe there were people who’d volunteer? Or was there something similar? There were Trumps out there- the Yangban’s Null split and shared powers across a group, Citrine could make adjustments, Othala was granting regeneration right now. Maybe get a bunch of them to boost someone’s powers to the ultimate?

Or some kind of biological effect- we’d taken out plenty of biotinkers over the years leading up to now, whackos who’d snagged bits of Bonesaw’s files and got inspired to commit horrors. There was stuff in there about modifying coronas to modify powers, or even remove limiters, rendering the powers always on, always maximum.

My eyes caught on Bonesaw, who was attaching a leg to a man, fingers a blur as she connected muscle and sinew and tendons.

“Whaaaat are you thinking?” Anchorage asked slowly.

“Something crazy,” I said, getting up from my seat, using my improvised crutches and the empty legs of my armour to move towards the most feared Biotinker of them all.

“Bonesaw.”

“Yo,” Bonesaw said, sealing the skin on her patient and sticking a tag to the bunk.

“I have something to ask you.”

“Shoot.”

“I saw your files. Stuff about modifying people’s brains to change their powers.”

Bonesaw spun around to face me. “You know they’ll kill me if I start doing anything like that.”

“Not if I volunteer.”

Bonesaw looked stunned, but I didn’t stop talking. “We’re losing. We need something to tip the scales. I need something to tip the scales.”

The Butchers exploded with shouting, demanding, reasoning. I pushed them all down, and felt cool greyness in my mind without them.

“If it was that easy, I’d have done it for the Slaughterhouse Nine,” Bonesaw pointed out. “I tried it on a few clones, and things got messy.”

“I’m not thinking it’s easy,” I said quietly.

“You’re probably going to be messed up. Like, lose your mind kind of messed up.  I can’t guarantee how it’ll all reconnect in the end. Maybe run this by Panacea first?”

I glanced over at Panacea. She was facing away, too far to hear any of this.

“She’ll stop me.”

And maybe she’d be right to. This was a betrayal.

“…no,” I decided, feeling only a little spike of shame with how numb I was. “Leave her out of it for now. Let her focus on her work.”

“Okay, but she’s going to figure it out pretty fast,” Bonesaw said. “And I’ll need some serious tools to get into your head. Like, a whole lab. And I don't have door access.”

Going to a secondary location with the most infamous wet tinker in the world- an insane idea.

I thought of the mountain of flesh, of Scion crushing Queen of Swords into the ground, of Gavel lasting maybe two minutes total.

“Door,” I said. “To a lab.”

A portal opened to a room of sterile steel and sharp things. Bonesaw trotted inside.

I followed.

Afterword
